This section contains a general description of the facts that gave rise to the present dispute and that the Arbitral Tribunal considers relevant for the adjudication of the dispute. Further reference to other specific facts and the evidence supporting them are described subsequently when particular claims are considered in the present Final Award.

Premium is a company organized under the laws of Panama and was the sole shareholder of another Panamanian company, Broxton Inc., which owned all of the issued and outstanding shares of Ingeniería y Tecnología de Servicios S.A.S., a Colombian simplified stock company (“ITS”).10
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 2.

Mr. Palacio is a petroleum engineer and has worked in the industry of oil and gas services in Colombia for more than 20 years providing cementation services. For fifteen years he worked for Tucker Energy Services as a field engineer. For his last eight years with the company, Mr. Palacio was manager of operations and sales for Tucker Energy Services.11
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 6 and Mr. Palacio’s Witness Statement I, ¶ 3. Mr. Palacio founded ITS in 2007. He was in charge of business development and became its general manager.12
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 7 and Mr. Palacio’s Witness Statement I, ¶ 3.

ITS was first incorporated as a unipersonal company in 2007, and in 2010 was transformed into a simplified stock company. Through Broxton, Claimant and Additional Parties directly and indirectly owned 100% of the shares of ITS.13
Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 13.

ITS provides cementation services to oil and gas production companies in Colombia which involves highly specialized and skilled services during the well formation process that ate crucial for the safe operation of oil and gas wells.

Ms. Hernández is married to Mr. Palacio and also works in the oil and gas production services industry in Colombia. She is the legal representative and part owner of a separate business known as Petrodynamic Petroleum Services S.A.S. (“Petrodynamic”). Petrodynamic was a supplier to ITS.

Superior Energy is a Houston-based international oil and gas service company, organized under the laws of Delaware, offering drilling-related solutions to energy producers established in 1989.14
Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 7. Initially it was an oilfield products manufacturing firm but eventually branched out into services, and now it offers a full inventory of specialized tools for drilling, production and well workover activities.15
Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 8.

In 2007, Superior Energy entered the Colombian oil and gas market and in December 2012 Superior Energy created Superior Colombia to continue to expand its business in the oil and gas sector in Colombia.16
Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 11-12.

In 2012, Mr. Palacio and Ms. Hernández decided to sell ITS. During the sale process, Mr. Palacio met and had negotiations with at least three companies that were interested in purchasing ITS, including Superior Energy.17
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 9 and Mr. Palacio’s Witness Statement I, ¶ 7.

Mr. Palacio and Superior Energy met in Houston, Texas, to discuss selling ITS. They settled on US$ 24,000,000 price for the purchase. After the Houston meeting but before the Parties had reached an agreement on all terms, Mr. Palacio obtained a lucrative contract for ITS with Pacific Rubiales Energy (“Pacific”). Accordingly, ITS became more valuable. Thus, the Parties renegotiated the price to US$ 28,000,000.18
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 11.

Parties exchanged several drafts during the negotiations of the SPA. In February 26, 2012, Premium proposed to include a reference to activities carried out by Petrodynamic, recently disclosed as ITS’ supplier, regarding the lease of vehicles within the terms of Section 10.17. Eventually, the Parties agreed to include a definition for the “Petrodynamic Services” in Section 1 of the SPA and to further modify Section 10.17 to include the phrase “except for the Petrodynamic Services.”19
Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 22.

As a result, Section 6(a) of the SPA was added to the covenants set forth in Section 10.17 of the SPA to enforce a penalty in the event Mr. Palacio participated in Petrodynamic Services during the term of his Employment Agreement or during a period of two years after the termination of the said agreement (the “Non-Compete Period”).20
Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 23. The revised and definitive text of Sections 10.17 and 6 (a) provides as follows:
“Section 6 Covenants
(a)
Notwithstanding anything herein to the contrary, the Key Individual undertakes not to participate in the Petrodynamic Services and that all dealings and contracts which may be entered into between ITS and Petrodynamic Petroleum Services S.A.S. (and its affiliates, if any) will be at “arms-length” and will not involve, directly or indirectly, the Key Individual in the decision making process.”
“Section 10.17 Use of Industrial Secrets and Goodwill
(a)
Seller expressly acknowledges that Purchaser is acquiring all of the industrial secrets and goodwill of ITS in order to successfully expand and enhance its business in the provision of services to the oil and gas industry.
(b)
Seller and Beneficial Owners expressly covenant and agree that they shall not use any of the industrial secrets and goodwill, nor will otherwise carry out any activity that could undermine the value of these assets. Except for the Petrodynamic Services (and subject to the covenants in Section 6) the Seller and the Beneficial Owners further covenant and agree that if Seller or Beneficial Owners provide services to the Colombian oil and gas industry within the 2 years following the date of termination of the Employment Agreement of the Key Individual, due to the complexity of the Colombian oil and gas industry it would be reasonable to assume that, in doing so, Seller and Beneficial Owners will be using the transferred industrial secrets and goodwill, that the Seller and the Beneficial Owners would be engaging in unfair competition and unfair trade practices by using industrial secrets and goodwill that they have sold to Purchaser for consideration and thus no longer own, and that the value of the industrial secrets and goodwill will necessarily be undermined by such unauthorised use.
(c)
Without prejudice to the Seller’s and Beneficial Ownes’ right to disprove the above assumption (i.e. by demonstrating that, in participating in the Colombian oil and gas industry, they are using industrial secrets and goodwill other that those transferred herby), Seller and Beneficial Owners covenant and agree that, except for the Petrodynamic Services (and subject to the covenants in Section 6), the Purchaser Price shall be adjusted downwards by a certain percentage in the event that the Seller or the Beneficial Owners participate in the Colombian oil and gas industry within the next two years, as follows: (i) 20% if such participation takes place within 1 year after the date of termination of the Employment Agreement of the Key Individual, (ii) 15% if such participation takes place within .51 years after the date of termination of the Employment Agreement of the Key Individual, and (iii) 10% if such participation takes place within 2 year after the date of termination of the Employment Agreement of the Key Individual.
(d)
Purchaser may, without prejudice to any other method of recovery, deduct the amount of such downward adjustments or damages from any monies due or to become due to Seller. The payment or deduction of such damages shall not relieve Seller or the Beneficial Owners from their obligations to abstain from using the transferred industrial secrets and goodwill, or from any other of their obligations and liabilities under this Agreement.
(e)
The provisions of this clause are intended solely to preserve and fairly reflect the value of the transferred industrial secrets or goodwill in order to allow Purchaser to fairly and successfully expand and enhance ITS’ business in Colombia. If the provisions of this Article 10.17 are deemed too broad for that purpose by an authority of competent jurisdiction, such provisions shall nevertheless be valid and enforceable to the extent that the court deems necessary for such protection.”

On Match 1, 2013, the Parties executed the SPA21
Exhibit C-1 and R-1, SPA.. Under the SPA, it was agreed that the price would be US$ 28.000.00022
Section 2.2 (a) of the SPA: “The total purchase price payable by the Purchaser to Seller for the Broxton Shares on the Closing Date shall be the amount of US$ 28,000,000, minus: (I) the Base Closing Indebtedness (which, for avoidance of doubt, includes the Estimated Open Purchase Orders); and minus (II) the Holdback Amounts, (the amount paid on the Closing Date together with the Holdback Amounts are collectively referred to as the “Purchase Price”.)” (the “Purchase Price”) to be paid (i) US$ 25,500,000 at the closing (subject to certain adjustments) and (ii) two holdbacks of US$ 1,250,000 each, payable 12 and 24 months after the closing23
Section 2.2 (b) of the SPA: “With respect to the Hold back Amounts, the amount of US $ 1,250,000 shall be paid to the Seller on the date that is twelve months after the Closing Date (“Holdback Amount No. 1”), and the amount of US$ 1,250,000 shall be paid to the Seller on the date that is twenty-four months after the Closing Date (“Hold back Amount No. 2”) (together the “Holdback Amounts”) minus any claims pursuant to Section 8.5.” (the “First Holdback Amount” and the “Second Holdback Amount”, respectively). Superior Energy guaranteed payment of the Purchase Price.24
Section 2.2 (d) of the SPA: “The parties hereto agree that the performance of the obligations related to the payment of the Purchase Price by the Buyer, as set forth in Sections 2.2(a) and 2.2(b), shall be guaranteed by Buyer’s ultimate parent company, Superior Energy Services, Inc., in its capacity as intervening party hereto. The guarantee hereby granted by Superior Energy Services, Inc. will be automatically terminated, regardless of whether any subsequent written instrument is executed by the parties hereto, on the earlier of the date the Holdback Amounts are remitted to Seller’s bank account or notice is provided to Seller pursuant to Section 8.5, indicating no further Holdback Amount s are owed to Seller.”

The Parties also agreed in the SPA that Superior Colombia had the right to withhold the Holdback Amounts in order to offset any amounts owed by Premium, including any amounts related to their indemnity obligations under the SPA.25
Section 2.1(c) of the SPA: “Notwithstanding anything herein to the contrary, Purchaser has the right to withhold any portion of the Holdback Amounts in order to offset any amounts owed by Sellers to Purchaser arising or related to any of Sellers’ obligations hereunder, including without limitation, any amounts related to Sellers’ indemnity obligations.” Any claims made under the Holdback Amounts were to be submitted under the terms of Section 8.5 of the SPA.26
Section 8.5 of the SPA: “The Purchaser shall have the option of claiming all or any part of any Purchaser Damages under Section 8.2, by notifying the Seller Representative that the Purchaser is claiming the amount of such Purchaser Damages (or the Purchaser’s good faith estimate of such amount if unliquidated, pending the final determination thereof against the Holdback Amounts. Any such claim against the Holdback Amounts shall be made on or before following of the Closing Date: (i) twelve (12) months for the Holdback Amount No. 1, and (il) twenty-four (24) months for the Holdback Amount No, 2, by delivery of written notice to Seller Representative, stating the nature of and basis for such claim with reasonable specificity (including the applicable provision of this Agreement). If the Seller objects to the amount of all or part of any claim by the Purchaser against the Holdback Amounts, then the Seller shall, within 30 days of receipt of such claim, provide written notice (an ‘Objection Notice) to the Purchaser setting forth Seller’s objections. If the Seller sends the Purchaser an Objection Notice, then within fifteen (15) calendar days after receipt of an Objection Notice, the Purchaser and the S eller shall work in good faith to reconcile and resolve the differences. If the parties cannot mutually resolve such differences during such fifteen (15) day period, the Purchaser may proceed to determine the amount of Purchaser Damages payable to the Purchaser without prejudice to the Seller’s right to settle the issue by arbitration as contemplated in Section 10.2. Notwithstanding anything in this Section 8.5 to the contrary, the Purchaser shall also be entitled to assert any claim for Purchaser Damages directly against the Seller without making such claim against the Holdback Amounts.” Additionally, the Parties agreed that, without prejudice to any other method of recovery, Superior Colombia could deduct the amount of any downward adjustments or damages due to Seller as agreed to under Section 10.17 of the SPA.27
Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 28.

The SPA was subject to its first amendment on January 21, 2014, where the parties agreed to modify the Preamble and Sections 2.3(a)(i), 2.3(b)(i) and 2.3(b)(ii), and Exhibit C, clauses 2 and 3 of the SPA (the “First Amendment to the SPA”).28
Exhibit R-006. Later in June 2016, the arbitration clause in Section 10.2 of the SPA was amended in the Second Amendment to the SPA with regard to the process of nomination of the Arbitral Tribunal.29
Exhibit R-024.

Superior sought to keep Mr. Palacio as an ITS’ employee after the execution of the SPA. Indeed, Mr. Palacio had extensive knowledge of the industry and a close relationship with the main oilfield operators, particularly Ecopetrol and Pacific Exploration hsihtasamp; Production Corp. Thus, Mr. Palacio played a key role in the successful implementation of Superior Colombia’s expansion plan. Superior negotiated an employment agreement with Mr. Palacio, which was eventually added as an exhibit to the SPA30
Exhibit R-004. (the “Employment Agreement”).31
Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 20. Also, under the SPA, the Parties used the term “Key Individual” to refer to Mr. Palacio within the SPA.32
Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 28.

Superior Colombia had a Supply Chain Manager named Julio Bula Miranda (“Mr, Bula”), who became responsible for purchasing materials and equipment needed by ITS and Mr. Palacio continued to work for ITS after the closing as business manager for ITS meanwhile Superior installed its own person in the position to whom Mr. Palacio would report. In May and June 2013 Superior had yet to install that person and Mr. Palacio continued to manage ITS’ business until 30 July 2013, when he resigned his position as business development manager of ITS in a written letter33
Exhibit C-2. to Mr. Villamarín, Superior Energy’s country manager for Colombia.34
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 18 and Mr. Palacio’s Witness Statement I, ¶ ¶ 15-17.

On August 1, 2013, Mr. Palacio executed a services agreement with ITS for the provision of technical assistance in oil and gas sales and operations (the “Services Agreement”).35
Exhibit R-005. During the performance of the Services Agreement, Mr. Palacio had day-to-day access to information regarding ITS’ products, prices, clients, suppliers and business plans, among others. Mr. Palacio further kept in touch with the large Colombian oilfield operators through his work on behalf of ITS.

On or about 1 March 2014, Superior Colombia paid Premium the First Holdback Amount of US$ 1,250,000.00.36
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 20.

On September 17, 2014, Superior Energy’s Ethics and Compliance Department received an email from Mr. Bula claiming that since the execution of the SPA, “Petrodynamic, owned by Mr. Palacio is a main supplier of parts for the operation” and that they “cannot purchase from other companies, even if we have a better price, because current employees that used to be from ITS will complaint [sic] that those parts ‘don’t work” (the “Complaint”).37
Exhibit JD-002. Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 42.

As a consequence of the Complaint, Superior Energy launched a compliance investigation in October 2014 and engaged BDO USA LLP (“BDO”). The team led by Mr. Daves at BDO was tasked to investigate and assess the veracity of the allegations included in the Complaint, in relation to conflicts of interests and failures to comply with purchasing protocol.38
Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ ¶ 43-44.

On February 25, 2015, Superior Colombia delivered a claim notice under Section 8.5 of the SPA (the “First Claim Notice”)39
Exhibit R-007. informing Mr. Palacio that due to a breach of his contractual obligations, it would exercise its contractual right to withhold the Second Holdback Amount.40
Respondent0Æs Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 46. Therefore Superior Colombia refused to pay the Second Holdback Amount of US$ 1,250,000 when it came due on 1 March 2015.41
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 25.

On March 19, 2015, Mr. Palacio presented his response to the First Claim Notice42
Exhibit R-025. (the “Objection Notice”) requesting that the Second Holdback Amount be paid in full, including all late payment interests.43
Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 47.

Following the procedure laid down in Section 8.5 of the SPA, the Parties carried on negotiations regarding the claims under the First Claim Notice.44
Exhibit R-026. On May 8, 2015, Superior Colombia and Premium held a meeting where they discussed the First Claim Notice and the Objection Notice.45
Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 48-49.

The Parties had a meeting on the first week of August 2015 to assess the impact of the potential breaches of the SPA and continue the negotiations to settle the dispute.46
Exhibit R-031.

On October 2015, the Parties held a meeting in Miami where Superior Colombia offered Mr. Palacio further documentation regarding the bases of its claims and the parties agreed that Mr. Palacio and his counsel would review the documentation and provide their comments and responses thereto within 30 days following the date of the meeting.47
Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 50-53. The Parties failed subsequently to reach any agreement.
On January 22, 2016 Claimant filed the Request for Arbitration.

The present arbitration seeks to resolve the claims submitted by the Parties to the Arbitral Tribunal. The claims transcribed below result from the presentations made by the Parties during this arbitration.

title.bd: CLAIMANT’S AND ADDITIONAL PARTIES REQUEST FOR RELIEF

item.p:
In the Request of Arbitration, Claimant seeks an award against Respondents for the US$ 1,250,000 for the Second Holdback Amount48
Request for Arbitration, ¶ 44.; interest from March 1, 2015 on the holdback amount pursuant to Colombia’s applicable interest rate of 21.32 percent per annum49
Request for Arbitration, ¶ 45. and payment of the costs and expenses, including attorneys’ fees.50
Request for Arbitration, ¶ 46.

In the Reply to Counterclaims and Answer to the Additional Parties, Claimant and the Additional Parties request that the Counterclaims be denied in their entirety51
Reply to Counterclaims and Answer to the Additional Parties, ¶ 39. and seek payment of their costs and expenses, including attorneys’ fees.52
Reply to Counterclaims and Answer to the Additional Parties, ¶ 40.

In the Terms of Reference, Claimant seek an award for payment of (i) US$ 1,250,000 for the Second Holdback Amount, (ii) interest thereon from March 1, 2015 at the rate set forth by Colombian law, i.e., 21.32 percent per annum, and (iii) attorneys’ fees pursuant to Colombian law.

As for the defenses to Respondents’ Counterclaims, Claimant and the Additional Parties request that the Tribunal (i) declare that they did not breach the SPA; (ii) order Superior Colombia to reimburse them pursuant to Colombian law for the attorneys’ fees incurred in defending the Counterclaims; and (iii) order Superior Colombia to pay the costs of the arbitration pursuant to the ICC Rules.53
Terms of Reference, ¶ 64. Claimant and Additional Parties specifically request that, according to Rule 37.4 of the ICC Rules, the Tribunal fix the costs of the arbitration to be borne completely by Respondents.54
Terms of Reference, ¶ 59.

In the Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, Claimant states that Superior Colombia and Superior Energy ate in default of paying the balance of the Purchase Price and seeks payment of an awatd of US$ 1,250,000 jointly and severally against Respondents55
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 35., plus interest56
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 38. and costs.57
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 39.

In their Memorial of Reply Respondents request that the Tribunal enter an award:62
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 152.
a.
Declaring that it lacks jurisdiction over any and all claims submitted against Superior Energy;
b.
If the Tribunal finds that it has jurisdiction over Superior Energy, dismissing all claims with respect to Superior Energy as inadmissible;
c.
Dismissing all relief requested by Sellers in the Memorial of Claims, Answer to Counterclaims, and Reply to the Answer to Claims;
d.
Granting all of Respondents’ procedural requests in section V hereof and order the parties to comply with such procedural requests forthwith;
e.
Ordering Claimant, on a joint and several basis, to pay to Superior $5,784,468.33 for damages plus the maximum permitted interest under applicable law and all attorneys’ fees and other costs incurred in these proceedings; and
f.
Granting all of Respondents’ other petitions for relief in the Memorial of Counterclaims and Answer to Claims.

Finally, in their Memorial of Rejoinder Respondents request the Tribunal to enter an award:63
Respondents’ Memorial of Rejoinder, ¶ 83.
a.
Declaring that it lacks jurisdiction over any and all claims submitted against Superior Energy;
b.
If the Tribunal finds that it has jurisdiction over Superior Energy, dismissing all claims with respect to Superior Energy as inadmissible;
c.
Dismissing all relief requested by Sellers in the Memorial of Claims, Answer to Counterclaims, and Reply to the Answer to Claims;
d.
Ordering Claimant, on a joint and several basis, to pay to Superior $5,784,468.33 for damages plus the maximum permitted interest under applicable law and all attorneys’ fees and other costs incurred in these proceedings; and
e.
Granting all of Respondents’ other petitions for relief in the Memorial of Counterclaims, Answer to Claims and Reply to Answer to Counterclaims.

The Tribunal notes that Superior Energy has raised jurisdictional objections. Also, Claimant and Respondents have both asserted claims against each other based on alleged breaches of the SPA. The Parties have also sought specific decisions from the Tribunal regarding the admissibility of certain claims and the evidentiary value of certain witnesses’ evidence.

In light of the above, the Tribunal will first address the jurisdictional and admissibility objections (A.). The Tribunal will then decide on the issues relating to the introduction of new claims during the proceedings and the evidentiary value of specific witnesses’ evidence (B.). Finally, the Tribunal will deal with the merits of the case addressing first Claimants’ claims (C.) and then Respondents’ counterclaims (D.).

When addressing these issues, the Tribunal will first describe the Parties’ position as set out by them in their submissions made throughout the Arbitration and will then examine them in light of the Parties’ different contentions. While the Arbitral Tribunal has taken into account all of the Patties’ submissions and arguments, the Tribunal will only refer to those facts and arguments that it considers relevant for the Tribunal’s findings and the adjudication of this dispute. To the extent that there are facts or arguments which are not expressly referred in the Tribunal’s reasoning, it is because they do not change the findings reached in this Final Award.

Respondents have raised jurisdictional objections on grounds that the Arbitral Tribunal does not have any jurisdiction over Superior Energy (the “Jurisdictional Objection”). Alternatively, Respondents submit that the claims asserted by Claimants against Superior Energy are inadmissible. This section sets forth the Parties’ positions and the Tribunal’s decision on this matter.

Respondents argue that the Arbitral Tribunal does not have jurisdiction over Premium’s claims against Superior Energy. They allege that Superior Energy is not a party to the arbitration agreement in the SPA and did not consent to arbitrate any claims arising under Section 2.2(d) of the SPA. In any event, and without implying an admission of jurisdiction, Respondents submit that claims against Superior Energy ate inadmissible pursuant to the terms set forth in the SPA and under Colombian law.64
Terms of Reference, ¶ 66.

Respondents allege that Superior Energy, as an independent legal entity, did not consent to the arbitration clause and executed the SPA for one sole reason which was evidenced by its signature in the signature line stating “[e]xclusively for the purposes of Section 2.2(d)” of the SPA. Thus, according to Respondents, Superior Energy executed the SPA in those narrow terms, that did not include the arbitration agreement.65
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 55.

Furthermore, Respondents state that both the cover page and the preamble of the SPA set out the parties: Superior Colombia, Premium, Mr. Palacio, and Ms. Hernández. Superior Energy is markedly absent from the list of contracting parties. If Superior Energy had agreed to arbitrate this dispute, either the signature line of the SPA or the SPA itself would have been drafted differently and that the plain text of the contract demonstrates otherwise.66
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 56.

Respondents allege that under Colombian law the arbitration clause must contain the essential elements of a contract, including object and consent, according to general theory of contracts and obligations, and that the signature of a party does not necessarily means that is a party to that contract or that is bound by the contract’s arbitration clause. Furthermore, even as a party to the SPA the binding effects of an arbitration agreement depend on a clear and binding “expression of will.”67
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ ¶ 57-58.

Respondents note that the Bogotá Superior Tribunal affirmed the principle of separability of the arbitration clause from the agreement itself:68
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 58,
“[Article 118 of Decree 1818 of 1998] pointed out the autonomy between the arbitration clause and the contract, to the extent that the former is an agreement that may be contained in a contract or in a schedule thereof, but as “an agreement”, which it is, it shall be endorsed by all persons intervening therein… [T]he conclusion that the arbitration clause is an independent and private legal transaction is more strongly confirmed, and therefore, it cannot be asserted that its amendment or termination in a company agreement can be carried out by the will of a corporate majority, but, on the contrary, the unanimous decision of the parties that entered into, or joined, such agreement is required for such purpose.”69
Exhibit RL-017, Bogota Superior Tribunal, Civil Chamber, judgment dated December 5, 2012.

Respondents also rely on jurisprudence of the Constitutional Court, which has further noted that an arbitral tribunal’s jurisdiction is subject to a “positive manifestation of will” and that deciding a dispute by an arbitral tribunal cannot be unilaterally imposed by another party:
“The Constitutional Court has been emphatic in highlighting the importance of the principle of empowerment [habilitación] as one of the essential components of arbitral jurisdiction. In fact, according to the criterion of the Court, the possibility of resorting to arbitral justice necessarily depends on the presence of empowerment; that is, a positive manifestation of will by the individuals that expect to settle their conflicts before that jurisdiction. As per the aforementioned [court], ‘empowerment of arbitrators by all and every contracting party is an imperative constitutional requirement, without which arbitration justice is not applicable.’ In developing the above, the Constitutional Court has also stated that, due to the exceptional nature of arbitration, empowerment to resort to these bodies should come from a voluntary and free act by the contracting parties. This simply means that empowerment of arbitration justice cannot come from unilateral imposition of will.”70
Exhibit RL-018, Corporations Superintendence, Case No. 2015-800-14, decision dated August 10, 2015.

Respondents add that Superior Energy and Superior Colombia are separated and independent legal entities and that it was Superior Colombia, and not Superior Energy, that assumed the obligations as “Purchaser” of the SPA.71
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 59.

Respondents note that Claimant have failed to provide any ground under which Superior Energy is bound by the arbitration clause.72
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 60.

Alternatively, Respondents state that if the Tribunal finds that it has jurisdiction over Superior Energy, then Superior Energy’s duties under the SPA, including with respect to the arbitration agreement, are automatically terminated in accordance with the express terms of the agreement and intent of the Parties.73
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 62. Section 2.2(d) of the SPA provides that Superior Energy’s obligations under the SPA, and therefore its status as a signatory thereto, is “automatically terminated… on the earlier of the date the Holdback Amounts are remitted to Seller’s bank account or notice is provided to Seller pursuant to Section 8.5.”74
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 63 and Sections 2.2 and 8.5 of the SPA.

Respondents add that it is undisputed that Superior Colombia gave such notice to Claimant upon delivery of the First Claim Notice on February 25, 2015, a three-page explanatory letter that stated that it was sent “pursuant to Section 2.2(c), Section 8.2 and Section 8.5” of the SPA, therefore Superior Energy’s obligations and relation to the SPA terminated on that date. Additionally, under Colombian law Superior Energy’s guarantee obligations would be activated only if Superior Colombia is in breach of the SPA, which Respondents deny.75
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ ¶ 64 and 65.

Claimant argues that pursuant to Colombian law, an arbitral tribunal may exercise jurisdiction over a dispute where all parties are signatories to a written arbitration agreement. Thus, signatory entities and/or individuals are entitled to submit their dispute to arbitration as claimants, and any other signatory entities and/or individuals may be properly named as respondents.

Claimant further indicates that, in the present case, as an intervening party and signatory to the SPA, Superior Energy has agreed to arbitration and thus the Arbitral Tribunal has jurisdiction over Superior Energy.76
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 31.

The Tribunal notes that no objections were raised as to the existence of an arbitration agreement under the Rules. Further, the Jurisdictional Objection raised in these proceedings only relates to Premium’s claims against Superior Energy.

Superior Energy is a signatory party of the SPA. Superior Energy has also assumed specific obligations under the SPA. In fact, according to clause 2.2(d) of the SPA, Superior Energy became a guarantor of the purchase price agreed under the SPA.

Clause 2.2(d) establishes:
“(d) The parties hereto agree that the performance of the obligations related to the payment of the Purchase Price by the Buyer, as set forth in Sections 2.2.(a) and 2.2(b), shall be guaranteed by Buyer’s ultimate parent company, Superior Energy Services, Inc., in its capacity as intervening party hereto. The guarantee hereby granted by Superior Energy Services, Inc., will be automatically terminated, regardless of whether any subsequent written instrument is executed by the parties hereto, on the earlier of the date the Holdback Amount are remitted to Seller’s bank account or notice is provided to Seller pursuant to Section 8.5, indicating no further Holdback Amounts are owed to Seller”.

At the core of the present dispute lies the question of whether Claimant is entitled to receive payment of the balance of the Purchase Price agreed under the SPA, i.e., US$ 1,250,000, which Superior Energy expressly agreed to guarantee according to the terms of the SPA. The Tribunal has no doubt that this claim falls squarely within the scope of the guarantee established by Superior Energy under the SPA.

Superior Energy rightly notes that it signed the SPA “[e]xclusively for the purposes of Section 2.2(d)”. Section 2.2(d) contains a guarantee of payment of the purchase price which has been established by Superior Energy. Thus, to the extent that Superior Energy has agreed to guarantee payment of the purchase price under the SPA, the Parties (specifically Claimant) are entitled to enforce this contractual commitment according to the mechanism chosen under the SPA which is arbitration before the ICC. If arbitration would not proceed to enforce the most basic obligation on the part of Respondents, which is to satisfy payment of the Purchase Price, then the Parties’ reliance on the arbitration agreement established in the SPA would be seriously impaired.

For the same reasons, the Tribunal is not persuaded that the mere fact that Superior Energy is not mentioned in the cover page or the preamble of the SPA implies that it did not consent to arbitration agreement under the SPA.

In short, the Tribunal finds no valid reasons to conclude that, while Superior Energy agreed to guarantee the Purchase Price of the SPA, it did not become bound by the arbitration clause contained in the SPA to seek the payment of said Purchase Price. In any event, the arbitration clause shall only apply to Superior Energy as far as its obligation to guarantee payment of the Purchase Price is concerned.

Superior Energy also raises an alleged inadmissibility of the claims asserted against Superior Energy on two distinct grounds. First, Superior Energy asserts that its guarantee automatically terminated when Superior Colombia sent the First Claim Notice to Claimant on February 25, 2015, a three-page explanatory letter that stated that it was sent “pursuant to Section 2.2(c), Section 8.2 and Section 8.5” of the SPA. Second, according to Superior Energy, under Colombian law its guarantee obligations would be activated only if Superior Colombia is in breach of the SPA, which Respondents deny.

The Tribunal cannot follow Superior Energy’s interpretation under section 2.2(d) of the SPA that its contractual guarantee has terminated with the sending of the First Claim Notice. The Tribunal notes that there is a dispute among the patties concerning Superior Colombia’s compliance with Section 8.5 when sending the First Claim Notice to Claimants77
See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 209; 273-278 and 296-304.. This is a matter that concerns the merits of the dispute which the Tribunal can only assess if those claims are considered admissible in the first place.

In addition, the facts leading to Respondents’ decision to withhold payment of the balance of the Purchase Price, i.e., the Second Holdback Amount of US$ 1,250,000, are all prior to the date of the First Claim Notice. Claimant’s claims rest on the most basic premise that Respondents’ decision not to release the Purchase Price in full was unlawful and did not honor the terms of the SPA. Hence, the Tribunal is not inclined to declare that Claimants’ claims under the SPA became inadmissible due to the existence of the First Claim Notice, when Claimant is precisely attacking the basis of Respondents’ decision to withhold payment of the purchase price communicated through the First Claim Notice.

In other words, Claimant’s claim for payment of the Purchase Price in full is based on facts which occurred prior to the First Claim Notice. Even Respondents have conceded that the alleged breaches of the SPA which entitled Superior Colombia to withhold the Second Holdback Amount occurred prior to said retention.78
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 195. Again, to determine if those breaches actually existed and gave rise to a lawful right of retention pursuant to the SPA and Colombian law, the Tribunal must examine the merits of the dispute. Thus, the First Claim Notice does not produce the effect of barring Claimant’s claims against Superior Energy as a matter of admissibility. This ruling is of course without prejudice to the Tribunal’s decision on the merits of the dispute.

In the same vein, the question of whether there has been a breach of the SPA on Respondents’ side belongs to the merits of the dispute. Accordingly, the Tribunal cannot rule at this stage that Superior Energy’s guarantee obligations should not be activated without entertaining the merits of the claims asserted against both Respondents. Consequently, the allegation of inadmissibility is also rejected.

In conclusion, the Arbitral Tribunal rejects Respondents’ Jurisdictional Objection and inadmissibility allegations and decides that it has jurisdiction over both Superior Energy and Superior Colombia to rule on Claimant’s claims against both Respondents.

title.bd: NEW CLAIMS AND EVIDENTIARY VALUE OF WITNESSES’ EVIDENCE

item.p: The Parties have filed objections concerning the admissibility of certain claims, and the evidentiary value of some of the witnesses’ evidence introduced in the record.

Specifically, Respondents have requested Mr. Villamarín’s witness statement to be dismissed as he failed to appear as witness at the Hearing. Also, Claimant has argued that Mr. Daves’ evidence as a witness presented by Respondents is improper and requested it to be dismissed.
The Tribunal will address each of these issues separately.

Claimant argues that Superior Colombia has attempted to insert new counterclaims in its Memorial of Reply by asserting as new counterclaims the alleged breaches under (a) Section 6.3 of the SPA and (b) Sections 4.6 and 4.14 of the SPA (the “New Claims”).

Claimant submits that, besides being legally flawed, these claims are procedurally barred because Superior did not assert them in the Terms of Reference and Claimant object to their consideration in this proceeding.79
Claimant’s Memorial of Rejoinder, ¶ 2 and footnote 1.Claimant refer to the allegations argued on Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 27-29 and 121-127.

In its opening statement Claimant reiterates that it rejects these claims and any claim that has not been included in the Terms of Reference and further notes that any argument made of evidence presented by Claimant to contradict those new claims are in no way a waiver for such claims to be included in the Arbitration.80
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 21, lines 7-23.
Respondents made no arguments regarding the Claimant’s accusation of the introduction of new claims.

Article 23(4) of the ICC Rules provides:
“After the Terms of Reference have been signed or approved by the Court, no party shall make new claims which fall outside the limits of the Terms of Reference unless it has been authorized to do so by the arbitral tribunal, which shall consider the nature of such new claims, the stage of the arbitration and other relevant circumstances.”

The Tribunal notes that Superior Colombia’s New Claims were not included in the Terms of Reference executed by the Parties and the Tribunal and were only filed by Superior Colombia when submitting its Memorial of Reply. At this stage, Claimant was left with limited ability to submit their defenses to the New Claims.

Additionally, the Tribunal finds no excuse, justification or valid reason as to why Superior Colombia introduced the New Claims only when filing its Reply. The basis for the New Claims did not depend on circumstances or facts unknown to Respondents at the time of execution of the Terms of Reference. Further, the nature of the New Claims was similar to those other claims concerning Claimant’s alleged breaches of the SPA which were included in the Terms of Reference. But they still represent distinct claims from those included in the Terms of Reference. Specifically, these claims relate to sections 6(3) of the SPA concerning the Claimant and Additional Parties’ obligation to take any action “as may be necessary to carry out the purposes and intents of this Agreement” which was not addressed before signing the Terms of Reference. Likewise, these claims also refer to alleged breaches of sections 4.6 and 4.14 of the SPA, which contain independent representations and warranties which had not been invoked before as the basis of alleged breaches, despite the fact that other alleged breaches of Representations and warranties under section 4 of the SPA had already been included in the Terms of Reference81
¶ ¶ 412 of this Final Award)..

Under these circumstances, the Tribunal concludes that the New Claims should be declared inadmissible as they have been filed belatedly outside of the time-limit established by Article 23(4) of the Rules without any reason justifying such delay. Therefore, the Tribunal will neither entertain any arguments, nor take any decisions, based on these allegations of breach.
Claimant submits that the witness statement of Mr. Daves is improper and should not be considered by the Tribunal.

According to Claimant, in presenting this testimony, Superior asks the Arbitral Tribunal to delegate its task to establish the facts of the case82
Art, 25 of the ICC Roles, to its hired gun, Mr. Daves adopting an entirely new approach to proving one’s case in an ICC arbitration. Claimant goes on to allege that “one side hires an accountant who does not understand the series of meetings and their language, where a colleague who does understand the prescient witnesses asks questions and listens to answers, but somehow takes contemporaneous notes of the interviewees’ responses.” At some point after each of these meetings ends, he creates an MS Word file with bullet points setting forth his understanding of what his colleague understands these witnesses to have said in a different language. The witnesses are not given any opportunity to review, modify or clarify any of the statements attributed to them. After agreeing that all witness’ testimony will be in the form of witness statements signed by the person who will later be subject to examination at the hearing, Superior instead culls out a small handful of these Word files, submits witness statements of the hired gun setting forth what his “investigation” allegedly found, and asks the Tribunal to adopt his findings”.83
In the event that the Tribunal decides to allow Mr. Daves’ testimony and to consider his Word files, Claimant states the Tribunal should have a fuller understanding of what is contained in Mr. Daves’ Word files and submits as an exhibit the entirety of the documents produced by Superior in response to the Tribunal’s order to turn over “all documents created or modified during any of the interviews of any of the 18 people mentioned in paragraph 7(p) of Mr. Daves’ Witness Statement including (a) handwritten notes of Mr. Daves, and (b) computer files containing notes of Mr. Daves” to be considered if the Tribunal overrules the Premium Parties’ objection. Exhibit C-98. Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ ¶ 45-46.

Claimant relies upon the procedural rules and guidelines governing this proceeding, including Procedural Order No. I,84
Procedural Order No, 1, ¶ 5.3: “All witness evidence on which a party relies shall be submitted in the form of a written Witness Statement or Statements dated and signed by the witness in question. Witness statements shall constitute direct evidence (evidence-in-chief).” Further, ¶ 5.8: “[i]n all cases, a party will seek to ensure that a Witness Statement reflects the witness’s own account of relevant facts, events and circumstances as reflected in the Witness Statement.” Finally, ¶ 5.6: [i]f a witness is called to appear at the hearing and fails to do so, the Tribunal shall disregard the witness’ Witness Statement(s).” the ICC Rules, the Terms of Reference,85
Pursuant to the Terms of Reference, the applicable procedural rules governing this arbitration include the ICC Rules, and those contained in the present Terms of Reference. Further, pursuant to the Terms of Reference, in exercising its discretion, the Arbitral Tribunal shall be guided, but not bound, by the 2010 IBA Rules on the Taking of Evidence in International Commercial Arbitration, and the 2013 IBA Guidelines on Party Representation in International Arbitration, Terms of Reference, ¶ 99. the 2010 IBA Rules on the Taking of Evidence in International Commercial Arbitration86
Pursuant to Article 9 of the 2010 IBA Rules on the Taking of Evidence in International Commercial Arbitration, “[t]he Arbitral Tribunal shall, at the request of a Party or on its own motion, exclude from evidence … any … statement, [or] oral testimony” due to inter alia, “considerations of fairness or equality of the Parties that the Arbitral Tribunal determines to be compelling.” Furthermore pursuant to Article 4.1 of the 2010 IBA Rules on the Taking of Evidence in International Commercial Arbitration, “each Party shall identify the witnesses on whose testimony it intends to rely and the subject matter of that testimony.” Under Article 4.4, the Arbitral Tribunal may order each Party to submit “Witness Statements by each witness on whose testimony it intends to rely…” Under Article 5, each Witness Statement’s content must comply with requirements such, us (a) name and address of the witness; (b) full detailed description of the facts (c) a statement of the original language of his testimony; (d) an affirmation of the truth and (e) the signature and mention of date and place. and the 2013 IBA Guidelines on Party Representation in International Arbitration. Claimant submits that Superior is seeking to circumvent all these rules governing this because Mr. Daves’ interviews and his notes should not be considered for several reasons.87
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ ¶ 48-57.

First, Claimant asserts that Respondents try to use Mr. Daves’ testimony to introduce witness evidence and testimony describing alleged facts, events and circumstances upon which Mr. Daves has no personal knowledge. Mr. Daves states that he “obtained personal knowledge of the matters’88
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves II, ¶ 3. and that his witness statements “reflect my own account of the relevant facts, events and circumstances.”89
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves II, ¶ 3. Clearly, Mr. Daves did not obtain “personal knowledge of the matters” and the statements allegedly made by these witnesses at best represent regurgitated, secondhand, indirect evidence. As made clear by the rules abovementioned, witness evidence can only be introduced and relied upon if it is contained within dated and signed witness statements and the entire objective of witness statements (personal knowledge of the facts with an opportunity for cross-examination) would be subverted if a witness who did not submit a witness statement was permitted to be heard through the witness statement of another witness.90
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ ¶ 58-61.

Secondly, Claimant states that to permit the use of Mr. Daves’ witness statement would allow Superior to circumvent Claimant’s ability to cross-examine witnesses who provide evidence upon which Superior relies. Cross-examination is a cornerstone of international arbitration. Not only is the assessment of a witness’ credibility crucial, but cross-examination also allows the Tribunal to obtain a firsthand account of the witness’ recollections and for statements to be put into their full and proper context.91
According to Claimant, The importance of cross-examination in international arbitration is highlighted in Procedural Order No. 159 and Article 4.7 of the 2010 IB A Rules on the Taking of Evidence in International Commercial Arbitration, pursuant to which the witness statement of a witness who does not appear for testimony at the hearing shall be excluded. Claimant rejects Superior’s defense that they will have the opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Daves because this opportunity does not revert the fact that Claimant is unable to question the individuals with the firsthand knowledge.92
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ ¶ 62-63,

Third, Claimant points out that the fact that the interviews required a translator raises significant concerns relating to the accuracy and reliability of Mr. Daves’ notes from these interviews. Indeed, the translator, Mr. Jiménez, is the true source of Mr. Daves’ secondhand information.93
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ 66. On its closing statement, Claimant rejects Mr. Daves’ testimony that the interviews were conducted in English because Mr. Palacio and Ms. Hernández do not speak fluent English.94
Tr. Day 4, 17 November 2017, p. 785, lines 18-24 and p. 786, lines 9-14.

Finally, Claimant argue that there is no way to confirm the accuracy and completeness or to authenticate the evidence presented by Mr. Daves relating to the interviews.95
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ 67.

Respondents request the Arbitral Tribunal to ignore Claimant’s request to disregard Mr. Daves’ witness statement and its exhibits because Claimant provides no reasons to do so and have failed to demonstrate the fact that the witness statement breach any applicable law, procedute, or guideline.96
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 148.
Respondents add that Claimant will have ample time to cross-examine Mr. Daves and ask him questions at the Hearing.

Furthermore, according to Respondents, Mr. Daves is an expert in forensic accounting and the oil and gas industry with decades of experience. He also has extensive knowledge of ITS, Petrodynamic and the circumstances of the disputes at hand.

Finally, Respondents assert that Mr. Daves’ testimony and notes are of the utmost importance to Respondents’ submissions and will further the Tribunal’s ability to determine the truth of the matters at hand.97
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 149.

The Tribunal recalls that Procedural Order No. 1 establishes specific rules regarding witnesses’ evidence. Section 5.3 provides: “All witness evidence on which a party relies shall be submitted in the form of a written Witness Statement or Statements dated and signed by the witness in question. Witness statements shall constitute direct evidence (evidence-in-chief).”

Section 5.8, in turn, establishes that: “[i]n all cases, a party will seek to ensure that a Witness Statement reflects the witness’s own account of relevant facts, events and circumstances as reflected in the Witness Statement.”

The Tribunal also notes that it has discretion to determine the evidentiary value of the witnesses’ written statements and particularly of Mr. Daves’ witness statement.98
Procedural Order N° 5, ¶ 54: “Secondly, any objections or concerns raised by Claimant and Additional Parties pointing to Mr. Daves’ credibility as witness or about the accuracy of his statement entails a question of value of Mr. Daves’ testimony as evidence, which the Tribunal will duly assess when rendering the Final Award. In so doing, the Tribunal shall take into account the assertions made by both parties and the evidence as a whole submitted in the present case and, especially at the hearing.”

Claimant asserts that Mr. Daves’ recollection of facts as set out in his witness statement stems from his interviews in Colombia made under circumstances in which he could not have had any personal knowledge or understanding of what transpired at those interviews. This is so because these interviews were conducted in Spanish and Mr. Daves did not have command of Spanish language and had to attend those meetings with the assistance of an interpreter.

The Tribunal notes that Mr. Daves has provided opinion on other matters different from those obtained only at the interviews and has also reviewed related documents99
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves I, ¶ ¶ 25-34 and Witness Statement of Mr. Daves II, ¶ 6-10.. This alone is a reason not to declare Mr. Daves’ witness statement inadmissible.

In respect of those statements that resulted from the interviews conducted by Mr. Daves in Colombia, the Tribunal notes that several facts ate undisputed among the Parties: first, that the interviews were in fact conducted in Spanish; second, that Mr. Daves did not and does not have command of Spanish, and; third, that in taking notes of those interviews Mr. Daves was assisted by an interpreter from Spanish to English.

In the Tribunal’s view, the fact that (i) Mr. Daves’ statement is based on his personal notes and, (ii) the interviews were conducted in Spanish and as a result, those personal notes were obtained through the assistance of a Spanish translator, certainly affects the reliability of his testimony which is, to that extent, secondhand information, but it does not entirely deprive ex ante his statement from any evidentiary consideration. Hence, the Tribunal will pay close attention to the contents of Mr. Daves’ written testimony, his live examination at the Hearing (which included Claimant’s extensive cross examination of Mr. Daves), and other witnesses’ statements and contemporaneous documents relevant to those matters on which Mr. Daves has provided his testimony.
This objection is therefore dismissed. However, the relative weight to be given by the Tribunal to Mr. Daves’ testimony claims not otherwise corroborated must necessary be reduced.

Procedural Order N° 6 established that Mr. Villamarín would testify at the Hearing via video link provided that (i) he be made available to appear during November 14 or November 15, 2017; and (ii) that the Patties and Mr. Villamatín agree to test the video feed in advance of the Hearing, so that no time is lost at the Hearing.100
procedural Otdet N° 6, ¶ 27.

On November 15, 2017, during the second day of the Hearing, Mr. Villamarín was made available to testify via video link. However, Respondents objected to Mr. Villamarín’s appearance arguing that although they accepted that he declared remotely, they asked Claimant, not the Tribunal to allow someone from their legal team to be with him, not to interrupt but to make sure that he is there and that he has no notes, since they are not seeing him live. Mr. Villamarín refused to have someone present in the room. Respondents then asked the Tribunal to approve their request to have someone present in the room.101
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 271, lines 11-24; p. 272, lines 2-6.

Claimants replied, correctly, that this condition was not raised at the time the agreement regarding Mr. Villamarín’s remote testimony was made, and Procedural Order N° 6 does not require for counsel from Superior to be present during the testimony.102
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 272, lines 11-19. Claimant also noted that this request was only made the day before103
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 274, lines 6-7. and that the only concern expressed by Superior was about someone in the room coaching Mr. Villamarín.104
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 275, lines 2-8. Also Claimant represented to the Tribunal that they instructed Mr. Villamarín not to have before him any materials and that most likely the Tribunal would instruct him not to review anything during the course of his testimony.105
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 274, lines 8-16. Also that there was no one in the room with him or coaching him with respect to his testimony.106
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 274, lines 17-21.

Moreover, Claimant stated that they asked Mr. Villamarín to have someone present and he strongly objected and argued that the Respondents’ request had the effect of witness intimidation.107
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 272, lines 19-25.

Respondents argue that this is the common practice in international arbitration. They also note that this is the first time that a witness being seen during his testimony is considered to be witness intimidation since, if he were to declare live in the Hearing Respondent’s counsel would have listen to him and made him questions during cross-examination.108
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 275, lines 9-22.

After taking into consideration the position from both Parties, the Arbitral Tribunal considered that there was a genuine disagreement as to the rules applicable for the examination of a witness through video conference. The fact that Procedural Order N° 6 does not address the particulars is because it is the Tribunal’s understanding that it is customary that both Parties are present in situ in the witness’ examination: first, this serves to ensure that the witness is not being assisted or taking into account written notes or other information besides his own recollection of the facts, and; second, this helps counsel to show documents or assist the witness in any other way.109
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 276, lines 21-25; p. 277, lines 2-25.

On this basis, the Tribunal instructed the Patties to make arrangements in order to make sure that they were represented by counsel where the witness was located to ensure that these key elements of videoconference examination may be achieved.110
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 278, lines 2-8. The Tribunal agreed to defer Mr. Villamatín’ testimony if needed.111
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 279, lines 3-8.

After the decision of the Tribunal, Claimant sought to make arrangements for Mr. Villamarín to testify in presence of counsel for both Parties and informed the Tribunal accordingly.112
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 284, lines 11-21. At that time, Claimant informed the Tribunal that Mr. Villamarín had communicated to their client Mr. Palacio that Mr. Villamarín had that he received a phone call from Mr. Luis Mayor, Superior Energy’s Business Development Manager for Latin America (“Mr. Mayor”), two days before the day scheduled for his testimony during the hearing. During this call, Mr. Mayor reportedly asked Mr. Villamarín if he was in New York, “on Fifth Avenue” (i.e., where the Hearing was taking place) and that they needed to talk because Superior Colombia was considering getting into business with Frank’s, the company in which Mr. Villamarín worked at the time. Because of this phone call, Mr. Villamatin expressed concern for retaliation (i.e., that potential business was being offered in order to affect his willingness to testify called by Claimant) and that he therefore was considering not to testify at all.113
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 286, lines 7-22. Later that same day Claimant confirmed that Mr. Villamatín would not testify.114
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 519, lines 5-11.

Given the arguments raised by the Parties, specially contacts made by a senior official for business development from Superior Colombia to suggest Mr. Villamarín the prospect of business opportunities, and the fact they there was no agreement regarding the effect of Mr. Villamarín’s lack of attendance to the Hearing, the Arbitral Tribunal decided to further hear both Parties on this issue. The Tribunal granted Claimant’s request for Mr. Palacio (who had heard from Mr. Villamarín) to be heard on this matter,115
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 522, lines 17-25. and also asked Respondents to make arrangements for Mr. Mayor to appear before the Tribunal by videoconference during the Hearing.116
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 530, lines 23-25. The Tribunal made absolutely clear that there would be no examination from either party and that the questions would be made only by the Tribunal.117
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 530, lines 7-10.

Mr. Palacio responded the questions made by the Tribunal that same day118
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 534-537. and on the next day of the Hearing, on November 16, 2017 Mr. Mayor testified by videoconference and responded the questions put forward by the Tribunal.119
Tr. Day 3, 16 November 2017, p. 551-562. The Tribunal reserved its decision the evidentiary value of Mr. Villamarín’s witness statement for this Final Award, which is indicated below.

Given the decision by Mr. Villamarín not to testify, Claimant states that Superior had suggested that notwithstanding the failure to appear for testimony, Superior would agree to have Mr. Villamarín’s written witness statement accepted into evidence on condition that it is noted Respondents’ inability to cross-examine Mr. Villamatín.120
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 519, lines 12-22. Claimant’s position is it cannot agree with Respondents’ request to note its inability to cross-examine Mr. Villamarín.121
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 519, lines 23-24. Instead, Claimant wishes to stipulate to have Mr. Villamarín’s written declaration accepted into evidence with the additional note that Superior waived its right to cross-examine Mr. Villamarín.122
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 519, lines 24-25; p. 520, lines 2-5.

Claimant argues that the reason that Mr. Villamarín decided not to testify was because of the phone call made by Mr. Mayor and as a result of his actions Claimant and the Additional Parties were deprived of their opportunity to present their case.123
Tr. Day 3, 16 November 2017, p. 563, lines 22-25; p. 564, lines 2-5. Mr. Mayor was evidently aware of Mr. Villamarín’s imminent testimony in this matter when he made his business development call, Claimant argues. His awareness of the proceedings taking place in New York was reflected in his question to Mr. Villamarín whether he was on “Fifth Avenue,” the location where the Hearing was taking place.124
Tr. Day 3, 16 November 2017, p. 564, lines 6-19. In light of that awareness, Claimant argues, Mr. Mayor’s call to suggest there is business that Mr. Villamarín could obtain from Superior was designed to alter or eliminate his testimony in support of the Claimant. Mr. Mayor mentioned the possibility of new bids and the creation of alliances for services between Superior and Mr. Villamarín’s company and that this is consistent with the concerns expressed by him that his role in these proceedings could jeopardize his job.125
Tr. Day 3, 16 November 2017, p. 566, lines 4-25.

Lastly, although Mr. Mayor thought it was reasonable for him to believe that Mr. Villamarín would have some responsibility in Colombia with respect to what was happening in Brazil regarding a potential alliance between Superior Energy and Mr. Villamarín’s company, Claimant argues that it did not have the opportunity to confirm the truthfulness of Mr. Mayor’s testimony.126
Tr. Day 3, 16 November 2017, p. 567, lines 2-9.

Claimant concludes that the resulting refusal of Mr. Villamarín to testify resulted from interference by Respondents with Claimant’s rights to present testimony, and that the only way to amend this interference is for the Tribunal to accept Mr. Villamarín’s witness statement and deem that Respondents waived their right to cross-examine Mr. Villamarín and that any evidence regarding firing Mr. Villamarín is stricken from the record.127
Tr. Day 3, 16 November 2017, p. 567, lines 4-25 and p. 568, lines 7-17.

Respondents’ position is that Respondents have been deprived of the right to cross-examine Mr. Villamarín due to his failure to appear at the Hearing.128
Tr. Day 3, 16 November 2017, p. 569, lines 10-16

Respondents recall that they proposed to Claimant that Mr. Villamarín’s witness statement remains in the record while noting that Respondents were not able to cross-examine Mr. Villamarín.129
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 521, lines 4-8.

Respondents, however, reject Claimant’s counterproposal to note that they waive their right to cross-examine Mr. Villamarín because the only reason for his absence was beyond the control of Respondents and it was Claimant’s burden to produce the witness. The consequence of that is that the testimony should not be in the record anymore. So they refuse to waive their right of cross-examination.130
Tr. Day 2, 15 November 2017, p. 521, lines 9-21.

Respondents assert that according to Procedural Order No. 1: “[i]f a witness is called to appear at the hearing and fails to do so, the Tribunal shall disregard the witness’ Witness Statement(s).”131
Procedural Order N° 1, ¶ 5.6.
The Tribunal notes that paragraph 5.6 of Procedural Order No. 1 applies when a witness has failed to appear at the Hearing without any valid reason or good cause.

In the instant case, the Tribunal is persuaded that Mr. Villamarín was ready to appear at the Hearing. It is true that there were differences among the Parties on whether Mr. Villamarín’s appearance by videoconference should be allowed with the presence of lawyers from Respondents at the place of location of Mr. Villamarín, and the Tribunal was prepared to make that ruling in case the Parties did not come to terms. The Tribunal does not construe the Respondent’s request to have a representative of Respondent’s counsel present with Mr. Villamarín for his testimony as anything but ordinary and reasonable and does not infer therefrom any attempt by counsel for Respondent to interfere with the examination.

But the situation evolved and Mr. Villamarín ultimately did not appear as a witness at the Hearing for other reasons, specifically alleging that he had been approached by Mr. Mayor, an employee from Superior Colombia who apparently believed Mr. Villamarín was already at the Hearing but had not yet testified, to suggest business opportunities together between Superior and Mr. Villamarín’s current company. This fact has been confirmed by Mr. Palacio132

The Tribunal finds it is not acceptable nor justified for a high-ranking employee of Respondents to approach one of Claimant’s witness right before his live examination at the Hearing, with the prospects of future business opportunities, because to a reasonable person this implies an inducement to favor the person making the offer of new business. When such an inducement is knowingly offered to someone who is about to serve as an adverse witness in an arbitration hearing, it is prima facie evidence of an attempt to interfere in the proceedings. To the extent that Mr. Villamarín is no longer an employee of Claimant, the Tribunal considers a valid reason for Claimant to justify Mr. Villamarín’s lack of attendance to the Hearing based on contacts made by Respondents suggesting potential business together with Mr. Villamarín.

Under these circumstances, the Tribunal expresses its serious dismay in having to conclude on the evidence that Respondents’ senior business development official successfully attempted to interfere with the presence of a witness. The Tribunal is also dismayed with the interference and delay this caused during the Hearing. However, the Tribunal observes that this interference was exposed in time to prevent it from having any further effect than the desired effect to prevent Mr. Villamarín’s appearance. Due to the fact that Mr. Villamarín had already submitted a witness statement, the ironic effect of this interference was to deny Respondents the opportunity to cross examine him.

The Tribunal believes that this negative consequence was adequate under the circumstances to deter any further such conduct and preserve the order of the proceedings, although even that effect is abated somewhat. That is because the Tribunal notes that it received and did not exclude any witness testimony and documentary evidence offered by Respondents relating to the issues on which Mr. Villamarín testified in his witness statement. Due to Respondents’ ability to submit such testimony and evidence for the Tribunal’s consideration, the Tribunal believes that any impact of allowing the Villamarín statement in the absence of specific cross-examination is minimized, proportional, and just.

The Tribunal determines therefore that Claimant’s request is granted to the extent that the Tribunal will admit Mr. Villamarín’s witness statement and it shall be a part of the record, and Respondents’ request to exclude it is denied. The Tribunal has only made here a decision on the procedural aspect of admission of the witness statement, but it shall determine the evidentiary value of Mr. Villamarín’s witness statement, by and when confronting it with all the other evidence submitted by the Parties throughout this arbitration.

title.bd: The First Claim Notice was in compliance with the terms of the SPA

title.bd: Respondents’ are exempted from paying the Second Holdback Amount due to Claimant and the Additional Parties’ breach of the SPA

item.p:
Respondents argue that under Colombian law, Claimant’s breach of the SPA exempts Superior Colombia from paying the Second Holdback Amount and entitles Superior Colombia to exercise the penalties and enforcements mechanisms incorporated in the SPA to address such breach. Colombian law precludes claims for breach of contract when the claiming party itself is in breach of the contract. Article 1609 provides the called exceptio non adimpleti contractus which is an express exemption to a patty’s duty to perform its obligations under a contract when the other party has failed to perform its obligations under the said contract:287
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ ¶ 158-160.
“In bilateral contracts, no party would be deemed in default by not performing an agreement, while the other party has not performed its part, or has not agreed to perform it in the required form and time.”288
Exhibit RL-022.

Respondents contend that the exceptio non adimpleti contractus exempts a party from its obligation to perform a contract under the general rule of pacta sunt servanda. According to the Constitutional Court, the purpose of this exemption is to prevent “that one of the parties tries to take advantage of the contract and requires the other party to perform, while it itself does not perform or agrees to perform its respective obligations.”289
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 161 and exhibit RL-026. Pursuant to Colombian jurisprudence290
Exhibits RL-027and RL-028. and scholarly writings291
Exhibit RL-029. the elements of the exceptio non adimpleti contractus are present in this case: (i) the SPA provides for reciprocal obligations; (ii) the breach of the material covenants and material obligations on the SPA; and (iii) the breaches happened before Superior was required to pay the Second Holdback Amount.292
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ ¶ 161-163.

Respondents submit that the SPA provides for bilateral or reciprocal obligations which are imposed on Superior Colombia and on Premium and the Additional Parties: (i) Superior Colombia was obliged to purchase Broxton shares and pay the Purchase Price and (ii) Premium and the Additional Parties were obliged to sell the Broxton shares and comply other obligations and covenants such as Sections 10.17; 6 and 7 of the SPA.293
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ ¶ 165-166.

Respondents asserts that the SPA provides for material covenants in Section 6 and material obligations in Section 10.17.294
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ ¶ 167-189.

The covenants in Section 6 are material for the following reasons: (i) because the underlying legal interest it seeks to protect, that is, to prevent conflicts of interest295
Superior’s Code of Business Ethics and Conduct of 2011 and Superior’s Code of Business Ethics and Conduct of 2013 both defined conflict of interests, exhibits R-070 and R-071. and that may arise from Mr. Palacio’s personal relationship with Petrodynamic, a company owned and managed by his wife, Ms. Hernández;296
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 168. (ii) the materiality of the covenants in Section 6(a) of the SPA led Superior Colombia to incorporate similar obligations in the Employment Agreement,297
Exhibit R-004, Clause 2 of the Employment Agreement. the Services Agreement;298
Exhibit R-005, Clause 10 of the Services Agreement. and Superior Colombia’s Code of Conduct also aimed at preventing conflicts of interests from arising;299
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 170. and (iii) reflects and protects the fiduciary duties that Mr. Palacio owes to ITS because, under Colombian law he is not only obliged to comply with the express covenants in Section 6(a), but also with the implied duties imposed by the principle of good faith.300
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 172.

Likewise, Respondents avers that obligations established in sections 10.17 (b) and 10.17 (c) ate material because they (i) provide for specific covenants to preserve the value of ITS and allow Superior Colombia to enhance and expand ITS’ business in Colombia, including a non-compete covenant imposed on Claimant and Additional Parties and (ii) protect the same legal interests protected by the Employment Agreement and later by the Services Agreement.301
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ ¶ 177 and following, further elaborated in Respondent’s Memorial of Counterclaims Section II.B.1. See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 374-378.

Respondents allege that the parties expressly acknowledged that Superior Colombia purchased all of ITS’ industrial secrets and goodwill302
Section 10.17(a) of the SPA: “Seller expressly acknowledges that Purchaser is acquiring all of the industrial secrets and goodwill of ITS in order to successfully expand and enhance its business in the provision of services to the oil and gas industry in Colombid”. which were material for Superior’s strategy to expand in the Colombian gas and oil industry. Therefore, the Parties agreed that Premium and Additional Parties could not use them or do anything to undermine their value because it would constitute unfair competition and unfair trade practices.303
Section 10.17 (b) of the SPA. Section 10.17 (b) also incorporates an assumption of the use of these assets by provision of services in the industry unless (i) the services fall within the Petrodynamic Services or (ii) the services did not include the purchased industrial secrets and goodwill.304
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ ¶ 177-178.

Also, Respondents argue that under the Employment Agreement, Mr. Palacio is prohibited from rendering services to an employer other than ITS, or work on his own.305
Exhibit R-004, Clause 2 of the Employment Agreement. In turn, under the Services Agreement, Mr. Palacio is prohibited from providing his services to companies that competed with ITS.306
Exhibit R-005, Clause 10 of the Services Agreement.

Finally, Respondents describes that the breaches of the SPA occurred prior to the retention by Superior Colombia of the Second Holdback Amount. Pursuant to section 2.2(c) of the SPA, Superior Colombia was required to pay the Second Holdback Amount “on the date that is twelve months after the Closing Date”, that is, in March of 2015. In turn, Premium was obliged to comply with Sections 6(a), 10.17(b), and 10.17(c) since the date of execution of the SPA.307
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 195.

As a starting point, the Tribunal notes that pursuant to the terms of the SPA, Superior Colombia has a right to retain the so-called “Holdback Amounts” only if certain conditions are met. Specifically, this right to withhold payment or reduce the Purchase Price arises from disparate provisions of the SPA such as inter alia Section 2.2 (c), Section 8.0, particularly 8.5, and Sections 10.17(b) and 10.17(d) of the SPA.

Section 2.2 (c) of the SPA establishes Superior Colombia’s right to withhold payment in the following terms:
“Notwithstanding anything here to the contrary, Purchaser has the right to withhold any portion of the Holdback Amount in order to offset any amounts owed by Sellers to Purchaser arising or related to any of Sellers’ obligations hereunder, including, without limitation, any amounts related to Sellers’ indemnity obligations.”

Section 8.5, in turn, sets out the requirements that Superior Colombia needs to fulfil to withhold payment of the Holdback Amount due to damages caused by Claimant:
“8.5 Claims under Holdback Amounts.
The Purchaser shall have the option of claiming all or any part of any Purchaser Damages under Section 8.2, by notifying the Seller Representative that the Purchaser is claiming the amount of such Purchaser Damages (or the Purchaser’s good faith estimate of such amount if unliquidated, pending the final determination thereof) against the Holdback Amounts. Any such claim against the Holdback Amounts shall be made on or before following the Closing Date: (i) twelve (12) months for the Holdback Amount No. 1, and (ii) twenty-four (24) months for the Holdback Amount No. 2, by delivery of written notice to the Seller Representative, stating the nature of and basis for such claim with reasonable specificity (including the applicable provision of this Agreement). If the Seller objects to the amount of all or part of any claim by the Purchaser against the Holdback Amounts, then the Seller shall, within 30 days of receipt of such claim, provide written notice (an “Objection Notice”) to the Purchaser setting forth Seller’s objections. If the Seller sends the Purchaser and Objection Notice, the Purchaser and the Seller shall work in good faith to reconcile and resolve the differences. If the parties cannot mutually resolve such differences during such fifteen (15) day period, the Purchaser may proceed to determine the amount of Purchaser Damages payable to the Purchaser without prejudice to the Seller’s right to settle the issue by arbitration as contemplated in Section 10.2. Notwithstanding anything in this Section 8.5 to the contrary, the Purchaser shall also be entitled to assert any claim for Purchaser Damages directly against the Seller without making such claim against the Holdback Amounts.”

Sections 10.17 (b) and 10.17(c) are also key provisions as they both establish the right of Superior Colombia to reduce or adjust downwards the Purchase Price, in the form of a liquidated damages clause, in case of breach of the SPA by Claimant and/or the Additional Parties, in the following terms:
“(b) Seller and Beneficial Owners expressly covenant and agree that they shall not use any of the industrial secrets and goodwill, nor will otherwise carry out any activity that could undermine the value of these assets. Except for the Petrodynamic Services (and subject to the covenants in Section 6) the Seller and the Beneficial Owners further covenant and agree that if Seller or Beneficial Owners provide services to the Colombian oil and gas industry within the 2 years following the date of termination of the Employment Agreement of the Key Individual, due to the complexity of the Colombian oil and gas industry it would be reasonable to assume that, in doing so, Seller and Beneficial Owners will be using the transferred industrial secrets and goodwill, that the Seller and the Beneficial Owners would be engaging in unfair competition and unfair trade practices by using industrial secrets and goodwill that they have sold to Purchaser for consideration and thus no longer own, and that the value of the industrial secrets and goodwill will necessarily be undermined by such unauthorized use.
