(c) Without prejudice to the Seller’s and Beneficial Owners’ right to disprove the above assumption (i.e. by demonstrating that, in participating in the Colombian oil and gas industry, they are using industrial secrets and goodwill other that those transferred herby), Seller and Beneficial Owners covenant and agree that, except for the Petrodynamic Services (and subject to the covenants in Section 6), the Purchaser Price shall be adjusted downwards by a certain percentage in the event that the Seller or the Beneficial Owners participate in the Colombian oil and gas industry within the next two years, as follows: (i) 20% if such participation takes place within 1 year after the date of termination of the Employment Agreement of the Key Individual, (ii) 15% if such participation takes place within .51 years after the date of termination of the Employment Agreement of the Key Individual, and (iii) 10% if such participation takes place within 2 year after the date of termination of the Employment Agreement of the Key Individual.”

In the instant case, Respondents invoked these rights under the SPA when they sent the First Claim Notice to retain the Second Holdback Amount. In fact, Superior Colombia expressly stated that such notice was made “pursuant to section 2.2(c), Section 8.2 and Section 8.5” of the SPA308
Exhibit R-007 and Respondents’ Mem oxial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 75. and also relied on Section 10.17 of the same agreement.309
Exhibit R-031. Further, when describing the basis for its claim, Superior Colombia also indicated that the “Key Individual breached the covenants in Section 6(a) of the Agreement causing Purchaser Damages to Purchase”.310
Exhibit R-007.

The Tribunal is convinced that Superior Colombia’s right to withhold payment is clearly established and thus admissible under the SPA provided that certain conditions are met. Therefore, if properly exercised, Superior Colombia’s right to withhold the Second Holdback Amount cannot amount to a breach of contract as asserted by Claimant.
The critical point is, therefore, to determine whether Superior Colombia lawfully exercised its right to withhold payment of the Second Holdback Amount according to the terms of the SPA.

Taking into account the Parties’ submissions and allegations, the Tribunal considers that it must first assess if Superior Colombia fully complied with the formal requirements set out by Section 8.5 of the SPA to withhold payment of the Second Holdback Amount (a). If so, the Tribunal will determine if there wete breaches on the part of Claimant justifying Superior Colombia’s decision to withhold payment of the Second Holdback Amount (b).

title.bd: The First Claim Notice is in compliance with the formal requirements of Section 8.5 of the SPA

item.p: The Tribunal concurs with Respondents that the formal requirements laid down by Section 8.5 of the SPA for a notice to withhold payment are: (i) delivery of a written notice; (ii) delivery on or before the date for payment of the Second Holdback Amount; (iii) description of the nature and basis of the claim with reasonable specificity; and (iv) negotiations in good faith during a 15-day period following said delivery. In this regard, the Tribunal is persuaded that Superior Colombia complied with all these requirements.

As to requirements (i) and (ii), there is evidence on the record that a written notice was sent by Respondents on February 25, 2015 and received by Claimant on February 26, 2015.311
Exhibit R-007. Considering that the Second Holdback Amount was due on or about March 1, 2015. There is also evidence of negotiations entertained during at least a 15-day period312
Exhibit R-026. due to the existence of an Objection Notice sent by Claimant, conversations and meetings between the Parties for, at least, two months. Accordingly, the requirement (iv) is also satisfied.313
Section 8.5 of the SPA and Exhibits R-025 and R-031.

As to the requirement (iii), i.e. description of the nature and basis of the claim, the Tribunal is not convinced by Claimant’s allegations about an alleged indetermination of damages and lack of reasonable specificity.314
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 22. See Final Award, ¶ 209. As noted by Respondents, Section 8.5 of the SPA does not require Superior Colombia to make an exact quantification of the alleged damages, but a “good faith estimate of such amount if unliquidated, pending the final determination thereof.”315
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 144-145, In addition, the Tribunal agrees with Respondents that they wete not obliged to describe their claim in greater detail. The claim, on its face, is clear enough and provides sufficient detail to understand its nature and basis.

The First Claim Notice satisfactorily describes the basis for the claim since it states that the “Key Individual breached the covenants in Section 6(a) of the Agreement causing Purchaser Damages to Purchased”.316
Exhibit R-007. The Tribunal notes that such description does include “the applicable provision of the agreement” (i.e. Section 6(a) of the SPA), which satisfies the specific requirement established by the Parties regarding the determination of the basis for the claim.317
Section 8.5 of the SPA. In addition, section 1.1.1. of the First Claim Notice describes the content of such provision, and further explains that said section required Mr. Palacio not to participate in Petrodynamic Services and to remain at arms-length in dealings between Petrodynamic and ITS. In sum, Respondents clearly stated that the basis for their claim consisted in a breach of Section 6(a) of the SPA on the part of Mr. Palacio.

Conversely, the Tribunal finds that Respondents also sufficiently defined the nature of their claim because they clearly stated the specific circumstances by which Mr. Palacio would have breached Section 6(a) of the SPA.

Section 1.1.2 of the First Claim Notice describes those specific circumstances. In particular, Respondents stated that, prompted by a complaint received by the Ethics and Compliance Department of Superior Services, Inc., they conducted investigative procedures finding that “a. The Key Individual has been directly involved in business dealings between Petrodynamic Services and ITS after Purchaser indirectly acquired ITS in March 2013”, and “b. Purchaser of Petrodynamic Services have been made in contravention of ITS, Purchaser, and/or Superior Energy policies. As a result, ITS has paid higher prices to Petrodynamic Services that it would have paid to third parties”.

In addition, the Tribunal finds revealing that Claimant did reply to the First Claim Notice in specific terms and at the time made no objections to its formal requirements or lack thereof.318
Exhibit R-025.
In light of the above, the Tribunal concludes that the First Claim Notice did comply with the formal requirements set out by Section 8.5 of the SPA.

The Tribunal will now turn to the question of whether and if Superior successfully established that Claimant or the Additional Parties breached the SPA, allowing Superior Colombia to retain payment of the balance of the purchase price and subsequently offset said payment with the alleged damages and penalties invoked by Superior Colombia.

title.bd: Claimant’s breach of the SPA justified Superior Colombia’s right to withhold payment of the Second Holdback Amount

item.p:
In the First Claim Notice, Superior Colombia asserted that Claimant had breached the SPA to retain the Second Holdback Amount. In fact, Superior Colombia expressly stated that such notice was made “pursuant to section 2.2(c), Section 8.2 and Section 8.5” of the SPA319
Exhibit R-007 and Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 75. and also relied on Section 10.17 of the same agreement.320
Exhibit R-031. Further, when describing the basis for its claim, Superior Colombia also indicated that the “Key Individual breached the covenants in Section 6(a) of the Agreement causing Purchaser Damages to Purchase”.321
Exhibit R-007.

Respondents’ position is that Claimant breached (i) the material covenants in Section 6(a) of the SPA, (ii) the material obligations in Section 10.17 of the SPA, (iii) the covenants to act in good faith under Colombian law in the contractual and pre-contractual period of the SPA, (iv) Section 6.2 (a) and Section 7 (d) of the SPA concerning representation and warranties and (v) the non-compete and confidentiality requirements under the Employment Agreement and the Services Agreement.322
See Final Award, ¶ 422.

The Tribunal notes that Respondents’ counterclaims are based on the same allegations of Claimant’s breaches of the SPA described above. For the sake of brevity, the Tribunal refers to section D.3 of this Final Award323
See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 420-494. whereby the Tribunal has found, based on abundant evidence, that Claimant and the Additional Parties have breached the SPA. Specifically, the Tribunal has found that (i) Claimant and Mr. Palacio breached Section 6 (a) of the SPA by Mr. Palacio’s participation in the Petrodynamic Services and in dealings between ITS and Petrodynamic; (ii) Claimant and both Additional Parties breached Section 10.17 (b) of the SPA by the use of the industrial secrets and goodwill that was agreed not to use; (iii) Claimant and both Additional Parties failed to act in good faith in the celebration and execution of the SPA; and (iv) Claimant and Mr. Palacio breached the non-compete and confidentiality provisions of the Employment and Services Agreements. In light of the above, the Tribunal concludes that Claimant and the Additional Parties have breached the SPA, thus entitling Superior Colombia to lawfully withhold the Second Holdback Amount.
On this basis, the Tribunal finds that Claimant’s claim seeking reimbursement of the Second Holdback Amount should be dismissed.

Respondents assert that Claimant and the Additional Parties have breached several sections of the SPA.324
The Tribunal notes that the New Claims filed by Respondents consisting in Claimant’s alleged breach of Sections 6.3 of the SPA, and Sections 4.6 and 4.14 of the SPA have been, declared inadmissible. Therefore, these claims are neither described not decided in this Final Award. As a result of these alleged breaches, Respondents seek an award on damages.

The Tribunal will first set forth Respondents’ claims related to Claimant’s alleged breaches of the SPA and will then turn to the assessment of the damages sought by Respondents. As noted above, the Parties’ positions are described as presented by each patty.
Respondents identified a number of alleged breaches made by Claimant, which are described below.

title.bd: Claimant’s breach of Section 6 of the SPA

item.p:
Respondents claim that Mr. Palacio was bound by specific covenants under Section 6 of the SPA that provides:325
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 57.
“6. Covenants
(a) Notwithstanding anything herein to the contrary, the Key Individual undertakes not to participate in the Petrodynamic Services and that all dealings and contracts which may be entered into between ITS and Petrodynamic Petroleum Services S.A.S. (and its affiliates, if any) will be at ‘arms-length’ and will not involve, directly or indirectly, the Key Individual in the decision making process.”326
Section 6 of the SPA.

Therefore, Respondents’ position is that Mr. Palacio: (i) was prohibited from participating in any way in the “Petrodynamic Services”; (ii) had to remain at arm’s length and not be involved, directly or indirectly, in the decision-making process regarding any dealings and contracts between ITS and Petrodynamic; and (iii) entered into an obligation to ensure that all such dealings and contracts between ITS and Petrodynamic would be at ‘arms-length’ and would not involve him, directly or indirectly, in the decision making process.327
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 58. Also Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 59, lines 10-25.

According to Respondents, Section 6 (a) of the SPA imposed Mr. Palacio specific obligations and duties that could not be willfully disregarded and that under Colombian law must be complied in good faith. The principle of good faith in the negotiation, execution, performance, interpretation and termination of contracts is founded in Articles 1603328
Exhibit RL-003. Article 1603 Civil Code: “Contracts must be performed in good faith, and they therefore require not only that which is expressed in them, but all things that arise precisely of the nature of the obligation, or which by law belong to it.” of the Civil Code and 871329
Exhibit RL-005. Article 871 Commercial Code: “Contracts shall be performed in good faith and, they therefore, require not only that which is expressed in them, but to all things that correspond to their nature by law, custom, or natural equity.” and 863330
Exhibit RL-004. Article 863 Commercial Code: “The parties shall proceed in good faith free of negligence during the precontractual period, or otherwise they will be forced to compensate the damages caused by them.” of the Commercial Code. Also, the Supreme Court and arbitral tribunals have ruled that good faith has to be judged from an objective standpoint331
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 60-62 and exhibits RL-011 and R-008. and has been defined as “the loyal, honest and irreproachable conduct analyzed from an objective perspective, that is, with a specific standard determined by social usages and good customs”332
Exhibit RL-010. or “a genuine set of rules of conduct that are not prescribed by law, but implicitly contained in the legal system, and thus, in the presence of a given situation, impose on the individual the duty to undertake a conduct aimed not to disregard other parties juridical interests.”333
Exhibit RL-012.

According to Colombian courts and scholars, Respondents argue, good faith has a “gap-filling” purpose (función integradora) and therefore good faith imposes secondary duties not expressly provided in the contract.334
Exhibits RL-001 and RL-002. One of them is the duty of fidelity that implies that a party is bound to fully perform its obligations and to put first the interests of the person or entity she is representing (positive commitment) and to abstain from maintaining and initiating a relationship which may cause conflict of interests (negative commitment).335
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, 63-64 and exhibit RL-001. Also Tr. Day 4, 17 November 2017, p. 825, lines 6-15,

title.it: Mr. Palacio participated in the Petrodynamic Services, in violation of the Section 6 of the SPA

item.p:
In their opening statement, Respondents argued that Mr. Palacio breached Section 6’s prohibition to “participate in the Petrodynamic Services” (i.e., “(i) the rental of tractors for moving the cementing units and (ii) the sale of consumable items such as float equipment and centralizers”336
Section 1 of the SPA.) as early as one day after closing, when he became an indirect owner of Petrodynamic. Respondents state that they became aware of that situation during the Arbitration as a result of disclosure of the documents made by Claimants.337
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 32, lines 9-14. Mr. Palacio and Ms. Hernández each owned 50 percent of Premium and one working day after the Closing Date, Premium inserted approximately US$ 800,000 into Petrodynamic, in exchange Petrodynamic gave 1,449,200 shares to Premium.338
Exhibits R-132 and R-133. Ms. Hernández’s shares were diluted and Premium became the new effective owner of Petrodynamic, and the owners of Premium were Mr. Palacio and Ms. Hernández.339
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 54, lines 2-25. Therefore, Mr. Palacio became an indirect shareholder, and Respondents say that this ownership interest constituted evidence of a breach of his obligations under the SPA because it is one piece of evidence that tends to establish that Mr. Palacio engaged in the Petrodynamic Services and/or “dealings and contracts which may be entered into between ITS and Petrodynamic” and did not remain at “arms-length” from them.340
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 58, lines 2-9.

In their closing statement, Respondents contest Claimant’s and Ms. Hernández’s position that the operation was a loan and not a capital contribution and that there was a mistake in the bank forms. Respondents point out that Ms. Hernández testified on her first witness statement that she was the sole shareholder of Petrodynamic and on her third witness statement she declared she made an additional capital contribution to Petrodynamic and then stresses that Premium infused the cash and became a shareholder in December 2013 but said nothing about a loan.341
Tr. Day 4, 17 November 2017, p. 843, lines 6-22 They add that it is not credible the existence of a loan with no term, interests or repayment.342
Tr. Day 4, 17 November 2017, p. 845, lines 2-4.

Besides the alleged first breach of the SPA, Respondents assert that the evidence gathered by Superior Colombia shows that Mr. Palacio actively participated in the Petrodynamic Services within the two years following the termination of his relationship with ITS. The investigation lead by Mr. Daves, based on interviews with ITS’ employees and analysis of corporate documentation reached various conclusions.343
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 68-69.

Firstly, Mr. Daves concluded that Mr. Palacio was involved in pricing decisions concerning products sold by Petrodynamic to ITS and observed that “Mr. Palacio sent and received numerous emails to and from ITS personnel on behalf of Petrodynamic and was consistently identified during interviews as the contact person from Petrodynamic for questions regarding pricing.”344
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 69; Witness Statement of Mr. Daves, ¶ 10 and exhibit JD-016.

Second, BDO determined that Mr. Palacio had personally negotiated prices for Petrodynamic Services with ITS employees, on behalf of Petrodynamic. Mr. Villamarín stated in an interview that Mr. Palacio had been involved in discussions between ITS and Petrodynamic regarding flotation parts and truck rental prices.345
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves I, ¶ 16. Also, Respondents point to emails that Mr. Palacio exchanged with Mr. Bula as evidence that Mr. Palacio was responsible for negotiating pricing schemes for truck rental on behalf of Petrodynamic.346
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 70 and exhibits R-036; R-037 y R-038.

Third, BDO concluded that Mr. Palacio directly negotiated contracts with Petrodynamic’s suppliers while he was working at ITS. Specifically, BDO found a draft agreement between Petrodynamic and Joalsiar Setvicios S.A.S. (“Joalsiar”) for the supply of certain parts, including centralizers and floatation equipment. The draft agreement was sent by Jorge Sierra –an operations engineer at ITS and legal representative of Joalsiar– directly to Mr. Palacio. In the email, Mr. Sierra addressed Mr. Palacio as “patrón” (literally translated, this means “boss”) and told him that he was sending a contract for Mr. Palacio as they had previously talked about.347
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 71 and exhibit R-039. According to Mr. Daves when Mr. Sierra was first asked about the Petrodynamic-Joalsiar relationship Mr. Sierra denied involvement in the operation. Mr. Sierra explained that Joalsiar was his wife’s company and that he was not authorized to sign contracts on its behalf, according to Mr. Daves. When Mr. Daves asked Mr. Palacio about this topic, Mr. Daves says that Mr. Palacio acknowledged receiving a draft contract but stated that he did not sign it because the contract had to be signed by the representatives of Joalsiar and Petrodynamic, who were Mr. Sierra’s wife and Ms. Hernández, respectively.348
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves, ¶ ¶ 18-22 and exhibit R-040.

Respondents argue that before the acquisition, Joalsiar had provided services and flotation parts directly to ITS but after the acquisition Mr. Palacio conveniently placed Petrodynamic as an intermediary between them with the effect of crafting profits for Petrodynamic, at ITS’ expense, and incentivizing for Mr. Sierra on behalf of ITS to continue to buy products from Petrodynamic. Mr. Sierra approved 27 purchase orders for Petrodynamic’s products totaling US$ 1,724,597 between August 2013 and October 2014.349
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 73, Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 58-60, witness Statement of Mr. Daves, ¶ 24 and exhibit JD-013.

Fourth, Respondents assert that Mr. Palacio also acted on behalf of Petrodynamic when dealing with ITS’ clients, such as Emerald Energy and Baker Hughes, who would contact Mr. Palacio regarding potential business with Petrodynamic. Petrodynamic would then directly send price quotations to such clients.350
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 74 and exhibits R-041 and R-042.

Fifth, Respondents claim that Mr. Palacio further engaged in business dealings with other companies in the oil and gas industry on behalf of Petrodynamic. Within the year following the termination of his Employment Agreement —but while still working for ITS under the Services Agreement– Mr. Palacio received purchase orders and information requirements intended for Petrodynamic from clients such as Qmax Solutions Colombia and Baker Hughes. During this period, Respondents also point to evidence that Mr. Palacio dealt with suppliers on behalf of Petrodynamic.351
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 75 and exhibits R-039; R-043; R-044; R-045; R-046; R-047; R-048; R-049; R-050;R-051.

Finally, Respondents aver that Mr. Palacio was responsible for Petrodynamic’s daily operations and directed Petrodynamic employees to provide certain information on products or to issue invoices to clients352
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 76 and exhibits R-052: R-053; R-054; R-055. and received labor and accounting information pertaining to Petrodynamic.353
Such as external auditing firm KPMG or compensation fund Compensar. Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 76 and exhibits R-056: R-057; R-058. Also, that after having interviewed almost all the employees in ITS’ supply chain management team, they all confirmed that Mr. Palacio was the contact for all things concerning Petrodynamic within ITS.354
Exhibits JD-005 and JD-006; Witness Statement of Mr. Balsero II, ¶ 20 and Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 61.

Respondents assert that further instances of Mr. Palacio’s breach of Section 6 is demonstrated by documents produced by Claimant:355
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 56-57. (i) on December 29, 2014, Mr. Palacio negotiated float equipment prices with ITS supply chain employees thereby making decisions at Petrodynamic in respect to ITS;356
Exhibit R-081. (ii) on January 8, 2015, e-mails show that he was considered point of contact and received reports from Petrodynamic clients on part failures used in bids for Pacific entities357
Exhibit R-082. and (iii) on January 14, 2015, directed Petrodynamic employees and asked questions in negotiations with clients regarding shoe sales pricing.358
Exhibit R-083. In addition, e-mails sent or received by Mr. Palacio on behalf of Petrodynamic demonstrate that customers viewed him as the point of contact of the company and he personally used the e-mail “ventas@petrodynamic.com.co” to perform this role.359
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 54.

title.it: Mr. Palacio did not remain at arm’s length in the dealings and contracts between ITS and Petrodynamic

item.p:
Respondents claim that Mr. Palacio further breached Section 6 (a) of the SPA by directly and indirectly participating in dealings and contracts between ITS and Petrodynamic. Mr. Palacio personally approved and signed for ITS the authorization of three different purchase orders placed by Petrodynamic360
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 78 and exhibits R-059; R-060 and R-061. for a total of, at least, US$ 452,000.361
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 54. Also, Respondents allege that Mr. Palacio remained responsible for the purchase orders’ process from ITS to Pettodynamic and the price making decisions on behalf of Petrodynamic concerning items bought by ITS.362
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 78 and exhibits R-062; R-063; R-064; R-065; R-066; R-067; R-068; R-069.

Respondents refute Claimant’s defense that German Nichols told him to sign the purchase orders arguing that there is no evidence of these instructions despite being ordered by the Tribunal to do so produce this document363
Procedural Order No. 2. Respondents’ Redfern Schedule, Request No. 5.5. p. 75. and there is only evidence that he admitted to having signed the purchase orders, therefore breaching the SPA.364
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 55.

Respondents also refute Mr. Palacio’s assertion that he could not have participated in the Petrodynamic Services because it was Ms. Hernández who was in fact running the company. This claim is not supported by evidence and it is not credible that Ms. Hernández run Petrodynamic without Mr. Palacio’s management and participation. She has admitted she had no prior experience in the oil and gas industry365
Witness Statement of Ms. Hernández, ¶ 3. and she is a software system manager with training in information technology366
Exhibit R-084. in contrast with his husband who has broad experience in the oil and gas industry. Mr. Palacio himself has admitted to Mr. Daves367
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves II, ¶ ¶ 33-34. counseling Ms. Hernández in business matters and staying involved in Petrodynamic Services.368
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 63-66.

Respondents asserts that, as a result of Mr. Palacio’s involvement in the Petrodynamic Services and its dealings with ITS, he was able to transfer profit from ITS to Petrodynamic: ITS would buy significant amounts of flotation equipment from Petrodynamic previously bought from local vendors at significantly lower prices. Respondents assert that Premium benefited from Mr. Palacio’s privileged position in ITS and from his breach of the SPA. Respondents cite to the testimony of Mr. Daves that:369
Respondents0Æ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 79-80.
“During our review of ITS accounting records, we noted that flotation parts purchased from local vendors by ITS prior to the [Acquisition] were purchased from Petrodynamic at higher prices after the Acquisition. Mr. Palacio acknowledged this pattern of prices during our interview with him and explained that he was transferring a portion of the profit margin generated by ITS to Petrodynamic as some sort of tax strategy.”370
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves I, ¶ 15,

According to Mr. Daves, Mr. Palacio showed that he was fully aware of the profits margins of ITS as well as Petrodynamic’s stating that “the profit margin for ITS was 37% to 40%” and that “the profit margin on parts for Petrodynamics is 20% to 25%”.371
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves I, ¶ 15. Mr. Palacio admitted that he could manipulate the profit margins of each company. On October 28, 2014, Mr. Palacio handwrote a detailed notation of the profit, tax and commercial strategies of ITS and Petrodynamic, among other companies in the Colombian oil and gas industry.372
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 69 and exhibit JD-008. This knowledge allowed him to interpose Petrodynamic as a middleman between ITS and its suppliers at a price point that would beat international competitors and allow Petrodynamic to make a profit.373
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves II, ¶ ¶ 28-32. This margin could have instead been entering ITS’ balance sheet if Palacio had used the same network of suppliers that he did for Petrodynamic. The self-dealing is aggravated by the fact that, in particular for API-certified products sold by CTE, Petrodynamic earned an astronomical price margin of 156% to 246% depending on the product.374
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 70 and Witness Statement of Mr. Daves II, ¶ 31.

Respondents further add that evidence, specifically the interviews conducted personally by Mr. Daves, shows that Mr. Palacio de facto handled the relationship between ITS and Petrodynamic.375
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves, ¶ ¶ 10-14 and exhibits JD-004, Interviews of Victor Augusto Palacio Gaitán dated November October 27, 2014 and October 28, 2014; JD-005, Interview of Juan Carios Villamarín, dated October 27, 2014; JD-006, Interviews of Julio Bula dated October 20, 2014, October 27, 2014 and November 10, 2014 and JD-007, Interview of Diego Avella dated October 23, 2014. For instance, Mr. Palacio instructed ITS’ personnel to buy from Petrodynamic376
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves, ¶ ¶ 10-14 and exhibits JD-004; JD-005 and JD-006. and those purchase orders were summarily approved.377
Witness Statement of Ms. Diana Rojas, ¶ ¶ 7-11.

In addition, Respondents point to an e-mail chain dated April 9, 2013, as evidence that Mr. Palacio and Ms. Hernández supervised and instructed José Joaquín Mejía, an ITS’ employee at the time (“Mr. Mejía”), to perform daily tasks for the benefit of Petrodynamic. Specifically, Mr. Mejía asked Ms. Hernández to (i) give him some pending purchases orders from Petrodynamic to San Antonio (an ITS’ competitor) that were sent to him by Mr. Palacio but they were not received because of internet problems and (ii) activate the corporate e-mail of Petrodynamic with the purpose of not using the e-mail of “Petrodynamic”. As for this last point, Respondents understand the second “Petrodynamic” as a typo truly referring to ITS’ corporate e-mail. Therefore, Respondents conclude that Mr. Mejia was asking for the activation of the Petrodynamic’s corporate e-mail because he did not want to use the ITS’ corporate e-mail for dealings involving the Petrodynamic business.378
Respondents’ Memorial of Rejoinder, ¶ ¶ 34-35 and exhibit R-113.

Respondents state that Mr. Mejía was in charge of handling the ITS warehouse and internally within ITS he made sure that parts and products be acquired from suppliers, including those from Petrodynamic. Diana Rojas noted that “[p]urchases were decided by the operations personnel, requested on the phone and executed by the then-warehouse employee, [Mejía] and certain interns”379
Witness Statement of Ms. Rojas, ¶ 7. and that “[w]e were never explained how ITS had come up with a group of suppliers prior to the Acquisition by Superior Colombia, but I remember [Mejía] saying that he would keep on working with his roster of suppliers.”380
Witness Statement of Ms. Rojas, ¶ 9. Mr. Mejía eventually left ITS to work as a Petrodynamic employee.381
Respondents’ Memorial of Rejoinder, ¶ 36.

Respondents conclude that all the evidence points to Palacio and Hernández de facto controlling the relationship between ITS and Petrodynamic, at least through July 2013. Precisely during this time frame – when Palacio was also signing ITS purchase orders for Petrodynamic products – the prices for certain products and services that Petrodynamic sold to ITS increased compared to the prices it used to pay to other suppliers.382
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves I, ¶ ¶ 17 and 27. On October 2013, a couple of months after Mr. Bula started working at Superior Colombia, the first supply chain management procedure was put into practice 383
Witness Statement of Ms. Rojas, ¶ ¶ 10-12. and from that date on, and also following Mr. Bula’s request for discounts, the prices at which Petrodynamic sold products to ITS began to stabilize or decrease.384
Respondents’ Memorial of Rejoinder, ¶ 37 and Witness Statement of Mr. Daves I, ¶ ¶ 10-34.

In any event, Respondents maintain that the comparison between Petrodynamic’s prices and international companies such as Halliburton and Weatherford – which are certainly not Pettodynamic’s market peers, and which sell products of the highest quality and the highest technology, even when compared within the API-certified range – are not at issue in this Arbitration. What is at issue is Pettodynamic’s push out of other ITS suppliers and prices for products post-acquisition in order to improve Pettodynamic’s profit margin, and Mr. Palacio’s role in that decision and subsequent negotiations between Petrodynamic and ITS.385
Respondents’ Memorial of Rejoinder, ¶ 38,

title.bd: Claimant’s breach of Section 10.17 of the SPA

title.it: The covenants under Section 10.17 of the SPA

item.p:
Respondents’ position is that the whole Section 10.17 of the SPA is based on the premise that Superior Colombia acquired ITS’ business including its industrial secrets, goodwill and contacts, among other assets acquired, to successfully expand and enhance ITS’ business in the Colombian oil and gas industry.386
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 81-82. Section 10.17 (a) expressly provides:
“Seller expressly acknowledges that Purchaser is acquiring all of the industrial secrets and goodwill of ITS in order to successfully expand and enhance its business in the provision of services to the oil and gas industry in Colombia.”387
Section 10.17 (a) of the SPA.

The Colombian Supreme Court has defined “goodwill” as follows:
“The good name, the reputation, that a commercial establishment, or merchant, has before the market or the general public, namely, it refers to the specific factor of a business that has created a reputation, clientele and a network of correspondents of all types, combined with the trust that it instills in its suppliers, employees, financial institutions and, in general, in any person with whom it has dealings.”388
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 83 and exhibit RL-013.

In addition, Respondents cite to the Colombian Council of State which defined “goodwill” in the following terms:
“Traditionally Good Will is translated by the words Clientele or parish of a commercial house (the clients voluntarily attend this establishment due to the quality of the service provided and its reputation). In fact, this term adopts a broader definition and may be defined as the specific factor of a business that has known how to forge a name, a place, an establishment that succeeds and creates a clientele and a network of relationships and correspondents of all types, without the materialization of such elements. To the Good Will of the clients is added the favor and confidence of the suppliers, employees and the group of those with whom the establishment maintains relationships.”389
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 84 and exhibit RL-006.

Furthermore, Respondents point out that Section 10.17 (e) provides that “[t]he provisions of this clause are intended solely to preserve and fairly reflect the value of the transferred industrial secrets or goodwill in order to allow Purchaser to fairly and successfully expand and enhance ITS’ business in Colombia.”390
Section 10.17 (e) of the SPA. Because of this statements, the Parties agreed Section 10.17 to provide for specific covenants, penalties and enforcement mechanisms intended to preserve and fairly reflect the value of the transferred industrial secrets or good will for Superior to fairly and successfully expand and enhance ITS’ business in Colombia.391
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 86-88.

Respondents maintain that Section 10.17 (b) of the SPA provides that Superior Colombia acquired all the industrial secrets and goodwill of ITS. Accordingly, Claimant agreed that they would not use any of them nor “otherwise carry out any activity that could undermine the value of these assets.”392
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 89.

Respondents add that, consequently, the Parties agreed to assume that a breach of Section 10.17(b) would exist in the event Claimant provided services to the Colombian oil and gas industry within the 2 years following the date of termination of the Employment Agreement, but that Claimant could rebut this presumption by demonstrating that it (i) was a provision of Petrodynamic Services that did not violate the covenants provided for under Section 6(a) of the SPA; or (ii) Claimants did not use the industrial secrets and goodwill acquired by Superior Colombia.393
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 90.

As for Section 10.17 (c) of the SPA, Respondents argue that this Section establishes a price reduction that would apply “without prejudice to the Seller’s and Beneficial Owners’ right to disprove the above assumption”. Therefore, Respondents assert, Superior Colombia is entitled to the reduction in either one of the following two scenarios: (i) in the event Claimant participates in the Colombian oil and gas industry within the 2 years following the date of termination of the Employment Agreement and fails to demonstrate the provision was of Petrodynamic Services and did not use ITS’ industrial secrets and goodwill or (ii) in the event Mr. Palacio breaches any covenant in Section 6(a) within the same two years. This section does not require, Respondents say, proof of any damages or that such damages resulted from the breach, rather, the mere occurrence of one or more of these actions prohibited by Section 10.17 would entitle Respondents to a reduction of the Price corresponding to when such a violation occurs during the two years following the Agreement.394
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 91-93.

Section 10.17 (d) entitles Superior Colombia to deduct from sums owed to Claimant any amount resulting from (i) the downward adjustment of the Purchase Prices pursuant to Section 10.17 (c) and/or (ii) any damages derived from the breach of the SPA. Any payment or deduction does not relieve Claimant from any of its obligations under the SPA.395
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 88.

Additionally, Respondents emphasize that Mr. Palacio’s expertise and ITS’ business development and goodwill as well as the non-competition obligations were an important part in setting the Purchase Price. The portion of the Purchase Price that Respondents specifically allocated to goodwill is, Respondents assert, set forth in the Superior Energy’s subsequent Form 10-K filing with the SEC, made on February 27, 2014 as follows:
“In March 2013, the Company acquired 100% of the equity interest in a company that provides cementing services to oil and gas companies in Colombia. This acquisition provides the Company with a platform for continued expansion in the South American market area. The Company paid approximately $20.4 million at closing and repaid $3.0 million of the acquired company’s debt. The Company will pay an additional $3.6 million over the next two years, subject to the settlement of certain liabilities. Goodwill of approximately $15.1 million was recognized as a result of this acquisition and was calculated as the excess of the consideration paid over the net assets recognized and represents estimated future economic benefits arising from other assets acquired that could not be individually identified and separately recognized. None of the goodwill related to this acquisition will be deductible for tax purposes. All of the goodwill was assigned to the Production Services segment.”396
Exhibit R-079.

Respondents’ witness Mr. Ballard testified that Superior allocated US$ 1,315,789 for the value of the non-competition agreement and US$ 2,871,000 for the value of the customer relationships brought to the deal by Mr. Palacio.397
Respondent’s Memorial of Reply ¶ 97 and Witness Statement of Mr. Ballard, ¶ 5-6.

title.it: Claimant breached covenants under Section 10.17 of the SPA

item.p:
Respondents state that Claimant breached Section 10.17 (b) and 10.17 (c) of the SPA by (i) Mr. Palacio’s violation of the covenants in Section 6 during the Employment Agreement and within the two years following its termination and (ii) providing services to the Colombian oil and gas industry within the 2 years following the date of termination of the Employment Agreement.398
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 96-100, further elaborated in Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, section II A 5 ¶ ¶ 7-80.

Respondents maintain that it is undisputed that the Non-Compete Period extends to at least, July 30, 2015, given that the Employment Agreement terminated on July 30, 2013. But, Respondents argue that it should be deemed to extend to two years after termination of the Services Agreement, in November 30, 2014. Respondents argue Mr. Palacio’s termination of the Employment Agreement was anti-competitive (in order to escape the Non-Compete), and the fact that Services Agreement substantially continued Mr. Palacio’s prior obligations and his duties and responsibility remained largely the same, maintaining his access to ITS’ confidential information, its client lists and industrial secrets, and this access ended only when Ms. Rojas took leadership of ITS’s supply chain operation.399
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 88-89 and Witness Statement of Ms. Diana Rojas, ¶ 13.

Respondents reject the Claimant’s alleged carve out of “Petrodynamic Services” from the obligation not to compete in the Colombian oil and gas industry because the SPA provides a limited definition of the “Petrodynamic Services”400
Section 1 of the SPA: “Petrodynamic Services means (i) the rental of tractors for moving the cementing units and (ii) the sale of consumable items such as float equipment and centralizers, regardless of whether provided by Petrodynamic Petroleum Services S.A.S., its affiliate (s) or any third party.” and only covers Pettodynamic’s existing business line at the moment of the SPA and any goods or services not being provided at that time are not “Petrodynamic Services”.401
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 21. More importantly, the carve out was conditioned to the compliance of Section 6 of the SPA so it does not apply to Mr. Palacio because Section 6 prohibits him from participating in the Petrodynamic Services so his breaches of this section nullify the putative carve out.402
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 90-91. Also Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 56, lines 21-25; p. 57, lines 2-11. Porter Nolan, who was involved in the negotiations confirmed this:403
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 100
“Such carve-out did not and could not apply to Palacio. The intention of this parenthetical ‘(and subject to the covenants in Section 6)’ to prime (or control) over the Petrodynamic carve-out in 10.17 is echoed by the fact that the covenant in Section 6(a) specifically and intentionally begins by stating Notwithstanding anything herein to the contrary[….]’”404
Witness Statement of Mr. Nolan, ¶ 19.

In their closing statement Respondents reiterated their argument as for the way that Section 10.17 should be interpreted. First, there is a presumption and a general rule providing that neither Mr. Palacio nor Ms. Hernández can participate in the Colombian oil and gas industry and any participation would trigger that presumption. Second, the only exception for the participation in the oil and gas industry are the Petrodynamic Services understood as defined on the SPA -rental of tractors and the sale of floating equipment and centralizers- and performed exclusively by a company owned by Ms. Hernández. Furthermore, the effect of Section 6 (a) is that (i) Mr. Palacio cannot participate in the Petrodynamic Services; (ii) any dealings between ITS and Petrodynamic must be at arms-length; and (iii) if Mr. Palacio participates in the Petrodynamic Services breaches clause 10.17, triggers the presumption and the price reduction if the presumption is not disproved.405
Tr. Day 4, 17 November 2017, p. 830, lines 11-25; p. 831, lines2-19.

According to Respondents, any participation by Claimant in the Colombian gas and oil industry during the Non-Compete Period triggers the presumption established in Section 10.17 (b) of the SPA, that is, that Superior need not prove Claimant’s breach but rather, under such circumstances, it would be Claimant’s burden to disprove the presumption that Claimant used ITS’ industrial secrets or goodwill and undermine their value.406
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 92.

Respondents claim that Mr. Palacio’s “participation in the Colombian oil and gas industry” is evidenced by the following:407
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 92. (i) on December 9, 2013, Mr. Palacio sent an e-mail on behalf of Petrodynamic that provides quotes and discuss product pickups and billing with Baker Hughes a competitor of ITS;408
Exhibits R-086 and R-095. (ii) on March 1, 2013 through July 30, 2013, Mr. Palacio prevented ITS’ supply chain employees from reviewing other suppliers and personally approved purchase orders;409
Exhibits JD-006; JD 007 and Witness Statement of Ms. Rojas, ¶ 9. (iii) on January 20, 2015, Mr. Palacio shared the Petrodynamic price list used in the 2015 bid for Pacific with Estrella International Energy Services, a competitor of ITS;410
Exhibits JD-006; JD 007; R-087 and Witness Statement of Ms. Diana Rojas, ¶ 9. (iv) on February 19, 2015, Mr. Palacio disclosed to Petrodynamic employees certain of ITS’ open orders product type and prices for Tucker Energy, a competitor of ITS;411
Exhibit R-088. (v) on April 9, 2015, Mr. Palacio provided quotes and negotiated price discounts to Petrodynamic clients, many of whom were ITS’ competitors;412
Exhibit R-089 and R-096. and (vi) on May 31, 2015, Mr. Palacio proposed cementing parts and storage locations to Shlumberger, a competitor of ITS.413
Exhibit R-090.

In addition Respondents state that during the Non-Compete Period Mr. Palacio competed with ITS, through Petrodynamic, by actively participating in oilfield services, such as cementing services, pipeline cleaning and inspection services and the sale and rental of commercialized items other than consumable items, including selling petrochemicals and renting silos (cementing equipment) and bulk and frac tanks.414
Exhibits R-097; R-098; R-099; R-100 Petrodynamic was hired by ITS’ competitors such as Maren Fox S.A. and Tucker Energy Services S.A. to provide cementing services to Pacific, namely the plug and abandonment of Pacific oil wells and sale of gravel pack tools, which were a mainstay of ITS’ business.415
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 92 and Witness Statement of Mr. Balsero II, ¶ ¶ 21-22. These services are outside the scope of the Petrodynamic Services.416
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 93-94 and exhibits R-101; R-102; R-103; R-104; R-105; R-106; R-107; R-108; R-109; R-110.

Premium also breached Section. 10.17 (b), Respondents argue, by submitting a bid for the supply of reamer shoes to Pacific within the two years following the date of termination of the Employment Agreement. On December 19, 2012, ITS entered into a Supply Contract417
No. 5500002616, exhibit R-017. with Meta Petroleum Corp., a Pacific’s subsidiary, to supply reamer shoes for casing in the operation of the Rubiales and Quifa oil fields for the years 2012-2015 (the “Pacific Supply Contract”). Upon the scheduled termination of the Pacific Supply Contract, Pacific opened a new tender for the supply of reamer shoes for the next three years, Pacific’s call for tender N° RFP 15-00315 in which ITS was invited to participate.418
Exhibit R-008.

Respondents allege that they submitted their tender by the deadline on July 3, 2015, complying with all the legal, financial and technical requirements. On February 2, 2016, ITS was notified that the contract was awarded to another bidder.419
Witness statement of Mr. Balsero, ¶ 13. ITS became aware that Petrodynamic was awarded the contract only once Petrodynamic started to supply the reamer shoes to the Pacific’s oilfields, in the same place where ITS was providing cementing services.420
Witness statement of Mr. Balsero, ¶ 11. Petrodynamic submitted its bid in June 2015 at the latest,421
Witness statement of Mr. Balsero, ¶ 9. prior to the end of the Non-Compete Period. Superior adds that Claimant has failed to disprove that Mr. Palacio participated in Petrodynamic’s bid to Pacific.422
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 105-106. Also Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 111.-115 and Witness Statement of Mr. Balsero II, ¶ ¶ 6-12.

Respondents complain that this contract and the relation with Pacific was the jewel of ITS’ assets at time of the sale, and that Mr. Palacio himself estimated that this contract resulted in ITS acquiring assets that increased the value of ITS in US$ 2,000,000.423
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio I, ¶ 11. Mr. Palacio was listed as administrator of the contract and signed it on behalf of ITS. As a direct result of this new contract, Premium claimed during the negotiations that the value of ITS increased tremendously and, accordingly, ITS became more valuable. Palacio then negotiated an increase in the purchase price of ITS by US$ 4,000,000, of which at least US$ 2,000,000 reflected an increase in value from the new 2012 Pacific contract424
Respondents’ Memorial o f Reply, ¶ ¶ 11-113.

Mr. Palacio was in a unique position, Respondents stand out, to assist Petrodynamic win the bid over ITS. While at ITS he was directly involved in the negotiations and performance of the Pacific Supply Contact, was designated to administer it,425
Pacific Supply Contract, Clause 1.12, Exhibit R-017. and all notifications from Pacific related to the Pacific Supply Contract had to be addressed to him426
Pacific Supply Contract, Clause 1.15, Exhibit R-017.. Furthermore, Mr. Palacio continued to act as ITS’ administrator and person of contact for the Pacific Supply Contract until he left ITS on November 10, 2014. Therefore, Respondents argue, Mr. Palacio was in a unique and privileged position to acquire information on ITS’ costs, profit margins, business practices and technical capacity to supply reamer shoes to Pacific under the specific terms and conditions of the Pacific Supply Contract.427
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 107-108. Respondents believe that this bid by Petrodynamic is part of a broader strategy to capture ITS’ clientele.428
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 109.

Respondents deny knowledge alleged by Claimant by Superior that there was business being done between ITS and Petrodynamic. Claimant referred to information periodically provided on mandatory forms by Superior Colombia to Superior Energy’s internal audit department. Respondents refer to the testimony of Hal Williams, head of the audit department of Superior (“Mr. Williams”), to argue that although Related Patty Reports showing business between ITS and Superior Colombia were required to be provided under a procedure put in place by Superior Energy to ensure compliance with SEC reporting requirements and applicable accounting standards, the Internal Audit Department’s role is not to check for fraud or to oversee legal or financial operations of any kind.429
Witness Statement of Mr. Williams, ¶ 11. Moreover, these reports will raise for internal audit purposes only when the reported amounts are such that they will have a material impact on the Superior group’s reporting and/or balance sheet.430
Witness Statement of Mr. Williams, ¶ 12. Also Witness Statement of Mr. Nolan, ¶ ¶ 18-24.

title.it: Claimant has the burden of proof

item.p:
Respondents state that Claimant has the burden of proof to demonstrate that Mr. Palacio did not misappropriate ITS’ assets and use its goodwill and industrial secrets. Under Colombian law, Respondents argues, Claimant must provide sufficient evidence to demonstrate the alleged facts, in accordance with the rules of reasoned judgment.431
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 84 and exhibit RL-039. Claimant is required to provide sufficient evidence for the Tribunal to find the claims demonstrated according to the “rules of experience, logic and reason.”432
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 84 and exhibit RL-040. Other doctrine provides that the standard of proof to succeed in a civil claim is that of “prevalent probability”, exhibit RL-041.

title.it: The non-compete obligations of Section 10.17 are legally enforceable under Colombian law

item.p:
Respondents argue that, contrary to Premium’s assertions, the non-compete obligations of section 10.17 are valid and enforceable under Colombian law, which provides that parties to a sales contract may validly agree to restrict the seller’s ability to compete against the purchaser in a given market. These provisions must be ancillary to a business transaction, proportional and necessary.433
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 105-106 and exhibit RL-048.

Respondents assert that Section 10.17 complies with the above requirements. The parties explicitly agreed that the non-compete provisions were necessary to “preserve and fairly reflect the value of the assets” including ITS’ industrial secrets and goodwill and to prevent any activity that would “undermind” their value. According to Mr. Ballard, Superior paid Palacio “handsomely not to compete with ITS after acquisition”, or otherwise, “Superior could have started a new business from scratch in Colombia at much lower cost.”434
Witness Statement of Mr. Ballard, ¶ 12. Also, the non-compete obligation is proportional given that applies to a specific territory and for a limited period of time and because Claimant received an increased Purchase price in order to agree to such provisions.435
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 107-108 and Witness Statement of Mr. Ballard, ¶ 12. Therefore Respondents distinguish Section 10.17 from Claimant’s interpretation of it as a “post-employment non-compete restriction” of the kind prohibited by Colombian law.436
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 109.

title.bd: Claimant did not fullfill its contractual duties of care and did not act in good faith

item.p:
Under Colombian law, Respondents argue that parties to a contract owe each other an affirmative duty to act in good faith and also have duties not to breach implied covenant of good faith437
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 42, further elaborated in Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 60-65. and moreover, managers and directors owe the company for which they work additional duties of good faith, fair dealing and loyalty.438
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 43 and exhibits RL-029; RL-030; RL-031; RL-032; RL-033 and RL-034.

Respondents complain that Mr. Palacio and Ms. Hernández breached their duties of good faith by recruiting and hiring numerous employees from ITS who went to work for Petrodynamic.439
Witness Statement of Mr. Balsero I, ¶ 13. Some of them are Nidia Gutiérrez, a key employee that handled the administrative side of cementing contracts and financial analysis;440
Witness Statement of Mr. Balsero I, ¶ 14 and Witness Statement of Mr. Balsero II, ¶ 11. Ms. Monroy, an accountant at ITS;441
Witness Statement of Mr. Balsero I, ¶ 15. Mr. Mejía, who worked at ITS’ warehouse; Fredy Sarmiento who also worked at ITS’ warehouse (“Mr. Sarmiento”) and Adriana Lorena del Pilar Roa, an accountant assistant at ITS (“Ms. Roa”).442
Witness Statement of Mr. Balsero I, ¶ 17.

In addition, Respondents complain that Petrodynamic competed directly with ITS for the new Pacific’ (Meta) tender for the supply of cementing services.443
Witness Statement of Mr. Balsero II, ¶ ¶ 16-20.

title.bd: Claimant breached the representations and warranties of the SPA and the duty to act in good faith according to Colombian law

item.p:
Respondents also argue that Claimant breached Sections 6.2 (a)444
Section. 6.2 (a) of the SPA: “Subject to the terms and conditions herein provided, each party hereto shall use its reasonable best efforts to, as promptly as practicable (i) seek all necessary waivers, consents and approvals from other parties to Material Contracts, leases and other contracts, (ii) seek all consents, approvals and authorizations that are required to be obtained under any Colombian or other foreign law or regulation, (iii) lift or rescind any injunction or restraining order or other order adversely affecting the ability of the parties hereto to consummate the transactions contemplated hereby, (iv) effect all necessary registrations and filings, including filings with the Regulatory Authorities and submissions of information requested by any Government Authority, and (v) fulfill all conditions set forth in Article 7 applicable to it. Each party hereto further shall, with respect to any threatened or pending preliminary or permanent injunction or other order, decree or ruling or statute, rule, regulation or executive order that would adversely affect the ability of the parties hereto to consummate the transactions contemplated hereby, use its reasonable best efforts to prevent the entry, enactment or promulgation thereof, as the case may be”. and 7 (d)445
Section 7 of the SPA: “Purchaser may terminate this Agreement without liability of any kind if the following conditions are not satisfied by Seller or waived by Purchaser at or prior to the Closing Date: (d) Representations and Warranties. The representations and warranties of Seller, Broxton and ITS contained herein shall be true and correct in all respects as of the date of this Agreement and must be true and correct in all respect as of the Closing Date. Purchaser shall have received a certificate dated as of the Closing Date from Seller executed by Seller Representative by and on behalf of Seller and by an Executive officer of ITS with respect to the matters described in this Sections 7.1.” of the. SPA446
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ ¶ 95-96. and did not act in good faith in pre-contractual disclosure obligations under Colombian law during the negotiation of the SPA and due diligence process. Respondents argue that Premium violated the covenant to act in good faith under article 1603 of the Colombian Civil Code447
Exhibit RL-003. and article 863 of Colombian Commercial Code448
Exhibit RL-004., respectively, arguing that under Colombian law incomplete disclosure, affirmative misrepresentations, and failure to correct material omissions are all indicators of failure to act in good faith.449
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ ¶ 99-102.

Respondents describe the pre-contractual negotiations and due diligence beginning on October 2012 until the closing of the SPA on Match 1, 2013. On October 8, 2012, Superior sent to Premium and Mr. Palacio a due diligence checklist prepared by its legal counsel Baker hsihtasamp; McKenzie S.A.S. (“Baker McKenzie”) which included a request for a summary description “of all relationships with the shareholders of the Company (or companies affiliated with the shareholders)”450
Exhibit R-009. and Claimant did not reply to this particular section.451
Witness Statement of Mr. Trujillo, ¶ 4. On November 9, 2012, Baker McKenzie sent a second checklist452
Exhibit R-ll and Witness Statement of Mr. Trujillo, ¶ 5. with the same request and Premium answered on November 13, 2012, “N/A” and “No existen otras compañías del grupo.”453
Exhibit R-12; Witness Statement of Mr. Nolan I, ¶ 10; Witness Statement of Mr. Trujillo, ¶ ¶ 6-7 and Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ ¶ 103-106. On November 28, 2012, Baker McKenzie prepared a third information request and did not receive a response.454
Exhibit R-13 and Witness Statement of Mr. Trujillo, ¶ 8. The negotiations continued in November, December of 2012 and January and early February of 2013 time in which Claimant did not disclose, Respondents allege, the existence of Petrodynamic and its relation with Mr. Palacio or Ms. Hernández.

Respondents claim that they only learned that Petrodynamic was part of an affiliated455
Affiliate is defined in Section 1 of the SPA: “Affiliate (and, with a correlative meaning, “Affiliated”) shall mean, with respect to any Person, any other Person that directly, or through one or more intermediaries, controls or is controlled by or is under common control with such Person, and, if such a Person is an individual, any member of the immediate family (including parents, spouse and children) of such individual…” group that owned ITS only a few days prior to the closing of the SPA. On February 22, 2013, six days before the execution of the SPA, Claimant sent back a list of deliverables stating that there were no affiliates.456
Exhibit R-020 and Witness Statement of Mr. Nolan I, ¶ 12. But on February 25, 2013, three days later and only three days before the execution of the SPA, Claimant sent a portion of the disclosure schedule titled “Section 4.14 Transactions with Affiliates” which disclosed only that there was a vehicle lease agreement between ITS and Petrodynamic, but made no mention of the facts that Premium and the Additional Parties were the owners and operated Petrodynamic or that Petrodynamic sold additional goods, products, equipment or services to ITS.457
Exhibit R-021 and Witness Statement of Mr. Nolan. I, ¶ ¶ 13-14. Respondents’ Memorial of Rejoinder, ¶ 5 (d)-(f).

Respondents add that on February 26, 2013, two days before the Closing Date, Premium sent back the same checklist noting Petrodynamic as an affiliate for the first time.458
Exhibit R-014 and Witness Statement of Mr. Trujillo, ¶ 9. On the same day, Claimant sent proposed changes to the SPA inserting references to Petrodynamic and adding an exception to the non-compete provisions in Sections 10.17 (b) and 10. 17 (c).459
Exhibit R-022. Superior asked for additional information about Petrodynamic and its relation with ITS and the Additional Parties,460
Exhibit R-015. but Claimant did not send all the relevant information requested,461
Witness Statement of Mr. Nolan I, ¶ 17. and merely sent Petrodynamic’s certificate of existence and legal representation in which Ms. Hernández appear as sole legal representative.462
Exhibit R-016 and Witness Statement of Mr. Trujillo, ¶ 10.

Respondents submit that in response to Superior’s inquires, on February 26, 2013, Claimant only informed that Petrodynamic sold floating equipment and centralizers to ITS and the competitors San Antonio and Baker and that had a lease agreement with ITS. On the same day, Claimant also informed that Ms. Hernández owned Petrodynamic but said nothing about the relation between Petrodynamic and Mr. Palacio.463
Exhibit R-077 and Respondents’ Memorial of Rejoinder, ¶ 5 (g)-(k).

In reaction to the disclosures Respondents explain that some modifications were incorporated in the final version of the SPA: (i) The words “Petrodynamic Services” were included as a defined term in Section 1 of the SPA; (ii) Section 6(a) was included; and (iii) Section 10.17(b) and (c) now added the following terms: “[e]xcept for the Petrodynamic Services (and subject to the covenants in Section 6).”

According to Respondents, adherence with these provisions would have requited Claimant to disclose the all business dealings between Petrodynamic and ITS but failed to do so, and Claimant therefore breached the SPA as soon as it was signed on March 1, 2013.464
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 109. Respondents add that Section 10.11 states that Claimant and Additional Parties are jointly liable for all contractual purposes, and Section 10.12 says representations, warranties, covenants and obligations of Premium under the SPA are deemed to be made also by each of the Additional Parties465
Section 10.12 of the SPA. and therefore that they are jointly and severally liable466
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaims, ¶ ¶ 36-37 and Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 125-126. for the breaches of the representations and warranties.

Respondents rebuts Claimant and Additional Parties’ defense that Pettodynamic’s relation with ITS was “generally known… throughout the relevant time period”467
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 9. and Mr. Palacio’s assertion that they “discussed with Superior the relationship between Petrodynamic and ITS”468
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 14. stating that there is no evidence for these conclusions. Claimant never disclosed that Mr. Palacio was one of the owner and operators of Petrodynamic or even that he was involved in that company. On the contrary, Respondents argue that Claimant and the Additional Parties omitted information and affirmatively misrepresented their ownership and roles in Petrodynamic.469
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 45-46. If they had disclosed it, the Purchase Price would have been lower given the conflict of interest considering that Superior paid Additional Parties not to compete with ITS as part of said Purchase Price.470
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 44 and Witness Statement of West Ballard, ¶ 12. Also Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 121-127.

Respondents argue that it was not in good faith for Mr. Palacio to delegate responsibility (as Mr. Palacio says he did with Ms. Monroy in providing responses to the due diligence questionnaires) because delegation cannot absolve Mr. Palacio of his legal and good faith obligations and duties to refrain from making misrepresentations. Respondents also argue that the required good faith disclosures were not made when, during the due diligence process, Mr. Palacio’s counsel made available to Superior’s counsel a truck rental agreement between ITS and Petrodynamic. Although the truck rental agreement identifies Ms. Hernández as the legal representative of Petrodynamic,471
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 12. the agreement made no mention of Mr. Palacio. Also, Respondents argue that good faith is not fulfilled by providing disclosure in one contract buried in a data room.472
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 47-48. Also Tr. Day 4, 17 November 2017, p. 840, lines 6-22.

title.bd: Mr. Palacio breached the Employment Agreement and the Services Agreement

item.p:
Respondents’ position is that Mr. Palacio breached non-compete and confidentiality obligations contained in the Employment Agreement and the Consultant Agreement.473
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 128-129. As for the Employment Agreement, it required that while Mr. Palacio was an employee he was required to observe all ITS codes and policies, which include Superior’s Code of Ethics.474
Section 3 of the Employment Agreement He was also required to adhere to a confidentiality clause:
“All the information that may come to his knowledge related with the matters and businesses of the Company and in express form, he undertakes to maintain in the performance of his functions and outside them, the discretion, reserve and secrecy that the loyalty he owes to The Company…at all times, even after the termination of the employment agreement.”475
Section 3 of the Employment Agreement.

Respondents state that the Employment Agreement did not permit Mr. Palacio to “render services directly or indirectly to other employers or work on his account.”476
Section 2 of the Employment Agreement.

Respondents argue that the Consulting Agreement, entered into following the Employment Agreement, imposed upon Mr. Palacio the obligation to maintain “absolute discretion and confidentiality of the information that he becomes aware of by any means about the activities performed by [ITS] under penalty of breach of contract, and take responsibility for the damages that may be caused by this conduct.”477
Section 3 (g) of the Consultant Agreement. He was also prohibited from entering into contracts with ITS clients without prior written agreement of ITS.478
Section 2 (f) of the Consultant Agreement.

Respondents also argue479
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 130-131. that Palacio breached the Consulting Agreement’s confidentiality clause, lasting for three years after termination of the Consulting Agreement,480
Section 9 of the Services Agreement, (“[Palacio] specially undertakes to refrain from using, for its personal benefit…any knowledge obtained in connection with the activities, plans, programs, products or strategies of [ITS] or the information and documents to which it may have bad access throughout the performance of the services.) and the covenant481
Section 9 of the Services Agreement. that Palacio would act in good faith and with loyalty as “essential principles” in the employment relationship.

Respondents conclude that Mr. Palacio breached the Employment Agreement and Services Agreement by (i) failing to maintain confidentiality of ITS’ industrial secrets and client lists and (ii) failing to act in good faith as manager and employee of ITS.482
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 133.

Claimant and the Additional Parties highlight some facts regarding the origin of Petrodynamic. Claimant rely upon the testimony of Mr. Palacio and Ms. Hernández that the two of them formed Petrodynamic in 2011 to serve as a distributor of products and equipment because the products offered by certain competitors, such as Halliburton and Weatherford were very expensive.

They decided to set it up as a separate entity from ITS because competitors would not buy directly from ITS.483
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 8; Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 5 and Witness Statement of Ms. Hernández I, ¶ 5. During 2012, Petrodynamic’s business expanded and added customers and the services of distribution of parts and rent of storage tanks. Because of its multiple customers in Colombia, Petrodynamic was able to acquire consumable prices at the cheapest puces.484
Witness Statement of Ms. Hernández I, ¶ 9.

title.bd: Breach of Section 6 of the SPA

item.p:
In its closing statement, Claimant addresses Respondents’ allegations brought during the Hearing that Mr. Palacio participated on the Petrodynamic Services on the first working day after the execution of the SPA by becoming an indirect owner of Petrodynamic through Premium. Ms. Hernandez testified that she wanted to transfer money from Premium to Petrodynamic, both companies owned by her, but she used the wrong bank form, one that is for loans made to the company. However, that form carried a penalty of US$ 1,600,000 so she consulted with her attorneys and was told by them that it was proper and legal to submit a second form in place of the first, characterizing the funds received not as a loan but as an investment from Premium.485
Tr. Day 4, 17 November 2017, p. 784, lines 4-18.

Mr. Palacio also contradicts Superior’s allegations that he acted on behalf of Petrodynamic with ITS’ clients. He states that he occasionally used his relationships with the people at Petrodynamic to advance the interests of Superior (whose employees asked for help) and its customers, but not to put the interests of Petrodynamic over Superior. As for the senders of the e-mails provided by Superior, apparently many of them were simply mistaken about Mr. Palacio’s involvement with Petrodynamic due to his relationship with Ms. Hernández or previous interactions with him before the sale of ITS.486
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ ¶ 34-35.

Claimant and the Additional Parties rebut Respondents’ allegation concerning the relation between Mr. Palacio and Mr. Sierra from Joalsiar. The document attached to the referred e-mail was a favor asked by Mr. Sierra so that Joalsiar could show Bancolombia that it had a contract with Petrodynamic. As previously told to Mr. Daves, Mr. Palacio declined to sign the document and that agreement never existed between with Joalsiar.487
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 15; Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ ¶ 37-38 and JD-011. In addition, Joalsiar was not API certified so ITS did not buy from it. The suggestion that non-API certified parts bought from Joalsiar and sold to ITS as API certified items is not true because manufacturers brand their equipment as API certified, and this practice would have been noticed by Superior.488
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 16 and Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 39.

Mr. Palacio also denies the allegation reported by Mr. Daves that he instructed ITS’ personnel to buy from Petrodynamic or that he prevented ITS’ employees to review other suppliers. For instance, before the sale, ITS purchased from Petrodynamic certain chemicals used in the cementation process and after Superior Colombia’s stopped purchasing them from Petrodynamic.489
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio III, ¶ 27.

Claimant and the Additional Parties submit that Superior Colombia reached out to Mr. Palacio on various times to seek his assistance in securing price discounts from Petrodynamic and to facilitate the prompt delivery of the equipment required by Superior Colombia and that Mr. Palacio complied with Superior Colombia’s requirements.490
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ 13. These actions make clear that the parties understood that Section 6(a) of the SPA prohibited Mr. Palacio from making decisions regarding the prices at which ITS would buy from Petrodynamic, but did not proscribe Mr. Palacio from acting on behalf of Petrodynamic, whether to arrange for discounts and deliveries requested by ITS or otherwise.491
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ 14.

Claimant’s witness Mr. Villamarín states that after the Closing date ITS was able to purchase floating equipment at the lowest prices in Colombia for the specific type of equipment needed by it Mr. Villamarín hired Mr. Bula and on 2014 instructed him to investigate the prices and see if it was possible to buy floating equipment and lower prices than the prices of Petrodynamic, and Mr. Bula reported that Petrodynamic’s prices were the lowest prices available in Colombia for the products that were API certified.492
Witness Statement of Mr. Villamarín, ¶ ¶ 9-13. ITS continued to buy equipment through Petrodynamic as late as June 2015, after Superior notified Claimant that it would not pay the Second Holdback Amount.493
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 10-11; Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 32 and exhibit C-29.

According to Claimant and the Additional Parties, a comparison of pre-Closing invoices with post-Closing purchase orders demonstrates that Petrodynamic charged ITS less for certain API certified equipment and items after the Closing than before.494
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 12; Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 27 and exhibits C-14 and C-15. The items set forth in Superior Colombia’s analysis, Reamer Shoes 7” from API certified manufacturers, Premium charged ITS US$ 8,700 before the Closing but only US$ 6,900 or less after the Closing. Thus, when making a fair comparison before and after the Closing, ITS actually paid US$ 343,250 less than it would have paid if Petrodynamic had simply continued to charge ITS the same price.495
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 12; Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 28. In total, and according to the updated spreadsheet that Mr. Palacio once provided to Superior show savings of more than US$ 2,000,000 through February 2015.496
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 13 Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 31 and exhibit C-23.

Mr. Palacio rejects Mr. Daves’ allegation that the items sold by Petrodynamic from ITS are not API certified. He testified that he asked people from Petrodynamic to send him photographs of various pieces of flotation equipment for the Arbitral Tribunal to visualize the brands and that those photographs led him to conclude that the products were API certified.497
Exhibit C-96 and Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio III, ¶ 38.

Mr. Palacio further contests Mr. Daves assertions that some of the invoices used by him had no relation with the business relation between ITS and Petrodynamic and that they allegedly belong to unrelated companies. As for Invoice N° 0048498
Exhibit C-16. Mr. Palacio explains that it is addressed to “Consorcio Tiet Colombia Ltda-Ingenería y Teconología de Servicios”. Consorcio Tiet Colombia Ltda. is a Venezuelan company that had a joint venture arrangement with ITS at the time and bought the reamer shoes of that invoice together.499
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio III, ¶ 37.

Furthermore, Mr. Palacio argues that the interviews conducted by Mr. Daves and his colleague were entirely in Spanish, and Mr. Daves does not speak Spanish, so the interview notes are not reliable. In particular, Mr. Palacio denies having said that he understood that the Employment Agreement did not allow him to work for other companies; that after the sale he kept on buying locally made flotation equipment, and the reasons Mr. Daves states as why Mr. Palacio refused to sign the agreement with Joalsiar. He says that all these misunderstanding are attributable to translation issues.500
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio III, ¶ 40-43. He also denies the meaning given my Mr. Daves understanding of the handwritten notes or that he ever discussed a tax plan concerning ITS and Petrodynamic.501
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio III, ¶ 45-46.

Claimant affirms that under Superior’s policy of conflict of interest, Superior Colombia’s manager had the ability to wave conflicts502
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ 7. because Superior Colombia’s Code of Ethics expressly state that “[t]he company prohibits all conflict of interest unless specifically approved by the Company’s General Manager.”503
Exhibit R-091. In its closing statement, Claimant argued that Mr. Villamarín testified504
Witness Statement of Mr. Villamarín, ¶ 8. that Mr. Cervo explained to Mr. Villamarín the relationship between Mr. Palacio, Ms. Hernández, and Petrodynamic and that the arrangement of the relationship between them was approved by Superior.505
Tr. Day 4, 17 November 2017, p. 791, lines 9-25; p. 792, lines 2-25.

Claimant argues that the Petrodynamic business with Superior Colombia was not concealed but instead reported to Superior Energy, that on a quarterly basis, ITS gave to Superior Energy’s internal audit department a report (the related party transactions report required by Superior Energy) demonstrating ITS’s monthly business volume with Petrodynamic.506
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ 7 and exhibit C-97.

title.bd: Breach of Section 10.17 of the SPA

item.p:
Claimant and the Additional Parties claim that Petrodynamic did not use the industrial secrets and goodwill of ITS to set the prices of the equipment sold to ITS and that the information was based on the prices charged by competitors and of certified equipment. Petrodynamic was in the business of selling floating equipment in Colombia before the Closing Date and Superior did not purchase the industrial secrets necessary for that business. Moreover, the fact that certain old customers occasionally sent an e-mail to Mr. Palacio which we simply forwarded to Petrodynamic did not constitute the use of ITS’ industrial secret or goodwill.507
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 14; Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 40 and exhibit C-26.

Claimant and the Additional Parties state that Section 6 of the SPA only imposed upon Mr. Palacio an obligation to remain out of the business between ITS and Petrodynamic. Specifically, Mr. Palacio agreed that while he was managing ITS’ business, its dealing with Petrodynamic would be at arms-length and Mr. Palacio would not be involved in the decision-making process. Mr. Palacio testified that he abided by the prohibition in the SPA to avoid any involvement in the relationship between ITS and Petrodynamic so that ITS’ decisions about the equipment and services it was acquiring from Petrodynamic would be made at arms-length,508
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ ¶ 21-22. and thus did not violate the non-compete provisions of the SPA. Mr. Palacio also testified that he did not violate the non-compete provisions of the Employment Agreement,509
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 20 and ¶ 2 of the Employment Agreement. which only imposed upon him a duty not to work for Petrodynamic during the time of his employment.510
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 20.
