In addition, Claimant and the Additional Parties contend that Section 10.17 of the SPA addressed the fact that Petrodynamic was a vendor used by ITS by excluding Pettodynamic’s existing business line from the scope of the covenant not to compete.511
Sections 10.17 and definitions of the SPA. This Section also states that Superior Colombia was purchasing the industrial secrets and goodwill of ITS, but Claimant contends that Superior’s counterclaims do not come from these assets. Petrodynamic did not need them to set the prices of the equipment sold to ITS and later to Superior Colombia and the necessary information came for the prices charged by competitors and of certified products.512
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 40.

In its closing statement, Claimant and the Additional Parties underline the first phrase of Section 10.17 (c) of the SPA that provides “[w]ithout prejudice to the Sellers’ and Beneficial Owners’ right to disprove the above presumption” and conclude that they have disproved the presumption since there is no way that Ms. Hernández and Mr. Palacio used any industrial secrets or good will of ITS.513
Tr. Day 4, 17 November 2017, p. 816, lines 9-24.

As for the bid of the Pacific Supply Contract, Claimant and the Additional Patties reject Respondents allegations regarding the reamer shoes contract awarded by Pacific to Petrodynamic. Mr. Palacio testified that an e-mail sent from Pacific to Petrodynamic in April 2016 summarizing the results shows that eight companies were involved in the bid process and that ITS’ bid did not pass because it failed to comply with the technical requirements.514
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 17 and Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 36 Also, they allege that reamer shoes are considered by the industry as floating equipment and the sale of floating equipment by Petrodynamic was specifically excluded form Section 10.17 of the SPA.515
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio I, ¶ 28. In addition Mr. Palacio testified that Claimant and the Additional Parties did not rely on industrial secrets to submit the winning bid.516
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 5.

Ms. Hernández testified that she was the one that obtained this bid, although she acknowledged that she was unable to locate the e-mail delivering the invitation that would confirm her testimony. In addition, she says that on June 2010, ITS stopped using Petrodynamic as a supplier. Thus, Petrodynamic’s submission of the bid would have necessarily been based on selling reamer shoes obtained from a different supplier. Accordingly, any information that Petrodynamic or Ms. Hernández had with respect to reamer shoes ITS has obtained from Petrodynamic was outdated in July 2015 and irrelevant with respect to the bidding process.517
Witness Statement of Ms. Hernández III, ¶ ¶ 16-17.

Furthermore, Mr. Palacio explains that when he resigned in July 2013, ITS was working on a bid to provide cementation services to Pacific, not for the sale of reamer shoes, due on August 8, 2013. Mr. Palacio assisted ITS in this bid518
Exhibit R-075. to give continuity to ITS’ employees519
Exhibit R-073. and it was one of the two companies that prevailed in the bid process.520
Witness Statement of Mr, Palacio III, ¶ ¶ 16-17. As for the reamer show contract, it ended on its own terms on December 2015 or January 2016 when ITS had already stopped purchasing from Petrodynamic.521
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio III, ¶ 19.

In addition, Claimant and the Additional Parties assert that Respondents misunderstand the differences between the contracts negotiated by Mr. Palacio on behalf of ITS with Pacific. On one hand, there is Contract N° 5500002616 dated December 19, 2012, for the sale of reamer shoes522
Exhibit R-017. and, on the other hand, there is Contract N° 5500002450 dated January 9, 2013 for the provision of cementing services.523
Exhibit R-018. Respondents incorrectly state that Mr. Palacio himself estimated that the 2012 contract N° 5500002616 was very lucrative and, because of that contract, the value of ITS pre-Closing Date raised by US$ 4,000,000, which finally settled the Purchase Price.524
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 113. When Mr. Palacio actually said that he was referring to Contract N° 5500002450 for cementing services and not the contract for the sale of reamer shoes, which Superior Colombia lost in 2015 for technical reasons. Indeed, the 2013 Cementation Contract involved the core business of ITS and had a maximum value of US$ 30,741,473.70. Conversely, the 2012 Reamer Shoe Contract involved only the sale of parts and had a maximum value of US$ 3,174,820.80 and was not “very lucrative”.525
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio III, ¶ ¶ 10-12. Also Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ 6.

In its opening statement, Claimant and the Additional Parties emphasize that Superior Colombia paid US$ 28,000,000 on a company that had over US$ 60,000,000 in contracts for cementing services and only US$ 4,000,000 in contracts for the sale of reamer shoes. Furthermore, there is only one contract in the record with respect to ITS selling only reamer shoes and not as part of the provision of cementing services.526
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 12, lines 10-20.

In respect of the Non-Compete Period under the SPA, Claimant and the Additional Parties argue that a general rule under Colombian law is that contracts that directly or indirectly limit the production, supply, distribution or consumption of goods or services, and in general all kinds of practices, are prohibited527
Exhibit CL-9. because these types of agreements are contrary to free competition.528
Exhibit CL-10. This includes any agreement preventing a particular person from participating in a given market, a non-compete.529
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 18. However Claimant acknowledges that the Colombian Superintendency of Industry and Trade has determined that non-compete provisions are justified under Colombian law where they are necessary to a business transaction.530
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 19 and exhibit CL-011.

Furthermore, Claimant and the Additional Parties submit that postemployment non-compete restrictions are prohibited under the Colombian Constitution:
Work is a right and a social obligation and in all its forms enjoys the special protection of the state. Every person is entitled to a job under dignified and equitable conditions.531
Article 25, exhibit CL-12.
…
Every person is free to choose a profession or occupation. The law may require certificates of competence. The competent authorities will inspect and supervise the exercise of the professions.
Occupations, the arts, and work that do not require academic training are to be freely exercised, except for those which involve a risk to society.532
Article 26, exhibit CL-13.
…
Economic activity and private initiative must not be impeded within the limits of the public good. No one may require permits or licenses to exercise economic activity except when authorized by law.533
Article 333, exhibit CL-14.

Claimant and the Additional Parties explain that under Colombian law it is perfectly permissible for an individual to compete with their former employer when he is no longer an employee. Following the termination of the Employment Agreement, Mr. Palacio entered into a consulting agreement with ITS and was no longer an employee of ITS, but rather was acting as an independent professional.534
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 24. Mr. Palacio focused his efforts on business development, and occasionally used his relationships with the people at Petrodynamic to advance the interests of ITS and its customers.535
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 34. Through his relationship with Petrodynamic and by getting the lowest prices in Colombia, Mr. Palacio increased ITS’ business. Thus, according to Claimant, Superior Colombia received the full value of the assets it acquired from Premium.536
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 25.

Claimant and the Additional Parties content that Superior Colombia is not entitled to damages under the penalty clause. The Colombian Civil Code provides that “[h]aving clear knowledge of the intention of the contracting parties, one must adhere to it more than to the literality of the words”537
Article 1618 of Colombian Civil Code, exhibit RL-043. and that the clauses of a contract may “be interpreted by reference to those in another contract between the same parties and regarding the same subject matter. Or by the practical application that both parties, or one of the parties with the approval of the other party, have made of them.”538
Article 1623 of Colombian Civil Code, exhibit RL-043. Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ 11.

Claimant and the Additional Parties assert that the provisions of the SPA should be construed in that “...subsequent actions of the parties carried out during the performance of the contract, provided that such practical and concordant performance is carried out by both parties, or by only one of them with the acquiescence of the other”539
Exhibit RL-044., and that “[I]n case of discrepancy in the meaning of a contract, the Court warns that the judge should not limit himself to the text of the contract, but examine all the elements that allow the determination of the real intention of the parties, taking into account the practical results sought by them in celebrating the legal business.”540
Exhibit RL-045. Claimant’s Memorial of Rejoinder, ¶ 12.

Although Respondents urge the Tribunal to consider that the Non-Compete Period starts at the termination of the Services Agreement, not the Employment Agreement, Mr. Palacio rebuts this argument. Firstly, he states that he did not merely “switch” his title, he resigned it, terminated the Employment Agreement, and entered into the Services Agreement, with a new and more limited set of responsibilities and a more limited “non-compete” clause.541
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio III, ¶ 29. Secondly, even the shorthand phrase of “non-compete” is not actually accurate, he contends, because he agreed not to engage in unfair competition and unfair trade practices, thus not to use any industrial secrets and goodwill of ITS, but did not otherwise agree not to compete,542
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio III, ¶ 30. Third, the SPA is specific and provide that the two year period starts at the termination of the Employment Agreement.543
Section 10.17 (b) of the SPA AND Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio III, ¶ 31. Lastly, Mr. Palacio asserts that he was transparent with Superior in telling them from the moment of his decision that the reason for his resignation was to begin the Non-Compete Period, thus, he contends he would not have entered in the Services Agreement if that would have stopped or delayed the Non-Compete Period from elapsing.544
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio III, ¶ 31.

According to Claimant and the Additional Parties, Superior’s argument about goodwill is internally inconsistent and legally flawed. First, Mr. Ballard, quotes from Superior Energy’s public filing, which told its public shareholders that the goodwill recorded in relation to the acquisition of ITS “represents estimated future economic benefits arising from other assets acquired that could not be individually identified and separately recognized.”545
Witness Statement of Mr. Ballard, ¶ 5. In the next paragraph, Superior Energy was in fact able to individually identify and separately recognize the value of “non-competition agreement with Mr. Palacio” and “value of the customer relationships brought to the deal by Mr. Palacio.”546
Witness Statement of Mr. Ballard, ¶ 6. But Superior has not explained how it was possible to allocate value to something that could not be identified and recognized. They also failed to offer any sort of evidentiary support for Mr. Ballard’s statement.547
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ ¶ 24-26.

Furthermore, Claimant points out that Superior claims different values for the same items. Mr. Ballard claims that “we allocated $1,315,789 for the value of the non-competition agreement with Mr. Palacio and $2,871,000 for the value of the customer relationships brought to the deal by Mr. Palacio”548
Witness Statement of Mr. Ballard, ¶ 6. while Superior claims that it “allocated $1,363,202 for the value of the non-competition agreement with Mr. Palacio and $3,243,000 for the value of the customer relationships brought to the deal by Mr. Palacio.”549
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 117. Superior offers no support for the use of goodwill to establish a penalty clause. When an acquisition occurs, the Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) requires that any excess of the purchase price over the fair value of the assets acquired and the liabilities assumed be reported as goodwill as an accounting concept.550
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ ¶ 27-28.

title.bd: Contractual duties of care and good faith

item.p:
Claimant rejects Respondents’ allegation, concerning Mr. Palacio’s lack of good faith. The doctrine of good faith requires that: “[G]ood faith must be present throughout the contract… including the performance of the same… [T]o assess whether a particular subject acted in good faith it is imperative to examine… the conduct it deployed, but in an integral way, that is, as a whole.,,”551
Exhibit RL-036. The actions of the Parties in performing their obligations under the SPA make clear that Mr. Palacio’s actions in facilitating the discounts and deliveries requested by ITS were in accord with the mandates of the SPA.552
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ ¶ 22-23.

Also, Claimant deny assertions made by Mr. Balsero that, after the closing, Mr. Palacio and Ms. Hernández recruited personnel from the former ITS to work in Petrodynamic specifically Mr. Sarmiento, Ms., Monroy, Mr. Mejia, Ms. Gutiérrez and Ms. Roa. Ms. Hernández explains that Freddy Sarmiento never worked for Petrodynamic, Ms. Monroy and Mr. Mejía communicated with Superior while working in Petrodynamic with no concerns ever raised by Superior, Ms. Gutiérrez stopped working on ITS in April 2016 and then went to study to Canada and Ms. Ariana Lorena del Pilar left ITS and left it to work at a company called Quala and then she began to work in Petrodynamic.553
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ 8 and Witness Statement of Ms. Hernández III, ¶ ¶ 12-15. Also Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 19, lines 18-24.

title.bd: Breach of representations and warranties of the SPA

item.p:
Claimant cites the testimony of Mr. Palacio that there was no plan to divert profit from ITS554
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 26. to Petrodynamic and the testimony of Mr. Villamarín that the relationship with Petrodynamic was generally known by the relevant people in Superior.555
Witness Statement of Mr. Villamarín, ¶ 8. Moreover, Mr. Palacio testified that he offered during the negotiations that Petrodynamic would not do business with ITS to avoid any conflict of interest, but Superior refused because it was interested in getting the necessary equipment at the lowest price available.556
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 9 and Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 14.

In their closing statement Claimant and the Additional Parties state that, as explained by Ms. Hernández, in January 2012, long before Superior came along, she created Petrodynamic and tried to establish this company as a distributor in Colombia by contacting API certified manufacturers such as CTE.557
See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 237 and 507-508. This was before the sale of ITS and was not a part of a tax plan, as Mr. Daves alleged in his testimony. Ms. Hernández would not have gone through all this if API certified items were not really required.558
Tr. Day 4, 17 November 2017, p. 800, lines 2-14.

Claimant and the Additional Parties reject Respondents’ allegations that the Additional Parties affirmatively represented to Superior that they had no affiliates companies. Mr. Palacio states that he is an engineer and not a corporate lawyer and that this was the first time being involved in the sale of a company. He delegated in Ms. Monroy the task of providing the attorneys with the documents and information that Respondents requested.559
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ ¶ 10-11. Mr. Palacio adds that a lease agreement was made available in the data room which clearly identifies Ms. Hernández as the legal representative of Petrodynamic.560
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 12.

Moreover, Mr. Palacio clarifies that Premium tried to provide Superior and Baker McKenzie everything that they requested. No one ever asked directly if any of the Additional Parties owned any other business in the oil and gas industry and if someone had asked he would have told them about Petrodynamic.561
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio III, ¶ 21.

title.bd: Breach of the Employment Agreement and the Services Agreement

item.p:
Claimant and the Additional Parties submit that the Tribunal should view the provisions of the SPA in the context of “the reality in which the parties are placed at the time of performing their obligations”.562
Exhibit RL-050. To properly assess the reality of the Parties’ performance under the SPA, the Tribunal should consider three major periods: (i) the employment period from March 1, 2013, to July 30, 2013; (ii) the consulting period, from August 1, 2013, to November 2014; and (iii) the final period which ends on July, 30, 2015. Claimant argues that in doing so, the Tribunal should view the provisions of the SPA in the context of “the reality in which the parties are placed at the time of performing their obligations.”563
Exhibit RL-050. Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ ¶ 16, 17 and 20.

On the first period, Claimant describes that Mr. Palacio was subject to the Employment Agreement. He acted as general manager while Superior hired a country manager, and thus, there was no higher-ranking employee who could act independently with respect to Petrodynamic. Mr. Palacio did not have any involvement in the business of Petrodynamic because that was dictated by the Employment Agreement and the general duties of an employee to his employer under Colombian law.564
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ 17.

During the second period, Claimant says that Mr. Palacio was no longer bound by the Employment Agreement, rejecting Superior’s argument that the Consulting Agreement should be deemed an extension of his employment. Claimant argues that the Consulting Agreement makes abundantly clear that Mr. Palacio is not an employee of ITS but rather is independent. Accordingly, the general obligations of an employee to his employer were not applicable. Mr. Palacio, nevertheless, understood that he would not provide his business development services to any competitor of ITS. With full knowledge that Ms. Hernández owned Petrodynamic, Superior Colombia did not ask that the Consulting Agreement restrict Mr. Palacio’s activity with respect to Petrodynamic.565
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ 17, Witness statement of Mr. Palacio III, ¶ 18, Witness Statement of Mr. Villamarín ¶ ¶ 8-11 and exhibit C-13. Mr. Villamarín and Mr. Bula repeatedly reached out to Mr. Palacio to act on behalf of Petrodynamic for the benefit of ITS, for instance, on or about September 2013, Mr. Villamarín discussed with Mr. Palacio obtaining a discount from Petrodynamic with respect to flotation equipment.566
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ ¶ 18-19, further elaborated on Claimant’s Memorial of Reply ¶ ¶ 58-62. See Final Award, ¶ 216.

In the third period, after the Consulting Agreement, Claimant alleges that Mr. Palacio had not been involved in ITS’ operations or Superior’s business for 16 months. Ms. Rojas and Mr. Bula had brought order to the chaos that had been ITS’ procurement processes and needs. Any knowledge Mr. Palacio may have had regarding ITS’ previous procurement procedures, therefore, was outdated and could not be used by Mr. Palacio to his advantage or to ITS’ or Superior Colombia’s detriment.567
Witness Statement of Ms, Rojas, ¶ ¶ 7-12. Pursuant to the Colombia Civil Code, Mr. Palacio was free to compete as he was no longer subject to any non-competition restrictions arising from either the Employment Agreement or the Consulting Agreement. ITS’ determination to stop purchasing equipment and materials from Petrodynamic had nothing to do with any competition between ITS and Petrodynamic and Superior, rather, determined that in light of the claims between the parties, it could not continue to do business with Petrodynamic, notwithstanding the clear business advantages for ITS to continue procuring equipment from Petrodynamic.568
Claimant’s Memorial or Rejoinder, ¶ ¶ 20-21.
In order to decide Respondents’ counterclaims, the Tribunal must determine whether there has been a breach of the SPA and a violation of Colombian law by Claimant.

As a starting point, Respondents assert that Claimant had breached the SPA when they sent the First Claim Notice to retain the Second Holdback Amount. In fact, Superior Colombia expressly stated that such notice was made “pursuant to section 2.2(c), Section 8.2 and Section 8.5” of the SPA569
Exhibit R-007 and Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 75. and also relied on Section 10.17 of the same agreement.570
Exhibit R-031. Further, when describing the basis for its claim, Superior Colombia also indicated that the “Key Individual breached the covenants in Section 6(a) of the Agreement causing Purchaser Damages to Purchased”.571
Exhibit R-007.

Respondents’ position is that Claimant breached (i) the material covenants in Section 6(a) of the SPA; (ii) the material obligations in Section 10.17 of the SPA; (iii) the covenants to act in good faith under Colombian law in the contractual and pre-contractual period of the SPA; (iv) Section 6.2 (a) and Section 7 (d) of the SPA concerning representation and warranties; and (v) the non-compete and confidentiality requirements under the Employment Agreement and the Services Agreement.572
See Final Award, ¶ 306.

Thus, in addressing Claimant and the Additional Parties’ alleged breaches of the SPA, the Tribunal will deal with the each of Respondents’ claims in the following order: (i) breach of Section 6(a) of the SPA, (ii) breach of Section 10.17 of the SPA; (iii) violation of the duty of care and good faith and breach of representation and warranties; and (iv) breach of the Employment and Services Agreement.

title.bd: Breach of Section 6(a) of the SPA

item.p:
The SPA was signed on March 1, 2013.573
The First Amendment of the SPA entered between the Parties on January 21, 2014 and the Second Amendment on June, 2016. Section 6 (a) establishes a covenant which, in essence, prevents Mr. Palacio from participating in Petrodynamic Services and from intervening in business dealings between ITS and Petrodynamic.574
Section 6(a) of the SPA: “Notwithstanding anything here to the contrary, the Key Individual undertakes not to participate in the Petrodynamic Services and that all dealings and contracts which may be entered into between ITS and Petrodynamic Petroleum S.A. (and its affiliates, if any) will be at arms-length” and will not involve, directly or indirectly, the Key Individual in the decision making process”.

Respondents allege that Mr. Palacio breached Section 6(a) of the SPA by participating in Petrodynamic Services and by not remaining at arms-length in dealings between Petrodynamic and ITS.575
In Respondents’ view, this breach would have also triggered the breach of Section 10.17(b), since, by way of breaching Section 6(a), the exception established in the non-compete provision in relation to Petrodynamic Services (Section 10.17(b) of the SPA) is misplaced. Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 62.

According to Claimant, Respondents’ allegations about Mr. Palacio participating in Petrodynamic Services and not remaining at arms-length (breach of Section 6(a) of the SPA) are not justified because they rely on Mr. Bula’s whistleblowing, and Mr. Bula himself had reported that the prices offered by Petrodynamic were the best of the market.576
Claimant’s Memorial of Reply, ¶ 10 and Mr. Villamarín witness statement, ¶ 12.

The Tribunal believes that the fact that the prices offered by Petrodynamic were arguably the best available prices in the market is not determinative of whether Claimant and/or the Additional Parties have breached the SPA (although these facts do beat on the damages issue).

Section 6(a) of the SPA is crystal clear in that Mr. Palacio cannot be involved in the Petrodynamic Services and in all dealings and contracts to be entered into between ITS and Petrodynamic and its affiliates, if any. Thus, even if Petrodynamic services would have resulted in better prices or savings for ITS, this is an ex-post analysis that does not and cannot justify Mr. Palacio’s involvement in dealings between ITS and Petrodynamic which is expressly prohibited under Section 6(a) of the SPA.

The key issue for the Tribunal to scrutinize is any involvement Mr. Palacio had in any activity that either comes within the definition of “Petrodynamic Services” and “all dealings and contracts which may be entered into between ITS and Petrodynamic….” The evidence shows that this provision was drafted upon learning about the business between Petrodynamic, owned by the sellers, and ITS, and under those circumstances, Superior bargained for Mr. Palacio to stay out of such activity as a protection against the sellers’ self-dealing to the disadvantage of Superior.

Tire language was written broadly, so any involvement in the Petrodynamic Services or dealings and contracts between ITS and Petrodynamic would literally fall within the definition of what is prohibited, but the Tribunal do not raise form over substance where the actions taken were performed at the request of and for the benefit of Superior Colombia as the Tribunal does not believe it is commercially reasonable to interpret Section 6 (a) to be intended to reach conduct that does not rise to “participating” in inter-company business except in some meaningful way, but the threshold for that is not very high.

The evidence relating to potential breaches of Section 6 of the SPA consists of the following: (i) Mr. Palacio personally approved and signed the authorization of three different purchase orders placed by Petrodynamic577
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 78 and exhibits R-059; R-060 and R-061. for a total of, at least, US$ 452,000;578
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 54. (ii) various emails to Mr. Palacio’s account at Petrodynamic evidencing that he had some level of responsibility at Petrodynamic for activities relating to the process of purchase orders from Superior Colombia to Petrodynamic, and price-making decisions on behalf of Petrodynamic concerning items sold to Superior Colombia.579
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 78 and exhibits R-062; R-063; R-064; R-065; R-066; R-067; R-068; R-069.

title.it: Mr. Palacio’s Second Signature on ITS [Superior Colombia] Purchase Orders to Petrodynamic

item.p:
Between May and June 2013, while he was formally an employee of Superior Colombia, Mr. Palacio “personally approved and signed the authorization of three different purchase orders placed with Petrodynamic.”580
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 5. In each case, the Tribunal has found that Mr. Palacio acted upon approval of the orders by Superior Colombia’s Controller, Mr. German Nicholls.

The Tribunal notes that there ate three purchase orders dated May 14, 2013, May 29, 2013, and June 7, 2013, which contain Mr. Palacio’s signature.581
Exhibits R-059, R-060, R-061. The Tribunal also notes that each of these purchase orders were signed by Mr. Palacio within the term of his Employment Agreement, which terminated on July 30, 2013.582
Exhibit C-02. Each of the three purchase orders, however, contains another approval signature, above Mr. Palacio’s name, showing prior approval by a Superior Colombia official whose role in such approval of purchase orders has not been disputed in this case by Superior. Furthermore, Mr. Palacio testified, and it is undisputed that Superior had not yet appointed a new country manager for the former ITS, and thus Mr. Palacio was left in that position by Superior Colombia at the time of these purchase orders. On these facts, the Tribunal has no difficulty concluding that the purchase orders were independently approved by Superior Colombia and so they do not amount to a breach of Section 6.

Accordingly, the Tribunal is not persuaded that these approvals evidence conduct by Mr. Palacio that rises to the level of meaningfully “participating in the Petrodynamic Services” and therefore it is not the sort of conduct that the Parties prohibited under any good faith interpretation of the SPA.

title.it: Mr. Palacio’s involvement in Petrodynamic Services and Business Dealings and Contracts between ITS and Petrodynamic

item.p: The Tribunal concludes, however, that other evidence demonstrates that Mr. Palacio did participate in the Petrodynamic Services and/ot in “dealings and contracts which may be entered into between ITS and Petrodynamic” based upon evidence which, taken together, demonstrates specific instances when Mr. Palacio made key decisions in running Petrodynamic relating to business dealings with Superior Colombia.

The Tribunal finds that, at least from some point in 2013, Mr. Palacio was the indirect owner of Petrodynamic and, as we find below, he had the market knowledge, skill, and experience, unlike Petrodynamic’s co-owner Ms. Hernandez, that uniquely placed him in the position of responsibility at Petrodynamic for at least some aspects of its business dealings with Superior Colombia. This conclusion is reinforced by specific emails to and from Mr. Palacio that were brought into evidence during the hearing, which revealed that Mr. Palacio had an email account at Petrodynamic and corresponded on at least those few occasions with Superior Colombia personnel about pricing and other substantive matters relating to business between the two companies. This and other evidence also demonstrates to the Tribunal’s satisfaction that Mr. Palacio provided services to the Colombian oil and gas industry, in violation of Section 10.17(b), as further discussed below583
See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 337-361.

At the latest by December 2013, Premium whose owners were Mr. Palacio and Ms. Hernandez, became one of Petrodynamic’s shareholders.584
Respondents’ Hearing Presentations, p. 35 et seq. and Tr. Day 1, November 14-, 2017, p. 263-264, lines 12-22. Hence, Mr. Palacio became indirectly — through Premium-owner of Petrodynamic.

This circumstance only came to light shortly before the Hearing in this matter, following Claimant’s disclosure of documents demanded by Respondents and authorized by the Tribunal.585
Tn Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 32, lines 9-14. As a result, it has been established that Mr. Palacio and Ms. Hernández owned 50 percent of Premium and one working day after the sellers received funds for the purchase price on the Closing Date, Premium inserted approximately US$ 800,000 into Petrodynamic, and in exchange Petrodynamic gave 1,449,200 shares to Premium.586
Exhibits R-132 and R-133. Ms. Hernández’s shares were then diluted and Premium became the new effective owner of Petrodynamic, and the owners of Premium were Mr. Palacio and Ms. Hernández.587
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 54, lines 2-25.

Ms. Hernandez attempted to explain this cash infusion and minimize Mr. Palacio’s apparent indirect ownership interest in Petrodynamic. The Tribunal is not persuaded by Mrs. Hernández’ explanation that, in reality, the operation was a loan and not a capital contribution588
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 78, lines 15-25, p. 90, lines 21-25, p. 91, lines 1-25. and that there was a mistake in the forms filed with the Bancolombia.589
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 79, lines 17-25, p. 80, lines 2-14, p. 92, lines 2-15 and p. 93, lines 5-19. This was an argument only raised to resist the production of documents sought by Respondents showing all ownership in Petrodynamic and Premium, as ordered by this Tribunal Furthermore, there is no document establishing the existence of a loan agreement or any documentation of any of the essential features of a loan, (like a repayment obligation, interest, and a due date) between Premium and Petrodynamic.590
In fact, the Tribunal finds that Ms. Hernandez was an unreliable witness on this point. She initially testified on her first witness statement that she was the sole shareholder of Petrodynamic until December 2013, ( ¶ 5) and on her third witness statement she declared she made an additional capital contribution to Petrodynamic and then stresses that Premium infused the cash and became a shareholder on December 2103 ( ¶ ¶ 4 y 5), but said nothing about a loan. The Tribunal agrees with Respondents that it is simply not credible the existence of a loan with no term, interests or repayment. But even if it were true that the initial contribution made by Premium was a loan and was subsequently converted into a capital contribution for tax reasons, this is irrelevant in the Tribunal’s view. The fact remains that Mr. Palacio injected a large amount of cash, the day after being paid the purchase price at closing of the SPA, and thereafter became an indirect shareholder of Petrodynamic, by December 2013, at the latest.

In addition, Mr. Palacio was asked directly by the President of the Tribunal about the ownership of Petrodynamic, and Mr. Palacio acknowledged that he injected to Petrodynamic the very profits that he received from the ITS’ sale, becoming the indirect shareholder of Petrodynamic:
“CHAIRPERSON CONEJERO: I have just one single question regarding the ownership of Petrodynamic. Could you explain me when did you acquire for the first time, directly or indirectly, shares from Petrodynamic?
THE WITNESS: I don’t know if this was already explained, but when we first received the profits of ITS sales in Panama, Maria Eugenia, my wife, needed resources for Petrodynamic and so she endeavored to get a loan to inject funds, but she used the wrong form. Sometime after we realized that, that money had come in the wrong way and so we needed to resolve this issue. And we sought legal advice as to what was the — the most convenient process for Petrodynamic. And so she discussed with the attorney and the accounting that in order to avoid the fine and for everything to meet the requirements, the legal requirements, that these funds that had come in as a supposed loan to Premium -- to make Premium a shareholder or a capital investment for Petrodynamic. It really wasn’t something that was sought after for me to become a shareholder of Petrodynamic through Premium.
CHAIRPERSON CONEJERO: So just to be clear about your answer. You’re saying that you became indirectly a shareholder of Petrodynamic through Premium through these correctional forms that appear at some point in 2013?
THE WITNESS: Towards the end of 2013, I believe, or 2014, Maria Eugenia is the one who handles all the bank efforts. I don’t have the exact date.
CHAIRPERSON CONEJERO: We have the record for that. I just wanted to clarify your answer. Thank you.
THE WITNESS: Right.”591
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 263, lines 12-25, p. 264, lines 1-25 and p. 265, lines 1-5.

In addition, Mr. Palacio confirmed that he was an owner of Petrodynamic under cross-examination by Mr. Dimitroff, who asked, “You were one of the owners [of Petrodynamic]?” and Mr. Palacio responded: “One could say so.”592
Tr. Day 1, November 14, 2017 page 228 lines 20-21.
But there is additional and abundant evidence pointing to Mr. Palacio’s involvement in the Petrodynamic Services or dealings and contracts between ITS and Petrodynamic.

First, the existence of emails exchanged between Mr. Palacio and Mr. Bula evidence that Mr. Palacio was responsible for negotiating pricing schemes for truck rental on behalf of Petrodynamic.593
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 70 and exhibits R-036; R-037 and R-038. Mr. Palacio was cross-examined about this at the Hearing:
“This is an email from Julio Bula sent directly to you and your wife, correct?
A. Correct.
Q. And in the email Mr. Bula says, “Good morning, Maria Eugenia, Victor. We are interested in receiving a quotation for the four trucks that are currently using under the all-cost modality. The all-cost modality should include drivers, gas, tolls, maintenance, et cetera.” This was sent by Mr. Bula with the signature line showing. That’s the supply – supply chain manager at Superior, correct?
A. Correct.
Q. Did you understand that he is asking you for a quotation for the truck prices for Petrodynamic?
A. He’s asking me to help them contract the -- all cost model for ITS.
Q. That’s right. What he’s asking you to do is provide a good price for ITS from Petrodynamic for the rental of trucks; is that correct?
A. He’s asking me for help -- to help ITS to get a good price.
Q. Well, frankly he’s asking both you and your wife for a price quotation, correct? He’s saying, “Good morning, Maria Eugenia, Victor.” The first person he addresses is your wife and you?
A. Yes, first my wife.
Q. Then you answered that email on January 2nd on the first page.
A. Yes.”594
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 210, lines 6-25 and p. 211, lines 1-16.

Second, there ate other instances showing Mr. Palacio’s involvement the Petrodynamic Services in documents produced by Claimant in this arbitration: (i) on December 29, 2014, Mr. Palacio negotiated float equipment prices with ITS supply chain employees thereby making decisions at Petrodynamic in respect to ITS;595
Exhibit R-081. (ii) on January 8, 2015, e-mails show that he was considered point of contact and received reports from Petrodynamic clients on part failures used in bids for Pacific entities;596
Exhibit R-82. and (iii) on January 14, 2015, he directed Petrodynamic employees and asked questions in negotiations with clients regarding shoe sales pricing.597
Exhibit R-83.

Third, Mr. Palacio was clearly involved in dealings between Petrodynamic and Joalsiar for the acquisition of products that fell squarely within the definition of the so called “Petrodynamic services.” The Tribunal has no difficulty concluding that this also constitutes a breach of section 6(a) of the SPA.

Evidence shows that on July 8, 2014, Mr. Palacio received an email from Mr. Sierra, Joalsiar’s representative, containing a draft of a full Supply Agreement between Joalsiar and Petrodynamic. The Tribunal notes that (i) such email was directed to Mr. Palacio to a Petrodynamic’s email address (ventaspetrodynamic@gmail.com); (ii) in the draft itself, Mr. Palacio appears as Petrodynamic’s legal representative; and (iii) the draft states that Petrodynamic “agrees to purchase the products supplied by SUPPLIER [Joalsiar] in order to resell them.”598
Exhibits R-039 and R-128.

The Tribunal is not persuaded by Mr. Palacio’s allegation that he did not negotiate with Joalsiar but rather did a favor at the request of Mr. Sierra.599
Mr. Palacio’s second witness statement and Respondents’ Hearing Presentations, p. 59. As a result of negotiations between Mr. Palacio and Mr. Sierra, a draft Supply Agreement was produced and the executed Supply Agreement, while ultimately signed by Ms. Hernández instead of Mr. Palacio, is the same as the draft sent by Mr. Sierra to Mr. Palacio as acknowledged by Mr. Palacio’s testimony at the Hearing.
“Q. Let’s move to a different topic. I’d like you to turn to Exhibit R-39, please. Are you there?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. This is an email to you from Jorge Sierra, correct?
A. Mail was sent to Petrodynamic?
Q. It was. There’s a ventaspetrodynamic@gmail.com, and right next to it is you.
A. And he also sent it to me, the email, correct.
Q. He sent it to both the Petrodynamic and your email, but the only person addressed to is you?
A. Correct.
Q. And did you sometimes receive email messages at the ventapetrodynamic@gmail.com account?
A. Sometimes.600
Tr. Day 1, November 14, 2017, p. 200, lines 3-22.
…
Q. And he attaches a draft contract?
A. Yes.
Q. I’d like you to turn to the contract that he sent to you. The contract parties here are Joalsiar Servicios SAS, represented in this act by Mr. Jorge Sierra, correct?
A. Yes, that’s what it says there.
Q. And the supplier is Petrodynamic, represented by you, Victor Palacio, correct? 03:53
A. That is written there.
Q. Okay. And under the first paragraph where he talks about the object, the draft contract says, “The purpose of this contract, the periodic or continued supply by the supplier of oil industry material such as centralization, float equipment, and other materials required for supporting the oil services activities.” Did I read that correctly?
A. Yes.601
Tr. Day 1, November 14, 2017, p. 201, lines 21-25 and p. 202, lines 2-16.
…
Did Petrodynamic ultimately sign a contract after that time since he was just sending you a draft?
A. Yes. I see here that it was signed by Maria Eugenia Hernández.
Q. That’sidentical to the draft that Mr. Sierra sent to you?
A. Yes, sir.”602
Tr. Day 1, November 14, 2017, p. 205, lines 18-20.

Hence, despite the fact that the final agreement between Joalsiar and ITS was signed by Ms. Hernández rather than by Mr. Palacio,603
Exhibit R-128. and regardless of whether the agreement was actually performed or not,604
Tr. Day 1, November 14, 2017, p.131, lines 7-9. the Tribunal concludes that Mr. Palacio did negotiate for Petrodynamic with Joalsiar and that such negotiation led to an agreement on the terms of the Supply Agreement ultimately executed between these companies.

Fourth, evidence also shows that Mr. Palacio acted on behalf of Petrodynamic when dealing with ITS’ clients, such as Emerald Energy and Baker Hughes, who would contact Mr. Palacio regarding Petrodynamic Services.605
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 74 and exhibits R-041 and R-082. The Hearing also assisted the Tribunal to establish this point:
“Q. I’d like to move to Exhibit R-82, please. This is an email that is from Baker Hughes. Do you see the email?
A. Yes, sir.
Q. And this is an email from Jose Enrique Sanchez Mendoza from Baker Hughes and he’s emailing you, correct?
A. Copying me.
Q. That’s right. He says, “Good afternoon, Jose and Victor.”
A. Copy to ventas, sales, not me.606
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 217, lines 19-25 and p. 218, lines 1-6.
…
Q. And he’s asking you as part of Petrodynamic to take a look at this failure report and determine what happened, why did this equipment fail?
A. He says Jose and Victor.
Q. Yes. So you were one of the people he was asking on behalf of Petrodynamic to look at what caused the float failure?
A. Yes.
Q. And in this capacity you were -- he was contacting you as a representative of Petrodynamic?
A. I don’t know why he would send that email to me.607
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 219, lines 21-25 and p. 220, lines 1-10.
…
Let’s move on. I’d like you to look at Exhibit R-86. This is another email from Baker Hughes, correct?
(…)
Q. This is an email from the ventas@petrodynamic.com.co email, correct?
A. Correct.
Q. And this is being sent to Baker Hughes, correct?
A. Yes, sir.
Q, And the person who is responding who’s sending this email from Petrodynamic is you. You see in the bottom it says, “Best regards, Victor Palacio.”
A. It was sent from the ventas email.
Q. That’s right.
A. It was sent from the ventas email. It could be someone from Petrodynamic.
Q. Take a look at the bottom of that email where it says, “Best regards, Victor Palacio.” Do you see that?
A. Yes, I see it.
Q. That’s you, isn’t it?
A. Yes.”608
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 220, lines 11-25 and p, 221, lines 1-19.

Fifth, Mr. Palacio further engaged in business dealings with other companies in the oil and gas industry on behalf of Petrodynamic. Within the year following the termination of his Employment Agreement –and while still working for ITS under the Services Agreement— Mr. Palacio received purchase orders and information requirements intended for Petrodynamic from clients such as Qmax Solutions Colombia and Baker Hughes and dealt with suppliers on behalf of Petrodynamic.609
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 75 and exhibits R.-043; R-044; R-045; R-046; R-047; R-048, R-049; R-050; R-051.

In the same vein, the Tribunal is not persuaded that Mr. Palacio did not participate in the Petrodynamic Services or in dealings and contracts between ITS and Petrodynamic because it was Ms. Hernández who was in fact running the company. This assertion is not supported by evidence, on the contrary, the great weight of the evidence allows the Tribunal to conclude or infer Mr. Palacio’s direct involvement. That is not only because of the foregoing communications with Mr. Palacio himself, but also because it is simply not credible that Ms. Hernández solely effected Petrodynamic’s provision of the Petrodynamic Services or its dealings and contract with ITS, without Mr. Palacio’s management and participation. That is because such business pertains exclusively to matters as to which he is an expert and she is not. Ms. Hernandez is a software system manager with training in information technology610
Exhibit R-084. and admitted she had no prior experience in the oil and gas industry,611
Witness Statement of Ms, Hernández, ¶ 3 and Tr. Day 1, November 14, 2017, p. 101, lines 4-25. in contrast with her husband who has broad experience in the oil and gas industry:
“Q. And your work of Petrodynamic was basically of the same nature of administrative nature; sales, payroll and taxes purchases, etcetera; is that correct?
A. Yes.
Q. So before working at ITS, you didn’t have any experience in the oil and gas industry; is that a fair statement?
A. No.”612
Tr. Day 1, November 14, 2017, p. 102, lines 12-20.
***
“Q. Is it true or is it not, that it is
Mr. Palacio the one who worked in the field and you did perform administrative work more than anything else?
A. Administrative,yes.
Q. So you never performed work on the field – oil and gas services in the field?
A. No. But administrative work, management of inventory, of staff.”613
Tr. Day 1, November 14, 2017, p. 104, lines 8-16.

In light of the above, the Tribunal finds that there is clear and conclusive evidence614
See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 435-452. pointing to Mr. Palacio’s direct involvement in the Petrodynamic Services and in dealings between ITS and Petrodynamic. Hence, the Tribunal concludes that Claimant and Mr. Palacio breached Section 6(a) of the SPA by Mr. Palacio’sparticipation in the Petrodynamic Services and in dealings and contracts between ITS and Petrodynamic.

title.bd: Breach of Section 10.17 of the SPA

item.p:
Section 10.17(b) of the SPA sought to preserve the value of ITS’ industrial secrets and goodwill. It does so by prohibiting Claimant and Additional Parties from using ITS’ secrets and goodwill during the two years following the termination of Mr. Palacio’s Employment Agreement, “or otherwise carry out any activity that could undermine the value of these assets.” To do so, it creates a rebuttable presumption that if they do so participate in the Colombian oil and gas industry, there would be a breach of this prohibition. However, Section 10.17 carves out from this prohibition the provision by Claimant and Additional Parties of what is defined as the Petrodynamic Services provided there is compliance with the restrictions thereon as set forth covenant in Section 6.615
Section 10.17(b) of the SPA: “Seller and Beneficial Owners expressly covenant and agree that they shall not use any of the industrial secrets and goodwill, nor will otherwise carry out any activity that could undermine the value of these assets. Except for the Petrodynamic Services (and subject to the covenants in Section 6) the Seller and the Beneficial Owners further covenant and agree that if Seller or Beneficial Owners provide services to the Colombian oil and gas industry within the 2 years following the date of termination of the Employment Agreement of the Key Individual, due to the complexity of the Colombian oil and gas industry it would be reasonable to assume that, in doing so, Seller and Beneficial Owners will be using the transferred industrial secrets and goodwill, that the Seller and the Beneficial Owners would be engaging in unfair competition and unfair trade practices by using industrial secrets and goodwill that they have sold to Purchaser for consideration and thus no longer own, and that the value of the industrial secrets and goodwill will necessarily be undermined by such unauthorized use”.

In the event there is a breach of Section 10.17(b), Section 10.17(c) of the SPA states that the Purchase Price would be adjusted downwards by a certain percentage based upon when the breach occurred, in order to compensate Respondents for diminution to the value of the business when its industrial secrets and goodwill were undermined by such breach.616
Section 10.17(c) of the SPA: “Without prejudice to the Seller’s and Beneficial Owner’s right to disprove the above assumption (i.e. by demonstrating that, in participating in the Colombian oil and gas industry, they are using industrial secrets and goodwill other that those transferred hereby) Seller and Beneficial Owners covenant and agree that, except for the Petrodynamic Services (and subject to the covenants in Section 6), the Purchase Price shall be adjusted downwards by a certain percentage in the event that the Seller or the Beneficial Owners participate in the Colombian oil and gas industry within the next two (2) years as follows: (i) 20% if such participation takes place within 1 year after the date of termination of the Employment Agreement of the Key Individual, (ii) 15 % if such participation takes place within 1.5 years after the date of termination of the Employment Agreement of the Key Individual and (iii) 10% if such participation takes place within 2 years after the date of termination of the Employment Agreement of the Key Individual.”

The Tribunal must determine if Claimant and Additional Parties breached the non-compete provision established in Section 10.17(b) of the SPA during the Non-Compete Period. That is, did Mr. Palacio and/or Ms. Hernández use the transferred industrial secrets and goodwill, which is presumed, if not rebutted, by Mr. Palacio’s provision of services in the Colombian oil and gas industry during the two years after the termination of his Employment Agreement. As stated above, the Tribunal finds that the evidence establishes quite easily that Mr. Palacio provided services in the Colombian oil and gas industry, and there has been no rebuttal of the presumption that in so doing, he used the industrial secrets and goodwill that he agreed not to use in Section 10.17(b). Specifically, the Tribunal finds that the evidence described above617
Specifically, Exhibits C-28, JD-020, R-083, R-086, R-087, R-088, R-089, R-090, R-095 and R-096 and, in general the evidence that made this Tribunal conclude the breach of Section 6 (a) of the SPA. See also Final Award, ¶ 312-336, ¶ ¶ 337-361 and ¶ ¶ 424-454. and the following paragraphs establishes Mr. Palacio’s participation in the Petrodynamic Services and other business between Petrodynamic and Superior Colombia, not in compliance with Section 6, to be a violation of 10.17(b).

In addition, the Tribunal finds additional evidence of Mr. Palacio providing services in the Colombian oil and gas industry, in violation of Section 10.17(b). Mr. Palacio breached this section by bidding for the Pacific Supply Contract, that Mr. Palacio previously obtained and managed for ITS.

Claimant and Additional Parties competed with Superior Colombia for the same Pacific Supply Contract that Mr. Palacio had obtained for ITS when he worked there.618
Respondents’ Hearing Presentations, p. 73 and seq. See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 354-357. Until 2015, ITS supplied Pacific with reamer shoes and that upon the termination of this contract Pacific opened a tender inviting other companies.619
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 68

Respondents note that on July 3, 2015, within the Non-Compete Period,620
See Final Award, ¶ 354. Petrodynamic submitted its bid to Pacific Rubiales to replace the 2015 reamer shoe contract. Respondents have proved that Petrodynamic won the bid and ITS lost it.621
Respondents’ Hearing Presentations, p.75 and Exhibit C-028.

Claimant’s position is that ITS lost the bid because its offer failed to comply with the technical requirements set forth in Pacific’s RFP.622
Claimant’s Reply to Counterclaims, ¶ 19-20. See Final Award, ¶ 397. The Tribunal however does not need to enter into the reasons why ITS lost Pacific Rubiales’ bid because the issue is simply whether or not the Additional Patties provided services in the Colombian oil and gas industry. They did. Mr. Palacio became the indirect owner of Petrodynamic as of December 2013, and he, unlike Ms. Hernandez, had the knowledge, experience, and skill (developed extensively at ITS) necessary to prepare a successful bid of this kind. The mere fact that Petrodynamic participated and won such tender within two years following the termination date of the Employment Agreement, evidences their provision of services in the Colombian oil and gas industry and would therefore create the presumption of a violation of the prohibition on using the ITS industrial secrets and goodwill that constitutes a breach of Section 10.17(b) of the SPA.

Section 10.17(b) of the SPA contains a presumption that Claimant would engage in unfair competition, and thus breach the covenant contained in said section, if Claimant or the Additional Parties (including both Mr. Palacio and Mrs. Hernández) as the “Beneficial Owners” would provide services to the Colombian oil and gas industry within two years following the date of termination of the Employment Agreement, when it establishes that:
“…the Seller and the Beneficial Owners further covenant and agree that if Seller or Beneficial Owners provide services to the Colombian oil and gas industry within the 2 years following the date of termination of the Employment Agreement of the Key Individual, due to the complexity of the Colombian oil and gas industry it would be reasonable to assume that, in doing so, Seller and Beneficial Owners will be using the transferred industrial secrets and goodwill, that the Seller and the Beneficial Owners would be engaging in unfair competition and unfair trade practices by using industrial secrets and goodwill that they have sold to Purchaser for consideration and thus no longer own, and that the value of the industrial secrets and goodwill will necessarily be undermined by such unauthorized use” (emphasis added)

Under the SPA, Claimant or the Additional Parties had the opportunity, and the burden, to rebut this presumption. Pursuant to Section 10.17(c) of the SPA Claimant or the Additional Parties could have done so by demonstrating that, in participating in the Colombian oil and gas industry (i.e. in participating and wining Pacific’s tender), they did not use industrial secrets and goodwill of ITS that were bought by Superior Colombia.

To attempt to meet this burden, Mr. Palacio testified that the bid was not prepared by him but instead it was Ms. Hernandez who prepared the bid, and she “was aware of the price of the supplier and knows the expenses for importation and knows what to present.”623
Tr. Day 1, November 14, 2017, page 228 lines 8-11, and page 229 lines 4-7. Nevertheless, Mr. Palacio admitted “but I was aware of everything.”624
Tr. Day 1, November 14, 2017, page 229 line 12. Mr. Palacio further admitted that he requested and obtained information from Pacific about the competing bids that were presented.625
Tr. Day 1, November 14, 2017, page 230 line 14 to page 232 line 11 and Exhibit C-28. He also admitted that his contact at Pacific who sent him this information was a relationship Mr. Palacio had developed while he worked at ITS, when he would, at ITS’ expense, entertain this contact, sometimes as lavishly as having ribeye steaks, Grey Goose Vodka, and Grand Marnier during what Palacio called “lunches — work lunches.”626
Tr. Day 1, November 14, 2017, page 233 line 2 to page 234 line 2 and Exhibit JD-020. As for Mrs. Hernández’s involvement, it is confessed by Mr. Palacio that she prepared the bid herself, thus also becoming engaged in providing services to the Colombian oil and gas industry within the time frame established by the SPA627
Tr. Day 1, November 14, 2017, page 228 lines 8-11, and page 229 lines 4-7.. The Tribunal, in the face of this evidence, does not credit Mr. Palacio’s attempt to distance himself from Petrodynamic’s bid to Pacific. The evidence is more than sufficient for the Tribunal to conclude that Mr. Palacio provided services to the Colombian oil and gas industry during the Non-Compete Period –that started on July 30, 2013 and extended for two years until July 30, 2015- and has not rebutted the presumption of his use of ITS industrial secrets and goodwill in connection with those services.

The Tribunal also finds evidence that Claimant and the Additional Parties breached Section 10.17(b) of the SPA by Petrodynamic’s provision of services to the Colombian oil and gas industry selling flotation equipment to ITS’ competitors during the Non-Compete Period628
Respondents’ Hearing Presentations, p.70. The evidence shows that Mr. Palacio assisted competitor Baker Hughes and sold flotation equipment to competitor Schlumberger.629
Respondents’ Hearing Presentations, p.69. This is clear evidence that the Additional Parties participated in the Colombian gas and oil industry by selling equipment to ITS’ competitors in the Colombian oil and gas industry.630
Exhibits R-083, R-086, R-087, R-088, R-089, R-090, R-095, R-096. Unlike the Pacific Supply Contract situation, Claimant and the Additional Parties did not offer any evidence in an attempt to rebut the presumption that Mr. Palacio used industrial secrets and goodwill of ITS when he assisted Baker Hughes and sold flotation equipment to Schlumberger when he did so, and the Tribunal finds it eminently reasonable to conclude that the presumption has been amply established by the evidence, which demonstrates a breach of Section 10.17(b).

The Tribunal cannot agree with Claimant’s defense that the non-competition clause contained in Section 10.17(b) of the SPA would be prohibited under the Colombian Constitution. Claimant and the Additional Parties rely on Articles 26 and 333 which establish the general principle that every person has a right to work and freely develop an activity, and that such activity must not be impeded within the limits of public good. Claimant and the Additional Parties have failed to establish that a non-compete clause that is limited both in temporal and material scope would go beyond the limits of public good and be invalid.

On the contrary, the Tribunal is convinced that non-competition clauses are valid under Colombian law in a purchase contract if they are proportional and necessary. In fact, the Tribunal notes that even Claimant and the Additional Parties concede that non-compete provisions are justified under Colombian law where they are necessary to a business transaction.631
Claimant’s Memorial of Answer to Counterclaim, ¶ 19 and exhibit CL-011.

In this case, the Tribunal concludes that this provision was necessary in order to preserve the value of ITS’ industrial secrets and goodwill, which naturally constituted a very significant part of the consideration to be received by Superior Colombia in exchange for the purchase price under the SPA, as Mr. Ballard testified.632
Tr. Day 2, 17 November 2017, p. 300, lines 2-12 and Tr. Day 2, 17 November 2017, p. 302, lines 2-9.

The Tribunal also finds that the provision was proportional since it had a limited application to the extent that it only prohibited the Additional Parties to participate in the Colombian oil and gas industry for two years after the termination of the Employment Agreement. There was no evidence offered to the contrary. Upon expiry of that period, the Additional Parties were free to entertain all type of business in the Colombian oil and gas industry, in direct competition with ITS.
For these reasons, the Tribunal concludes that Claimant and the Additional Parties breached Section 10.17(b) of the SPA.

title.bd: Violation of the Duty of Care and Good faith under Colombian law and Breach of Representation and Warranties

item.p:
Article 1603 of the Colombian Civil Code recognizes the general principle of good faith in the execution of contracts:
Article 1603 Civil Code: “Contracts must be performed in good faith, and they therefore require not only that which is expressed in them, but all things that arise precisely of the nature of the obligation, or which by law belong to it.”633
Exhibit RL-003.

Article 871 of the Commercial Code, in turn, requires good faith not only in the execution but also in the celebration of contracts.
Article 871 Commercial Code: “Contracts shall be celebrated and performed in good faith and, they therefore, require not only that which is expressed in them, but to all things that correspond to their nature by law, custom, or natural equity.”634
Exhibit RL-005.

Finally, Article 863 of the Commercial Code requites parties to act in good faith during the precontractual stage of contracts.
Article 863 Commercial Code: “The parties shall proceed in good faith free of negligence during the precontractual period, or otherwise they will be forced to compensate the damages caused by them.”635
Exhibit RL-004.

Thus, according to Colombian law both Parties must act in good faith, not only in the execution and the performance of the SPA through its termination, but also during the negotiations of the content of the SPA.

Good faith in pre-contractual stage requires due diligence in the determination of the content of the contract “in order to ensure that stipulations … reflect what was really discussed and negotiated between them and avoid suprising the other contractual party and defrauding his confidence.”636
Exhibit RL-007. FELIPE VALLEJO GARCÍA, EL CONCERTO DE BUENA FE EN LOS CONTRATOS, IN: ESTUDIOS DE DERECHO CIVIL OBLIGACIONES Y CONTRATOS, UNIVERSIDAD EXTERNADO DE COLOMBIA, 2003, TOMO III. This obligation is acknowledged as a “duty of information” in the negotiations which is the first and most important obligation related to good faith in the pre-contractual stage.637
Exhibir RL-001. ARTURO SOLARTE RODRÍGUEZ, LA BUENA FE CONTRACTUAL Y LOS DEBERES SECUNDARIOS DE CONDUCTA, 108 VNIVERSITAS 2004, p. 289.

Respondents assert that Claimant and Additional Patties did not act in good faith during the pre-contractual period which resulted in a breach of the representation and warranties of the SPA because of incomplete disclosure, misrepresentations and omissions of relevant information during the negotiations of the SPA and the due diligence process.

Evidence submitted by Respondents shows that their legal counsel, Baker McKenzie, sent a due diligence checklist that requested a description of relationships with the shareholders or companies affiliated with the shareholders in three different occasions: on October 8, 2012,638
Exhibit R-009. November 9,639
Exhibit R-011. 2012, and November 28, 2012.640
Exhibit R-013. Claimant responded to the request sent on November 9, 2012, by declaring that there were no other companies from the group.641
Exhibit R-012. As for the rest, Claimant did not respond to that section642
Exhibit R-009. at all or with all the information requested643
Witness Statement of Mr. Trujillo, ¶ 8.. On February 22, 2013, Claimant sent back a list of deliverables stating that there were no affiliates.644
Exhibit R-020 and Witness Statement of Mr. Nolan I, ¶ 12.

On February 25, 2013, only three days before the execution of the SPA and after months of negotiations, Claimant disclosed that there was a vehicle lease agreement between ITS and Petrodynamic, but gave no more information about the company, its owners, or the services that provided.645
Exhibit R-021.

It was on February 26, 2013, that Claimant disclosed Petrodynamic as an affiliate for the first time. Also Claimant proposed to establish an exception to the non-compete provisions of the SPA in relation with the lease of vehicles and equipment by Petrodynamic to ITS. Upon being inquired by Respondents to provide further information, Claimant informed that Ms. Hernández was the representative646
Exhibit R-016 and Witness Statement of Mr. Trujillo, ¶ 10. and owner647
Exhibit R-77. of Petrodynamic and that it sold products to ITS and its competitors San Antonio and Baker.

Asa result of these disclosures, Respondents made some modifications to the SPA adding the definition of “Petrodynamic Services,” the incorporation of section 6(a) and the exception of the Petrodynamic Services on the non-compete obligations, subject to section 6(a).

Also, the e-mails of the relevant time show that, to the contrary to Claimant’s allegation that Petrodynamic was generally known by Superior,648
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 14. See Final Award, ¶ 412. the first time that Superior had any information about Petrodynamic and its relation with Premium was on February 25, 2013, just three days before the Closing Date649
Exhibit R-77. On this e-mail David Cohn, from Superior Energy states that “Until today, we did not realize that Petrodynamic was a related company.” This e-mail shows that Respondents did not know about Petrodynamic and the kind of services that provides..

In summary, the Tribunal concludes that Claimant at first failed to disclose the very existence of Petrodynamic and affirmatively misrepresented that there were no affiliated companies to Claimant and the Additional Parties. The existence of Petrodynamic was lately disclosed, only three days before the Closing Date, and the true scope of the relation between Petrodynamic and Ms. Hernández was first touched upon only two days before the execution of the SPA. The Arbitral Tribunal considers that this late disclosure was contrary to good faith, especially considering the several requests made previously by Respondents regarding the existence of affiliates to Claimant and the Additional Parties.

Furthermore, the disclosure was not only late but also incomplete, since Claimant failed to describe to the real extent of the activities conducted by Petrodynamic and, as a consequence, misrepresented the true scope of what would come to be defined simply as the “Petrodynamic Services” as consisting only of tractor rentals and the sale of consumables such as float equipment and centralizers.

First, because Claimant only informed about Petrodynamic’s relation with Mrs. Hernández but did not mention Mr. Palacio and his involvement with this company. The argument made by Claimant that they made available a truck rental agreement between ITS and Petrodynamic that identifies Mrs. Hernández as representative of Petrodynamic650
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 12. See Final Award, ¶ 414. is not enough to deem the disclosure and good faith obligations fulfilled. On the contrary, to the extent that this document referred only to Mrs. Hernández, the disclosure is incomplete and distracts the recipient of the information -Respondents- from deepening the very nature of the disclosure.

Second, because the term “Petrodynamic Services” was described in a much more limited scope than the reality of the services actually provided by Petrodynamic and the number and name of its clients ITS’ competitors-. When disclosure was made, the Petrodynamic Services only referred to (i) the rental of trucks and (ii) the sale of floating equipment and centralizers. But in reality, Petrodynamic provided a number of services beyond the services disclosed, as Mrs. Hernández specifically recognized when being cross-examined by Respondents’ counsel Mr. Zuleta:
Q. Is it true, is it not, that Petrodynamic at that time rendered the sale of equipment using cementing process to other companies that were not simply cross centralisers and floatation products?
A. Yes, as required -- as the company is required, yes.
Q. For example, Petrodynamic rented or sold -- is it true or not that Petrodynamic at that time rented or sold compressors, bulk tanks, batch mixers, silos, and frac tanks?
A. Yes, we did rent them.
Q. And Petrodynamic provided cleaning services; is that correct?
A. Yes.
Q. And also sold screens and mesh used for gravel pack services?
A. Yes”.651
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 126, lines 11-25.

As for Pettodynamic’s clients, clearly there were more than were disclosed. Evidence shows that Petrodynamic was hired by ITS’ competitors such as Maren Fox S.A. and Tucker Energy Services S.A. to provide cementing services to Pacific.652
Exhibits R-101; R-102; R-103; R-104; R-105; R-106; R-107; R-108; R-109; R-110. Further, at the Hearing Mr. Palacio expressly acknowledged that there were more clients of Petrodynamic that the ones disclosed, when asked by Mr. Dimitroff:
“Q. And what you answer -- what your lawyer answered, with: “The vehicle lease is only with ITS. Petrodynamic sales of the float equipment and the centralized products is San Antonio and Baker.” That was the answer, correct?
A. Correct.
Q. Those are the only two competitors that you identified for Superior?
A. The only two that were put there, yes.
Q. That’s right, but, frankly, there were more people that Petrodynamic was selling as far as competitors of ITS?
A. Yes.
Q. Nowhere else after this were the additional competitors at ITS identified that Petrodynamic was dealing with?
A. I don’t remember.
Q. I’d like you to turn to Exhibit R-15. By the way, if there were any additional information provided to ITS, we’d have to look at – change that. If there was any additional information that you provided to Superior during the due diligence process, we just have to look at the record, but right now, sitting here today, you don’t remember anything else being given to Superior, do you?
A. No. I don’t remember anything else.”653
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 189, lines 18-25 and p. 190, lines 1-25.
…
“Q. You don’t provide any information about Petrodynamic’s other business with ITS’s competitors, but there were other business with other competitors at the time, wasn’t there?
A. Correct.
Q. And the very – I guess a day later, 9 on March 1st, you signed the SPA?
A. Yes, sir.”654
Tr. Day 1, 14 November 2017, p. 193, lines 3-10 (boldface emphasis added).

In failing to disclose the real scope of the services provided by and the clients of Petrodynamic, Claimant breached the “duty of information” inherent in the doctrine of good faith during the pre-contractual period. To the extent that the Additional Parties were engaged in the Petrodynamic services, and participated in the negotiation of the SPA (specially, Mr. Palacio), they also failed to comply with good faith duties to inform the reality of the Petrodynamic business prior to executing the SPA.

In respect of the performance of the SPA, Colombian law establishes that contracts must be executed in good faith, according to an objective standard of loyalty and correction, in the fulfilling of each party obligations.655
Exhibir RL-001. ARTURO SOLARTE RODRÍGUEZ, LA BUENA FE CONTRACTUAL Y LOS DEBERES SECUNDARIOS DE CONDUCTA, 108 VNIVERSITAS 2004, p. 289. The Supreme Court of Colombia has defined good faith as “the loyal, honest and irreproachable conduct analyzed from an objective perspective, that is, with a specific standard determined by social usages and good customs.”656
Exhibit RL-010. SUPREME COURT OF JUSTICE, JUDGMENT OF THE CIVIL CHAMBER DATED JULY 15, 2008.

As noted by the Tribunal, Mr. Palacio did not fulfill his obligations under the SPA in good faith since he participated in the Petrodynamic Services and was involved in dealings between ITS and Petrodynamic, notwithstanding the prohibition established in Section 6(a) of the SPA that expressly prevented him to participate in any way in the Petrodynamic Services and to remain at arm’s length in any dealings and contracts between ITS and Petrodynamic.

In addition to Mr. Palacio’s involvement in the Petrodynamic Services and the dealings with ITS, Mr. Palacio directly competed with ITS in the oil and gas industry when Petrodynamic presented a bid for Pacific Rubiales’ reamer shoes contracts in direct competition with ITS,that actually lost the bid to Petrodynamic. The presentation of the bid, with the aid of Mrs. Hernández, was made in violation of section 10.17 (b) of the SPA, but also in violation of the standards of good faith and loyalty that the SPA required from Claimant and the Additional Parties, not to engage in unfair competition and unfair trade practice during the Non-Compete Period.
In conclusion, the Tribunal concludes that Claimant and the Additional Parties failed to act in good faith in both the celebration and the execution of the SPA.

section.title: Breach of non-compete and confidentiality obligations pursuant to the Employment and the Services Agreement.

item.p:
The Employment Agreement was incorporated as an exhibit to the SPA. Under its Section 3, first paragraph, Mr. Palacio was bound to treat in a “strictly confidential form all the information that may come to his knowledge” related with ITS’ matters and businesses and “to refrain from revealing in detriment of the interests of the Company, confidential or secret information”. In addition, under Section 2, Mr. Palacio would not “render services directly or indirectly to other employers or work on his own account”.657
Exhibit R-004 and Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 97.

The Employment Agreement was terminated by Mr. Palacio on July 30, 2013. However, Mr. Palacio’s confidentiality obligations were deemed to survive the termination of the agreement.658
Exhibit R-004.

Immediately after termination of the Employment Agreement, effective as of August 1, 2013, Mr. Palacio and ITS the Services Agreement, by virtue of which Mr. Palacio had to provide technical assistance in ITS’ oil and gas sales and operations.659
Exhibit R-005 and see paragraph 99 of this award. Under Clause 10 of the Services Agreement, Mr. Palacio agreed to the following non-compete provision: “was obliged not to provide his technical support services in sales and operations associated with the hydrocarbon industry to companies that constitute direct or indirect competition to (ITS), during the duration of the agreement.”660
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 97 and Exhibit R-005.

The Services Agreement also contained a confidentiality provision by which Mr. Palacio had to “refrain from using, for its personal benefit or for the benefit any individual or entity, any knowledge obtained in connection with the activities, plans, programs, products or strategies” of ITS...”661
Clause 9 of the Services Agreement This agreement was terminated on November 1, 2014.662
Exhibit R-005.

For the reasons set out above663
Specifically, Exhibits R-004 and R-005 and the same evidence used to determine the breaches of Section. 6 (a) and 10.17 during the Non-Compete Period. See also Final Award, ¶ ¶ 374-378 and ¶ ¶ 424-468., the Tribunal concludes that Mr. Palacio also breached the non-compete and confidentiality (no use or disclosure) provisions of the Employment and Services Agreements, specifically when engaging in dealings for Petrodynamic during the term of the Services Agreement, and for allowing Petrodynamic — in Mr. Palacio’s capacity as an indirect owner — to benefit from knowledge obtained through his position at ITS in particular with regards to the terms and conditions of ITS’ offer in the Pacific’s bid.

title.bd: Reduction of the Purchase Price under Section 10.17 of the SPA

item.p:
Respondents claim that Mr. Palacio’s violations of Section 6(a) of the SPA entitles Superior Colombia to the reduction of the Purchase price by 20% and in the event the Arbitral Tribunal decides that there is no violation of Section 6, Claimant’s submission of the bid to Pacific for the supply of reamer shoes entitles to a reduction of 10%. As explained above, section 10.17(c) entitles Superior Colombia to a reduction of the Purchase Price in case of breach of Section 6(a) and 10.17(b) of the SPA.664
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 119-122. Respondents state that Claimant and Additional Parties are jointly and severally liable for the price reduction665
Respondent’s Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 6..

According to Superior, Mr. Palacio’s unauthorized participation in the Colombian oil and gas industry and breach of Section 6 (a), took place within one year after the date of termination of the Employment Agreement. Thus, Superior Colombia is entitled to the reduction of the Purchase Price by 20%.

Respondents recall that the Purchase Price was US$ 28,000,000 with two Holdback Amounts of US$ 1,250,000 each. They also note that Superior Colombia has paid Seller US$ 26,907,165.33, thus, the amount Superior Colombia effectively withheld against the Second Holdback Amount was US$ 1,092,834.67. The reduction of the Purchase Price by 20% is equivalent to US$ 5,600,000. Since Superior Colombia already withheld US$ 1,092,834.67 against the Second Holdback Amount, Superior Colombia is entitled to the difference between US$ 5,600,000 and US$ 1,092,834.67, which equals US$ 4,507,165.33 together with any applicable interest.666
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 125-128 and Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 117-120.

Respondents further state that if the Tribunal finds no unauthorized participation within one year after the date of termination of the Employment Agreement, the submission of a bid to supply reamer shoes to Pacific entitles Superior Colombia, in the alternative, to a 10% reduction of the Purchase Price. In this case, the reduction of the Purchase Price by 10% is equivalent to USD$2,800,000. Since Superior Colombia already withheld US$ 1,092,834.67 against the Second Holdback Amount, Supetiot Colombia is entitled to the difference between USD$2,800,000 and USD$1,092,834.67, which equals USD$1,707,165.33, together with any applicable interest.667
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 129-130.

title.bd: Damages for Mr. Palacio’s breach of Section 6(a) of the SPA

item.p:
Respondents also claim that Superior Colombia is entitled to damages of US$ 1,277,303, together with any applicable interest, based upon the result from BDO’s investigation.668
Witness statement of Mr, Daves I, ¶ ¶ 24-34. This investigation identified five flotation parts and the truck rentals experienced a shift in the purchase pattern after the date of acquisition.669
Witness statement of Mr. Daves I, ¶ 26.

Respondents note that, with regards to the flotation parts, invoices and purchase order prices for 7” Centralizers rose from US$ 94 from a local vendor up to US$ 150 when the payment was made to Petrodynamic instead of the previous local vendor. This price eventually decreased to US$ 110 after the prices were negotiated with Mr. Palacio and Petrodynamic.670
Witness statement of Mr. Daves I, ¶ 27.

This same dynamic was experienced in relation to the 7” Stop Collars/Rings. The accounting records show that when the payment was made to a local vendor the price was of US$ 10 per unit. When that same payment was directed to Petrodynamic the amount rose to US$ 18 for the exact same product.671
Witness statement of Mr. Daves I, ¶ 29. Along with the increase in price came a substantial increase in the amount of purchases verified.672
