Witness statement of Mr. Daves I, ¶ 30.

A similar change can be noticed for 7” Reamer Shoes, 9 5/8” Centralizers and 9 5/8” Stop Collars/Rings. The amount of losses experienced due to the difference between paying the local vendor and Petrodynamic was of US$ 472,030, US$ 12,005 and US$ 5,788 respectively.673
Witness statement of Mr. Daves I, ¶ ¶ 31-32. According to Mr. Palacio the increase in price of the products was due to the fact that Petrodynamic was required to supply only products from API-certified manufacturers to fulfill ITS orders. According to the BDO investigation, no support whatsoever was given for that assessment.

Finally, the investigation carried out by BDO makes reference to relevant differences In monthly rental prices for trucks. ITS paid Bancolombia COP$ 8,619,083 per month per unit, while Petrodynamic was paid a minimum of COP$ 10,000,000 or less per each comparable truck. An amount of US$ 216,872 could have been saved by ITS if the payment pattern had not shifted due to what, Respondents allege, must have been Mr. Palacio’s influence in negotiations and pricing.674
Witness statement of Mr. Daves I, ¶ ¶ 33-34.

Respondents conclude that if the Tribunal decides that Superior Colombia is not entitled to a reduction of the Purchase Price, Superior Colombia is still entitled to offset the US$ 1,277,303, together with any applicable interest, against the US$ 1,092,854.67 withheld by Superior Colombia. In addition, Superior Colombia is entitled to the difference between US$ 1,277,303 and US$ 1,092,834.67, which equals US$ 184,468.33, together with any applicable interest.

Respondents dispute Mr. Palacio’s allegation that the fact that Petrodynamic lowered twice the price on Centralizers 7” is not proof of prior overpricing but a result of market factors.675
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio I, ¶ 33. Respondents assert, through Mr. Daves’ testimony, that Mr. Palacio’s knowledge of the prices charged by Petrodynamic and the prices that ITS was willing to pay is not a reflection of market conditions.676
Witness statement of Mr, Daves II, ¶ 27. Also, Respondents urge the Tribunal to conclude that it is no coincidence that Mr. Palacio was signing purchase orders for Petrodynamic at the time that the prices were at their highest and that as his control over ITS’ purchases diminished the prices charged by Petrodynamic also declined.677
Exhibits R-059; R-060 and R-061 and Witness statement of Mr. Daves I figures 3 and 5.

Respondents also submit that although Mr. Palacio claims that the need for API-certified goods increased the prices, that is not supported by any evidence and Mr. Ballard testified he was not aware of any new demand for API-certified products after Petrodynamic started supplying cementing parts to ITS.678
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves I, figures 6 and 8; Witness Statement of Mr. Daves II, ¶ 26 and Witness Statement of Mr. Ballard, ¶ 15.

Respondents add that it is not true that Petrodynamic only began sourcing API-certified products manufacturers after the acquisition of ITS. Petrodynamic was the exclusive distributor in Colombia for CTE since at least 2012, which appears to be the provider that Petrodynamic refers to.679
Exhibit R-085. When Mr. Palacio explained to Mr. Daves that Petrodynamic supplies parts from Canada and India because its customers demanded API-certified parts,680
Exhibit JD-004. he was presumably including Petrodynamic’s other customers such as Calfrac Well Services and Tucker Energy Services.681
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 78-79.

Respondents also state that Claimant has not proved sales of API-certified products to ITS in the relevant time period. Superior Colombia located all contracts in force in that period and found that only one of fourteen mentioned the use of API-certified parts at all.682
Respondents’ Memorial of Rejoinder, ¶ 62 and exhibits R-114; R-115; R-116; R-l 17; R-118; R-119; R-120; R-121; R-122; R-123; R-124; R-125. Furthermore, Mr. Daves expressly denies having seen any evidence supporting Respondents’ API certified arguments;683
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves II, ¶ 11. and affirms that during his on-site visit to the ITS warehouse located in Villavicencio, Colombia, he found no indication of the alleged API certified branding in the centralizers when he personally inspected them.684
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves II, ¶ 13. Mr. Daves also testified that after reviewing the documents presented by Claimant he concluded that Petrodynamic ordered a very small quantity of parts from API certified manufacturers compared to the quantity that would have been required to fulfill ITS’ orders. He states that he only found a single pro forma from an API certified manufacturer (CTE) to Petrodynamic that does not prove the actual delivery or payment.685
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves II, ¶ 20.

Respondents refute Claimant’s assertion that the calculation on damages is deceitful. Claimant bases this assertion on an e-mail sent by Mr. Bula to Mr. Cervo on February 19, 2015, and April 16, 2015, regarding floating equipment prices concluding that Petrodynamic’s prices were the highest on the market.686
Claimants Memorial of Reply, ¶ ¶ 63-78. But this conclusion is based on a snapshot in time, contrary to the calculation of damages made between ITS’ acquisition until the end of Mr. Palacio’s Employment Agreement on November 2014. The quotations sent by Mr. Bula to Mr. Cervo are from December 2014 and January 2015, months after the relevant period of damages.687
Respondents’ Memorial of Rejoinder, ¶ ¶ 64-65.

Moreover, Respondents argue that the price comparison between Weatherford and Palacio that Mr. Bula sent to Mr. Cervo in February 2015 is unavailing because in first place, although Mr. Bula says that he has applied the “additional discount” asked from suppliers in December 2014,688
Exhibit C-63. the Weatherford prices are the same as those received from Weatherford in March 2014, with no discount.689
Exhibit C-62. Second, the price comparison accounts for Pettodynamic’s additional “discount on purchases” that Mr. Palacio promised to Mr. Bula in his email of November 27, 2014.690
Exhibit C-66. Third, Petrodynamic is not a competitor of Weatherford— international sellers such as Weatherford and Halliburton tend to be far more expensive than local sellers such as Petrodynamic. Therefore, the comparison of the two prices is not apt, like comparing apples to oranges.691
Respondents’ Memorial of Rejoinder, ¶ 66.

Mr. Daves also tebuts Mr. Palacio’s explanation that the prices charged by Petrodynamic to ITS actually decreased after the acquisition. Mr. Daves states that the documents cited by Mr. Palacio do not support his position. Invoice N° 0031692
Exhibit C-15. is made to an unrelated customer and it is not an example of an invoice paid by ITS. Also, Invoice 0048693
Exhibit C-16. also refers to an unrelated company in addition to ITS and it is not clear the role of ITS in this invoice.694
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves II, ¶ ¶ 6-8. Mr. Daves further adds that Mr. Palacio does not adequately explain why, before the acquisition, ITS purchased items directly from third-party vendors and after the sale, started to purchase directly from Petrodynamic instead of third parties and does not acknowledge that this shift occurred at a time when ITS could still said to be under his control.695
Witness Statement of Mr. Daves II, ¶ ¶ 9-10. See further rebuttal rom Mr. Daves in Witness Statement of Mr. Daves III.

Respondents claim that both contractual damages and consequential damages that derive from Claimant’s breaches of the SPA are explicitly cumulative and not mutually exclusive under Section 10.17(c) of the SPA696
Section 10.17(d) of the SPA; “Purchaser may, without prejudice to any other method of recovery, deduct the amount of such downward adjustments or damages from any monies due or to become due to Seller. The payment or deduction of such damages shall not relieve Seller or the Beneficial Owners from their obligation to abstain from using the transferred industrial secrets and goodwill, or from any other of their obligations and liabilities under this Agreement.” and under Colombian law.697
Exhibit RL-053. Respondents’ Memorial of Rejoinder, ¶ 58.

title.bd: Superior Colombia lawfully withheld the Second Holdback Amount

item.p:
Respondents’ position is that BDO’s investigation revealed several breaches of the SPA by Mr. Palacio. According to BDO’s findings, Mr. Palacio (i) had sent and received numerous emails to and from ITS personnel on behalf of Petrodynamic,698
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 133 and witness statement of Mr. Daves, ¶ 10. (ii) was consistently identified during interviews as the contact person for questions regarding pricing from Petrodynamic;699
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 133 and witness statement of Mr. Daves, ¶ 10. (iii) had signed three purchase orders placed with Petrodynamic on behalf of ITS;700
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 133 and witness statement of Mr. Daves, ¶ 11. (iv) had negotiated contracts with third parties on behalf of Petrodynamic;701
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 133 and witness statement of Mr. Daves, ¶ 22. and (v) had discussed and negotiated flotation parts and truck rental prices from Petrodynamic with ITS’ employees.702
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 133 and witness statement of Mr. Daves, ¶ ¶ 16-18.

In addition, BDO further established that, after the acquisition, ITS had stopped buying flotation parts from local vendors and started purchasing them from Petrodynamic at higher prices, thus incurring cost overcharges703
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 134 and witness statement of Mr. Daves, ¶ 15. and that truck rental prices offered by Petrodynamic to ITS were above market prices.704
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 134 and witness statement of Mr. Daves, ¶ 17.

According to Respondents, the conclusions of BDO constituted sufficient grounds for withholding the Second Holdback Amount, and Superior Colombia was therefore entitled to exercise its contractual right to withhold the remaining amount of the purchase price and did so in good faith.705
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 136.

As noted in the preceding section, Claimant and the Additional Parties reject Respondents’ claim for damages on grounds that it is deceitful and assert that Claimant did not breach the SPA. Thus, Superior Colombia is not entitled to claim damages pursuant to Section 10.17 of said agreement.706
See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 240-248.

Claimant and the Additional Parties also rebut Respondent’s position concerning the payment of US$ 26,907,165 made by Superior and affirms that Superior Colombia has paid approximately US$ 21,650,000 in two installments US$ 20,400,000 at the closing and the First Holdback Amount of US$ 1,250,000707
Witness Statement of Mr, Palacio II, ¶ 16..

They also contradict Superior’s allegation of having held back only US$ 1,092,834.67 and the basis of this calculation.708
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ ¶ 16-17 and Tr. Day 4, 17 November 2017, p. 822, lines 6-14. Further Mr. Palacio notes that the SPA contains procedures to adjust the Purchase Price post-closing for (a) the networking capital of ITS709
Section 2.3 (a) of the SPA. and (b) the indebtedness of ITS710
Section 2,3 (b) of the SPA. as of the Closing Date.

Premium asserts that the time for adjustments to the Purchase Price under either of these provisions expired years ago.711
Witness Statement of Mr. Palacio II, ¶ 18. Thus, adjustment to the Purchase Price should be rejected.

The Tribunal will first determine if Superior Colombia was entitled to withhold the Second Holdback Amount. Then it will assess if Superior Colombia has the right to claim damages pursuant to Section 10.17 and, if so, up to which amount. Finally, the Final Award will address the claim for other damages, resulting for an alleged excess in price paid by Superior Colombia to Petrodynamic.

title.bd: Superior Colombia’s entitlement to withhold the Second Holdback Amount

item.p:
The Tribunal has already established that Superior Colombia met all the formal requirements to withhold the Second Holdback Amount712
See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 296-304.

Pursuant to Section 2.2.(c), in connection with Sections 8.2, 8.5 and 10.17(d) of the SPA, a breach of any of the mentioned provisions granted Superior Colombia a right of retention over the Second Holdback Amount.

Section 8.2 of the SPA specifically establishes Claimant’s indemnity obligation. It provides the concept of Purchaser Damages and establishes Claimant’s obligation to indemnify Superior Colombia upon their occurrence. In general terms, Purchaser Damages are any losses, damages, claims, costs, interest, awards, judgments, penalties, and expenses arising out or resulting from a breach of any representation or warranty or any covenant or agreement made by Claimant.713
Section 8.2 of the SPA: “Subject to the Warranty Period set forth in Section 8.1, from and after the Closing Date, Seller shall indemnify, defend and hold harmless Purchaser and its successors and assigns, officers, directors, employees, agents and Affiliates (collectively, the “Purchaser Indemnitees”), against any and all Losses, damages, claims, costs, interest, awards, judgments, penalties, and expenses (collectively, the “ITS Damages”) or incurred by Purchaser (collectively, the “Purchaser Damages”), arising out of or resulting from: (a) any breach or inaccuracy of any representation or warranty made by Seller herein (in each case, without regard to any “Material Adverse Effect” or other materiality qualifier contained therein, except as to those portions of the representations and warranties requiring a list of the items referred to therein) or in any Transaction Document; (b) any breach of any covenant or agreement made by Seller contained herein or in any Transaction Document, or (c) any third party claims or third party liabilities of or against ITS arising directly or indirectly out of events or conditions occurring or existing on or prior to the Closing Date.”
Section 2.2 (c) of the SPA expressly states that Superior Colombia “has the right to withhold any portion of the Holdback Amounts” to offset any amounts arising from Claimant’s indemnity obligations.
As noted above, Section 8.5 of the SPA establishes the formal requirements that Superior Colombia must comply with when claiming Purchaser Damages against Claimant.

Likewise, Section 10.17(d) of the SPA states that Superior Colombia may deduct the amounts resulting from the downward of the Purchase Price from any monies due or to become due to Seller, such as the Second Holdback Amount. As noted,714
See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 305-308. a downward of the Purchase Price is authorized upon a breach of the non-compete provision on the part of Claimant (Sections 10.17(b) and 10.17(c) of the SPA).

In light of the findings made in the preceding sections715
See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 296-304 and ¶ ¶ 424-494., the Tribunal concludes that Superior Colombia has lawfully exercised its retention right over the Second Holdback Amount. In sum, the breach of Sections 6(a) and 10.17(b) of the SPA triggered Superior Colombia’s rights, under Sections 2.2(c), 8.2, 8.5, 10.17(c), and 10.17(d) of the said agreement, to retain the Second Holdback Amount.

title.bd: Damages pursuant to Section 10.17(c) of the SPA

item.p: The Tribunal notes that the breach of Section 10.17 (b) of the SPA occurred while the Services Agreement was still in force and within the first year after the termination of the Employment Agreement that commences on July 30, 2013, and ends on July 30, 2015. Therefore, the Purchase Price must be adjusted downwards in 20%, according to Section 10.17 (b)(i) of the SPA.

The Tribunal cannot follow Claimant’s allegations concerning the need to differentiate three periods: (i) the employment period; (ii) the consulting period; and (iii) the final period which ends on July, 30, 2015, because the SPA only recognizes the Non-Compete Period. To the extent that all Claimant’s actions that constituted a breach of Sections 6(a) and 10.17 (b) of the SPA were made during the first year of the Non-Compete Period, the adjustment of 20% of the Purchase Price is justified.

In this regard, the Tribunal has already established that at least the breach of Section 6(a) of the SPA occurred during the first year following the termination of the Employment Agreement.716
See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 424-452, Under these circumstances, pursuant to Section 10.17(c) of the SPA, the Purchase Price must be adjusted downwards in a 20%, which equals US$ 5,600,000.717
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaims, ¶ 127-128.

Claimant and Additional Patties are jointly and severally liable for this price reduction, based on Section 10.11 of the SPA718
Section 10.11 of the SPA: “For all legal and contractual purposes, Seller and the Beneficial Owners are jointly and severally liable hereunder”. that expressly establishes their joint and several liability, and Section 10.12 which states that Claimant’s obligations ate deemed obligations by each of the Additional Parties.719
Section 10.12 of the SPA: “The representations, warranties, covenants and obligations of the Seller under this Agreement are deemed to be made also by each of the Beneficial Owner”.

The Second Holdback Amount was US$ 1,250,000. Considering that Superior Colombia had, by the time it exercised its retention right, already paid Claimant US$ 26,907,165.33, the amount effectively withheld by Superior Colombia was US$ 1,092, 834.67.720
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaims, ¶ 27-128.

title.bd: Damages Resulting from Breach of Section 6(a)

item.p: The Tribunal finds that it cannot award any additional damages to Superior Colombia for the breaches of Section 6(a), but that Superior Colombia is adequately compensated for these breaches by the price reduction required by the parties’ agreement in Section 10.17(c).

Respondents and Mr. Daves contend that each and every one of the price differences that Mr. Daves found must be interpreted to evidence the improper participation in the Petrodynamic Services or other contracts and business dealings between Petrodynamic and ITS in each and every one of those circumstances. The Tribunal has not reached that conclusion, because it requires too much speculation about the actual conditions of the setting of each of the prices, and that is because there was no specific evidence given by Respondents that corresponds to each of the price differentials that connects the price differential to a breach of Section 6(a).

In turn, for the breaches of Section 6(a) that the Tribunal has found as outlined in this Award, Respondents have not submitted any evidence of the damages that flow directly from each such breach. The BDO investigation and Mr. Daves’ testimony does not establish any causal link between those specific instances of breach found by this Tribunal and the specific price differences demonstrated, in whole or in part.

For example, the Tribunal has found that it was a breach for Mr. Palacio to participate in the negotiation of the contract with Joalsiar, but there is no evidence of any products actually sold by Joalsiar to Superior Colombia or what the prices were in that case.

Additionally, although Mr. Daves testimony about the BDO investigation showed price changes post-closing, it did not show what the prices would have been if the product could have been obtained from another supplier. The Tribunal believes that this information is important to determine whether the price increases did not correspond to market conditions rather than result from the intervention by Mr. Palacio in business dealings between Petrodynamic and Superior Colombia in violation of Section 6(a). This information is also important to determine what the damages are from allegedly overpaying for parts due to Mr. Palacio’s involvement.

Although the Tribunal does not find that it can award damages as a result of the breaches of Section 6(a), nevertheless the identified breaches of Section 6(a) are significant because they serve the Tribunal to establish that Superior Colombia validly held back the Second Holdback payment and also that there was a violation of Section 10.17(b) which has a “carve-out” for the Petrodynamic Services only when Section 6(a) is not violated.

That is not to find, however, that the breaches did not cause harm, or that Respondents are not being compensated for this loss. On the contrary, the Tribunal has no difficulty concluding that the breaches of Section 6(a) had the effect of diminishing the value of what Superior purchased. The Tribunal concludes that the reduction in the Purchase Price required by Section 10.17(c) overlap therefore with the compensation for the breaches of Section 6(a) that the Tribunal has found.

That is because the reduction of the Purchase Price — by an amount negotiated and agreed upon by both parties before the SPA — is a fair approximation of the anticipated impairment of the value of the ITS business when its purchaser Superior Colombia does not receive the value of the asset it paid for. The prohibition contained in Section 6(a) against Mr. Palacio’s participation in the Petrodynamic Services and other contracts and business dealings between ITS and Petrodynamic serves to protect ITS and its purchaser, Superior, against the misuse by Mr. Palacio of ITS’ industrial secrets and goodwill, such as historic pricing and purchasing decisions. The value of the ITS business purchased by Superior Colombia was necessarily reduced when it did not maintain control of its industrial secrets and goodwill for purposes of avoiding misappropriation under Section 6(a) of such assets by one of Petrodynamic’s owners to facilitate Petrodynamic’s own business, just as much as when ITS did not maintain exclusive control under Section 10.17(b) of the ITS industrial secrets and goodwill. The parties themselves linked these concepts in Section 10.17(b).
Accordingly, the Tribunal does not award any separate or additional damages for breach of Section 6(a) and Superior Colombia’s claim for damages on this account is dismissed.

title.bd: Damages Resulting from Breach of the Duty of Good Faith

item.p: The Tribunal has not been made aware of any specific damages that Superior Colombia claims to have suffered as a consequence of these breaches of the duties of good faith separate and apart from the breaches of Section 6(a) and Section 10.17(b). Nevertheless, the breach of Section 10.17(b) by Mr. Palacio’s participation in the Colombian oil and gas industry during the Non-Compete Period carries with it an agreed-upon reduction in the Purchase Price to reflect the impairment of the assets of the industrial secrets and goodwill, which the Tribunal finds to be adequate compensation for the breaches recited above of the duties of good faith so that no additional recovery is necessary to compensate Superior Colombia.

The Tribunal reaches that conclusion as it is reasonable to assume that Superior Colombia would have insisted that it pay a lower purchase price if, instead of relying upon the seller’s good faith Superior Colombia was aware of the incompleteness of information provided by the sellers during due diligence. In a case where a reduction in the value of the thing sold had not been awarded, the Tribunal would perhaps expect to find evidence of damages flowing directly from each violation of, say, Section 6(a), but here, the effect of the breaches of the non-competition and unfair trade violations that have been established was, the Tribunal finds, to reduce the value of what the purchase price paid for, and there is no evidence of any additional or separate harm.

As to breaches of the duty of good faith in connection with conduct that the Tribunal finds to violate Sections 6(a) and 10.17(b), Respondents did not supply the Tribunal with any evidence of damages stemming from a breach of the duties of good faith that are separate and apart from the breaches of Section 10.17(b) and Section 6(a). Accordingly, the Tribunal finds that the evidence does not warrant the award of any separate damages for the breaches of the duty of good faith as they pertain to violations of Sections 6(a) and 10.17(b). This claim is, therefore, also dismissed.

In conclusion, the Tribunal awards Superior Colombia damages equivalent to a price reduction of 20% of the purchase price amounting to US$ 5,600,000721
See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 521-527.. However, it has been established that Superior Colombia retained the Second Holdback Amount for a sum of US$ 1,250,000. Moreover, at the time it exercised its retention right, Superior Colombia had already paid Claimant US$26,907,165.33, so the amount effectively withheld by Superior Colombia was US$1,092,834.67.722
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaims, ¶ 127-128. Accordingly, the amount of US$1,092,834.67 is to be deducted from the amount of US$ 5,600,000 awarded to Superior Colombia, so Claimant and Additional Parties are ordered to pay jointly and severally damages to Superior Colombia in the amount of US$4,507,165.33.

Claimant seeks interest on the Second Holdback Amount since the date when it became due on March 1, 2015, according to the Colombian legal regime for the non-payment of the price of a contract or legal regime of default interest. The legal regime is the one that must be paid by the debtor (breaching party) from the moment in which he is in default to pay a sum of money until the settlement or payment of that obligation. This is confirmed by the Financial Superintendence:723
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 36.
(…) The interests of default are those that the debtor must pay as compensation for the delay in which he has incurred (…). It is a way of repairing the damage suffered by the creditor in the event of the late non-compliance of the debtor or its full noncompliance (…)724
Exhibit CL-5, Concept number 2006000164-001 of 2006 issued by Colombia’s Financial Superintendence on February 15, 2006.

According to Claimant, this legal regime is regulated in article 884 of the Colombian Commercial Code725
Exhibit CL-6, Colombia Commercial Code, art. 884. that establishes that when no default interest is agreed, it will be equivalent to one and a half times the current banking interest, as set forth in the certificate issued by the Financial Superintendence of Colombia. Default interest is the representation of a simple interest, which is understood as the interest that an initial capital produces in a period of time, and which is not accumulated to the capital to produce the interest for the following period.

Claimant explains that interest rates are presented in an annually effective way (EA), that is, year overdue, so if the calculation of default interest will be made monthly, the rate must be converted to monthly overdue and must be updated quarterly, since the Financial Superintendence only certifies this rate for quarterly periods. Subsequently, all interest generated in the period of noncompliance is added up and will result in the amount payable by the debtor for interest in default.726
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 38. Claimant explains how the default interest is settled setting an example on ¶ 38

Respondents concede that Superior Colombia would be entitled to retain the Second Holdback Amount if the Tribunal determined that Claimant breached Section 10.17(b) of the SPA, but argues that if the Tribunal determines that there is no breach, no default interest should be awarded over the retained sums since Superior Colombia legitimately exercised its right of retention under the SPA.727
Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 123.

On the other hand, regarding Respondents’ counterclaims, Respondents claim interest on the sums resulting from both the reduction of the Purchase Price728
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ ¶ 128 and 130. pursuant to Section 10.17(c) plus interest on any damages for breaches of Section 6(a) and for beach of the duty of good faith.729
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 131. Specifically, Respondents ask the Tribunal to order Claimant the payment of interest on the sums awarded to Superior Colombia, as applicable.730
Respondents’ Memorial of Counterclaim, ¶ 138 (f) and Respondents’ Memorial of Answer to Claim, ¶ 197 (x). As for the amount, Respondents ask for the maximum permitted interest under applicable law731
Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 152 (v) and Respondents’ Memorial of Reply, ¶ 83 (d)., seeking “the maximum interest rate allowed from the date of issuance of the final award until the effective day of payment.”732
Respondents’ Submissions on Costs, ¶ 17.

As for Claimant’s claim of interest, the Tribunal has found that Respondents lawfully withheld the Second Holdback Amount in compliance with all the requirements established on the SPA and, on that basis, has dismissed Claimant’s claims.733
See Final Award, ¶ ¶ 305-308. Since Claimant’s claims against Respondents have been dismissed, the Tribunal must also reject Claimant’s claim for interest.

With regards to Respondents’ counterclaims, Respondents claim the maximum interest rate according to Colombian laws on the sums resulting of the downwards of the Purchase Price and other damages, from the date of issuance of the Final Award until the date of payment. The Tribunal notes that it has only granted Respondents’ claim for reduction of the Purchase Price so the interest claim will only be assessed in connection with this specific claim.

In determining whether to make an award of post-award interest, the Tribunal must first determine whether it is a matter of substantive rather than procedural law. The Tribunal believes it is a matter of procedural rather than substantive law. Although the substantive law of the SPA is Colombian law, the SPA itself is silent on the award of interest in connection with any breach thereof.

Further, the parties chose New York as their seat of arbitration. As explained below, New York law regulates specifically interest to be accrued on monetary judgments which is the case here. In this regard, procedural matters not otherwise governed by the ICC Rules should be settled upon by the Tribunal pursuant to Article 19 of the ICC Rules, which govern this arbitration according to the Parties’ agreement.

The Tribunal concludes therefore that the lex arbitri rather than lex contractus governs the request for post-award interest. Accordingly, the Tribunal shall determine the applicable interest pursuant to New York law.

As for the interest to be awarded, if any, the Tribunal first looks to the text of any applicable New York law. The statutory law of New York requires prejudgment interest, at the statutory rate of 9% in cases brought in New York state courts, but the New York Civil Practice Law and Rules (the “CPLR”) is silent on the award of pre-judgment interest in arbitration proceedings. CPLR Section 5001 establishes that an award of prejudgment interest is mandatory in cases in state courts. The CPLR states, in pertinent part, that “[i]nterest shall be computed from the earliest ascertainable date the cause of action existed, except that interest upon damages incurred thereafter shall be computed from the date incurred.” CPLR Section 5004 provides that the statutory interest rate shall be “nine per centum per annum”. As to post-judgment interest, Section 5003 of the CPLR provides, as to “Interest upon judgment,” that “Every money judgment shall bear interest from the date of its entry. Every order directing the payment of money which has been docketed as a judgment shall bear interest from the date of such docketing.” Once again, by referring to an “order,” the CPLR addresses cases brought in the courts of New York, but the CPLR is silent as to awards in arbitration proceedings.

The Tribunal finds very persuasive a recent report of the New York City Bar Association Committee On International Commercial Disputes, entitled “Awards Of Interest In International Commercial Arbitration: New York Law And Practice,” dated June 21, 2017 (the “NY City Bar Interest Report”). This report concludes that under New York law,
International arbitrators have discretion to apply or not to apply New York’s statutory prejudgment interest provisions to the determination of pre-award and post-award interest in an international commercial arbitration governed by New York substantive law and seated in New York, in the Committee’s view, for several reasons734
NYC Bat Interest Report, page 3, available at http://s3.amazonaws.com/documents.nycbar.org/files/2017155-Report_Awarding_of_Interest_INTCOMDI$_6.21.17.pdf.

As the Tribunal does here, the Report concludes this is true in substantial part because of a textual analysis. The text of the CPLR uses numerous terms indicating that these sections are intended to apply only to court proceedings, not arbitration. For these and for additional reasons cited there, the Tribunal concurs in that it enjoys the discretion to determine post-award interest and is not bound to follow the CPLR

In exercising discretion, the NY City Bar Interest Report suggests that arbitrators should consider a number of factors:
“New York courts acknowledge that, in the absence of express party agreement on the interest rate to be applied, arbitrators have discretion to determine interest based on a broad range of considerations. It may be appropriate for an arbitral tribunal to determine pre-award and post-award interest in accordance with New York’s prejudgment interest provisions if, by way of example only: evidence exists that the parties intended for the statutory prejudgment interest rate to apply, or no case is made in favor of applying a different rate, or the choice of interest rate would not have a significant economic impact one way or another. Arbitrators also have discretion to take into consideration that, as already noted, the NY Legislature adopted a fixed rate in part for the administrative convenience of the courts. Moreover, arbitrators may choose to consider to what extent New York’s nine percent rate differs from market rates prevailing during the pre-award period and/or economic factors specific to the parties such as their cost of funds….
In the Committee’s view, thoughtful consideration of two guiding principles common to New York law and to international arbitration — the freedom of contracting parties to agree on the terms of their relationship, and the compensatory purpose of interest— should guide arbitrators in prioritizing the many factors that they may consider in awarding interest in a particular case. Generally, the more clearly a factor reflects the intent of the parties, the higher the priority an arbitral tribunal should give to that factor. A focus on party intent generally leads to an examination of key factors in the following order: (a) contractual stipulations on interest rates to be applied to one or more aspects of the contract; (b) guidance that may be found in the arbitration rules chosen by the parties regarding the award of interest; (c) the substantive law governing the merits of the case; and (d) the arbitration law of the seat of the arbitration. An arbitral tribunal should consider these indicators of party intent in light of the underlying compensatory purpose of interest awards subject to narrow exceptions based on public policy…. A majority of the awards surveyed awarded interest, typically with little or no analysis, in accordance with New York’s prejudgment interest provisions.735
NYC Bar Interest Report Executive Summary, pages 3-5.” [italicized emphasis added.]

In terms of the parties’ intention, the Tribunal notes that the Patties here have not expressed any contractual stipulations on interest rates. Respondents, in turn, have merely sought interest pursuant to Colombian law as governing law under the SPA.
For the reasons set forth in paragraphs 553 to 555, the Tribunal has decided to apply interest pursuant to New York law (lex arbitri) rather than Colombian law (lex contractus).

In addition, the Tribunal has also taken into account other relevant elements to find that interest rate pursuant to New York law is more appropriate in the instant case such as, inter alia, that (i) the monetary awards contained in this Final Award are all expressed in US dollars and not in Colombian pesos, and (ii) the rate of interest in New York State Courts, which is of 9% on annual basis, is far more appropriate for an award expressed in US dollars than the maximum interest rate in Colombia which, according to the website for the Superintendencia Financiera de Colombia736
Information available at. https://m.superfinanciera.gov.co/jsp/Publicaciones/publicaciones/loadContenidoPublicaion/id/10097727/reAncba/1/c/00 is, as of May 30, 2018, equivalent to 30.42% on annual basis. Indeed, the interest rate under Colombian law is a maximum interest rate for any ordinary transaction, while the New York interest rate is set specifically for findings of liability resulting in an award of damages. Accordingly, it is the more specific and relevant for the relief granted by the Tribunal in this Final Award. In addition, the Tribunal concludes that as a maximum rate, the Colombian rate does not fairly represent market expectations for amounts expressed in US dollars, while it is reasonable to conclude that the prevailing rate in New York would be anticipated by market participants absent some specific agreement on another rate. Hence, the Tribunal shall apply the interest rate of 9% on an annual basis.

The Tribunal has also found that in accordance with New York laws, absent an agreement from the parties, interest is to be calculated on a simple, and not compound, basis.737
See, Marfia v. T.C. Ziraat Bankasi, 147 F.3d 83, 90 (2d Cir. 1998); Patane v. Romeo, 235 A.D. 2d 649 (3d Dep’t 1997).

Finally, in exercising its discretion, the Tribunal declines to award pre-award interest on the amounts awarded because the matter of liability for breach as well as the amount of damages to be awarded were matters that were fairly disputed and uncertain throughout the proceedings until the Final Award was determined. Thus, in the Tribunal’s view, this is the earliest ascertainable date on which damages were found to be due which should serve as a basis for calculation of interest.

Accordingly, the Tribunal concludes that Respondent shall be entitled to interest at the simple (not compounded) rate of 9% to be calculated, on an annual basis, on the amount of US$4,507,165.33 from the date of issuance of the Final Award until full and effective payment.

Premium argues that, under Colombian law738
Exhibit CL-8, General Process Code of Colombia, art. 365. and the ICC Arbitration Rules (Rule 37(4)), they are entitled to recover its attorney’s fees from Superior and all the costs of the arbitration.739
Claimant’s Memorial of Claim, ¶ 39.

Premium seeks an amount of US$ 852,453.38 plus COP 181,870,476.29.740
Claimant’s Submission on Costs, ¶ 1.

With regards to counsel Smith, Gambrell hsihtasamp; Russell, LLP (SGR); a filing fee of US$ 3,000.00 was paid when the Request for Arbitration with the ICC was put forward. The ICC has charged the parties a total of US$ 52,833.00 for administrative expenses and apart from that a projected amount of between US$ 110,310.00 and US$ 512,074.00 will be allocated as Arbitrators’ fees. Premium requests that all those expenses are directed to the Respondent.741
Claimant’s Submission on Costs, ¶ 7-10.

Premium also put forward the request of being awarded the totality of the US$ 798,424.00 spent on the SGRs representation during the arbitration.742
Claimant’s Submission on Costs, ¶ 14.

Claimant was also assisted by Sergio Iván Pérez Peñuela and his law firm. The costs incurred by them total COP 135,469,750.00 (excluding VAT).743
Claimant’s Submission on Costs, ¶ 19. This sum could be complemented with an extra US$ 62,500.00 if the Arbitrators decide to award the entire US$1,250.000.00 Holdback Amount, a decision that would grant the success fee signed with Mr. Pérez (5% of the Holdback Amount if awarded)744
Claimant’s Submission on Costs, ¶ 19-22..

In relation to both additional parties, Premium requests the reimbursement of travel expenses for two trips made to New York during 2017. The first one took place on 1 September 2017, and resulted in US$ 734.60 in air fares and US$ 451.70 for their hotel room the night before. The second trip, made in order to assist to the four days of hearings, accumulated a total of US$ 1,142.80 in airfare expenses and US$ 2,017.93 in hotel bills745
Claimant’s Submission on Costs, ¶ 23-25..

Claimant states that the Parties reached an understanding that they would share equally the interpreters’ fees and equipment rental costs for the first three days of the hearings, shipping costs for binders, catering expenses and the costs of refreshments in the various Hearing Rooms.746
Claimant’s Submission on Costs, ¶ 27. Premium paid in full the interpretation fees (US$ 5,250.00) and equipment rental costs (US$ 847.50) for the first three days of the Hearing. Respondents have represented that the shipping costs were US$ 562.90 and the catering/refreshment costs were US$ 1,185.41. Thus, Respondents have promised to pay the net balance US$ 2,174.60 in the next few days. Accordingly, Premium reduced the amount of costs sought by that amount.747
Claimant explains that the balance of the interpretation fees and equipment rental reflected in this submission was to allow the Additional Patties to understand the final day of the Hearing and thus was not subject to the parties’ cost-sharing agreement Claimant’s Submission on Costs, footnote 12.

In conclusion, Premium requested a declaration an award that Respondents pay them their costs of US$ 852,453.39 plus COP 181,870,476.29, plus amounts associated with the fees of the Arbitrators and Mr. Perez’s success fee.748
Claimant’s Submission on Costs, ¶ 28.

Respondents classify the costs incurred in this arbitration into five categories.749
Respondents’ Submissions on Costs, ¶ 2. On the first place, they mention Respondents’ payments to the ICC. These costs would add up to US$ 235,000.00, being composed by ICC administrative expenses and the Arbitrators’ fees and expenses as well.750
Respondents’ Submissions on Costs, ¶ 3-4, 12.

Second is the category of legal costs. The law firms that the Respondents hired for this arbitral procedure were Zuleta Abogados Asociados (that charged Respondent US$ 619,814.90) and Baker Hostetler (that charged Respondent US$ 695,728.14). Between both of them the legal costs charged rise up to a total of US$ 1,315,543.04.751
Respondents’ Submissions on Costs, ¶ 5-7, 12.

Third, Respondents ask for the disbursements incurred by external legal counsel. Under this concept are included airfare, accommodation, food and other incidental expenses, printing, copying, courier charges, telephone charges, and translations. The total amount associated would be of US$ 55,369.57.752
Respondents’ Submissions on Costs, ¶ 8, 12.

Fourth, Respondents mention the disbursements incurred by their party. This category includes the amounts spent by Respondent regarding the attendance of witnesses to the Hearing, including airfare, accommodation, food, visas, and other incidental expenses. These figures would have meant a total spending of US$ 209,308.62.753
Respondents’ Submissions on Costs, ¶ 9,12.

Finally, Respondents make reference to the amounts spent on Hearing costs and related disbursements, item related to the payment for the fees charged by the court reporter, interpreters, interpretation equipment vendor, post hearing shipment of documents to the Tribunal, and catering made available to the Tribunal and Tribunal Secretary. Those costs would reach a total of US$ 12,257.49.754
Respondents’ Submissions on Costs, ¶ 11-12.

In summary, the total amount sought after by the Respondents is of US$ 1,827,478.72.755
Respondents’ Submissions on Costs, ¶ 12.

Apart from the specifications of the different costs incurred on, Respondents request the Arbitral Tribunal that, in the event that they ultimately prevail in this arbitration, they are entitled to their costs on a full indemnity basis. If Respondents were to only prevail in a portion of their claims, they are entitled to their costs in proportion to their relative success.756
Respondents’ Submissions on Costs, ¶ 13.

Finally, Respondents finish their Submission of costs by asking the Arbitral Tribunal to order Claimant and Additional Parties to pay all the costs previously mentioned, plus the maximum interest rate allowed from the date of issuance of the final award until the effective day of payment.757
Respondents’ Submissions on Costs, ¶ 17.
Pursuant to Art. 37 (4) ICC Rules, “the final award shall fix the costs of the arbitration and decide which of the Parties shall bear them or in what proportion they shall be borne by the Parties.”

Art. 37 (5) ICC Rules establishes in turn that: “In making decisions as to costs, the Arbitral Tribunal may take into account such circumstances as it considers relevant, including the extent to which each party has conducted the arbitration in an expeditious and cost-effective manner.”

The Tribunal notes that Respondents prevailed in their defenses to Claimant’s claim, and in their claim for breach of the SPA and for price reduction. However, Respondents did not succeed in their jurisdictional objections and in their claim for other heads of damages different from the price reduction under the SPA.

In light of the outcome of this arbitration, and exercising its discretion to allocate costs, the Tribunal considers that Claimant and the Additional Parties should bear its own costs and seventy percent (70%) of the reasonable legal and other costs incurred by Respondents, save for the costs of arbitration fixed by the ICC Court, which in the Tribunal’s view should be borne entirely by Claimant and the Additional Parties. This is so because it was Claimant’s decision to abandon negotiation discussions among the Parties in order to commence this arbitration and both Claimant and the Additional Parties reject the entirety of Respondents’ counterclaims, but ultimately the prevailing parties in this case were Respondents. Under these circumstances, the Tribunal finds that the costs of arbitration fixed by the ICC Court should be borne exclusively by Claimant and the Additional Parties.

Putting aside Respondents’ payments to the ICC, the costs incurred by Respondents amount to a total of US$ 1,592,478.72 may be summarized as follows:
(a)
Legal fees: US$ 1,315,543.04.
(b)
Disbursements by external counsel (airfare, accommodation, food and other expenses, printing, copying, courier charges, telephone charges, and translations): US$ 55,369.57.
(c)
Respondents’ disbursements (attendance of witnesses to the Hearing, including airfare, accommodation, food, visas, and other incidental expenses): US$ 209,308.62.
(d)
Hearing costs and other related disbursements (court reporter, interpreters, interpretation equipment vendor, post-hearing shipment of documents, and catering): US$ 12,257.49.758
Respondents’ Submissions on Costs, ¶ 11-12.

The Tribunal takes no issues with the costs described under headings (b) to (d) of paragraph 586 which, in the aggregate, amount to US$ 276,935.68. Thus, Claimant and the Additional Parties are ordered to pay Respondents seventy percent (70%) of such amount, which is equivalent to US$ 193,854.98, for these costs.

As for the legal fees indicated under paragraph 586(a) which amount to US$ 1,315,543.04, the Tribunal does not dispute that these fees were effectively incurred by Respondents. However, the Tribunal believes that Respondents’ legal fees appear to be excessive in light of (i) the total amount in dispute and (ii) the legal fees incurred by Claimant and Additional Parties which are substantially lower than Respondents’ legal costs759
Claimant and Additional Parties spent in legal fees the amounts of USD$852,453.38 and COP 181,870,476.29 (Claimant’s Submission on Costs, ¶ 1).. Hence, the Tribunal, using its discretion under Article 37(5) of the Rules, deviates from the rule set out in paragraph 585 for the other costs, and order Claimant and the Additional Parties to pay the amount of US$ 900,000 for legal fees incurred by Respondents.

As for the ICC costs, as noted above, the Tribunal orders that Claimant and the Additional Parties should bear all the ICC costs which were fixed by the Court at its session of July 4, 2018 in the amount of US$ 455,000.00. At the same session, the Court ordered that each party would be reimbursed an amount of US$7,500,00. Taking into account that Respondents ultimately paid the ICC an amount of US$ 227,500.00, Claimant and the Additional Parties are ordered to reimburse Respondents said amount.

In conclusion, the Tribunal grants Respondents an award on costs for US$ 1,093,854.98 which results from awarding (i) US$ 900,000 for legal fees incurred by Respondents, and (ii) US$ 193,854.98 for other costs borne by Respondents during the arbitration. Respondents shall also be entitled to be reimbursed the amount US$ 227,500.00 for payments made to the ICC to cover the ICC’s costs and expenses.

Finally, the Tribunal also notes that Respondents sought interest on these sums according to the maximum interest rate allowed from the date of issuance of the Final Award until the effective day of payment. Respondents have not made any specific arguments as to which rate of interest should apply for an award on costs, and whether such a rate of interest should be determined according to the lex contractus (Colombian law) or the lex arbtitri (New York law). For the reasons set forth in paragraphs 553 to 565 above, the Tribunal has exercised its discretion to decide on the appropriate rate of interest for post-award interest and concludes that the same interest rate of 9% applicable pursuant to New York law should apply here. Accordingly, the Tribunal orders post-award interest on the costs of arbitration awarded in paragraph 590 according to a simple (not compounded) interest rate of 9% to be calculated, on an annual basis, from the date of issuance of the Final Award until full and effective payment.

For the reasons set forth above, the Arbitral Tribunal issues the following DECISIONS:
(a.)
TO DISMISS Superior Energy’s objections to the Tribunal’s jurisdiction and DECLARE that the Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide on all claims including those against Superior Energy.
(b.)
TO DISMISS all of Claimant’s claims.
(c.)
TO DECLARE that Superior Colombia lawfully withheld the Second Holdback Amount.
(d.)
TO DECLARE that Claimant and the Additional Parties have breached Sections 6(a) and 10.17 of the SPA and their duties of care and good faith.
(e.)
TO ACCEPT Superior Colombia’s counterclaim for reduction of the Purchase Price for an amount equivalent to US$ 5,600,000.00. As Superior Colombia has already withheld US$ 1,092,834.67, Claimant and Additional Parties are ORDERED jointly and severally to pay Superior Colombia the amount of US$ 4,507,165.33.
(f.)
TO REJECT Superior Colombia’s counterclaim for other damages.
(g.)
TO ORDER Claimant and the Additional Parties to pay Respondents the amount of US$ 1,093,854.98 for legal fees and other costs incurred in this arbitration.
(h.)
To DECIDE that Claimant and the Additional Parties shall bear all the costs of arbitration fixed by the ICC Court which amount to US$455,000.00. Accordingly, Claimant and the Additional Parties shall reimburse Respondents the sum of US$ 227,500.
(i.)
TO ORDER Claimant and the Additional Parties to pay an annual interest over the sums indicated in paragraphs 592(e.), 592(g.), and 592(h.), at the rate of 9%, calculated on a simple basis, from the date of issuance of this Final Award until the date of full and effective payment.
(j.)
All other prayers for relief which are not expressly granted are hereby DISMISSED.
